# Continuous Circuit Training Does Not Simultaneously Build Strength and Endurance; Interval Circuit Training Is a Better Fit

**What it is** — Research does not support the claim (made by some instructors and machine
manufacturers) that continuous circuit training (CCT) simultaneously develops
cardiovascular endurance and strength. Interval circuit training (ICT: high-intensity
loading with regular rest intervals) is described as more suitable for developing strength
and strength-endurance together. Supporting evidence cited: prolonged low-intensity
endurance training performed alongside strength training in the same phase seriously
compromises strength/power development, partly because fast-twitch fibres can start
behaving like slow-twitch fibres under prolonged low-intensity load; muscle biopsy studies
of distance runners' gastrocnemius after a marathon show necrosis and inflammation
detectable at least 7 days later, an abnormality not seen in comparable biopsies from
weightlifters, sprinters, or rowers after strenuous sessions. (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59.)

**Why it works** — Continuous, moderate-intensity circuit work trains the aerobic/oxidative
system and biases fibre behavior toward slow-twitch characteristics, which is a different
and partly conflicting neuromuscular target from the high-force, high-velocity, largely
fast-twitch demands of strength and power work; ICT's rest intervals let each work bout
stay in a higher-intensity, more strength/power-specific zone instead of drifting toward
an endurance stimulus.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when designing off-season/GPP programming
that needs to develop both conditioning and strength: the text's recommendation is to
prescribe cardiovascular training separately, in limited amounts, early in the off-season,
with higher-intensity resistance training emphasized later, and to use interval-style
(work/rest) circuits rather than continuous circuits when the goal includes
strength-endurance. **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own
conditioning priority stack for football (alactic and aerobic capacity/power first, with
glycolytic conditioning absorbed incidentally rather than programmed as a primary target;
`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34,
39`), though the baseline material does not itself cite this fibre-type mechanism.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is evidence against combining continuous,
prolonged low-intensity work with concurrent strength training in the same block, not an
argument against all conditioning; short, high-intensity interval conditioning is treated
as more compatible with strength/power goals. The gastrocnemius necrosis finding is
specific to marathon-distance running, not necessarily to all forms of aerobic
conditioning used in team-sport contexts.

**Example** — **Inference:** programming continuous, moderate-pace circuit stations as a
"two birds, one stone" strength-and-conditioning solution is not well supported by this
evidence; separating a short conditioning block from resistance training, or using
interval-format circuits with real rest between high-intensity efforts, is the better-
supported approach.

**Related** — [[claim--fiber-recruitment-not-simply-graded-by-force]].

# Muscle Adapts in Days; Tendon, Ligament, and Bone Take Weeks to Months

**What it is** — Muscle tissue adapts to increased loading within several days, whereas
connective tissues (tendon, ligament, joint capsule) and tissue systems with a high
connective-tissue content (bone, cartilage) only show significant adaptation and
hypertrophy after several weeks to months of progressive loading (McDonagh & Davies,
1984). Verkhoshansky states training prescription must account for the different
adaptation rates of all involved systems and avoid overtraining whichever system adapts
slowest; he recommends gradual load increases and avoiding impulsive/explosive methods
particularly during General Physical Preparation (GPP) and for relative novices to
strength training. (PDF p. 46, printed p. 35.)

**Why it works** — Muscle's adaptive machinery (protein synthesis, neural recruitment)
responds faster than the slower turnover and remodeling of collagenous tissue; a program
that progresses load at the muscle's adaptation rate can outpace what tendon, ligament,
and bone can structurally tolerate, which is a well-established mechanism in tendon and
connective-tissue injury research independent of this text.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly supports conservative, gradual load
progression in GPP/early training blocks and for novice athletes specifically, and argues
against introducing high-impulse plyometric or explosive work before a base period of
progressive loading has given connective tissue time to adapt. This is a mechanistic
rationale for why "the athlete feels ready for more" (muscle-level readiness) is not
sufficient justification for a rapid load jump (tendon/bone-level readiness lags behind).

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this passage gives no specific timeline (only
"several days" vs. "several weeks or months") and no athlete-population-specific data; do
not treat it as a precise dosing table. **Inference:** this is a general injury-risk
mechanism, not a substitute for clinical input from Athletic Medicine on a specific
athlete's tissue status or injury history.

**Example** — **Inference:** a novice athlete whose squat strength (muscle-level) is
progressing quickly should still have their loading ramp paced by a longer timeline
(weeks to months) appropriate to tendon and bone adaptation, not by how fast their 1RM is
climbing.

**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

# Classic Energy-System Percentage Tables by Sport (Fox & Mathews, 1974) — Football Listed at ~90% Phosphagen

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky reproduces Fox & Mathews' (1974) classic tables estimating
the percentage contribution of the short-term (phosphagen/ATP-CP), intermediate
(non-oxidative glycolytic), and long-term (oxidative/aerobic) energy systems to different
training modes and sports. American football is listed at 90% short-term, 10%
intermediate, 0% long-term — among the most phosphagen-dominant sports in the table,
comparable to golf (95/5/0) and volleyball (90/10/0), and far more phosphagen-dominant
than field hockey or soccer half-backs (60/20/20). Verkhoshansky himself cautions that
this "highly determinate" scheme, compiled decades earlier, has been questioned, that
figures for some events (he names the 1500m specifically) have since been revised, and
that it should not be used casually because it disguises moment-to-moment metabolic
demand shifts within a single sport. (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81.)

**Why it works** — The table estimates an average, whole-game contribution, whereas actual
play consists of short high-intensity bursts (plays) separated by long rest (huddles,
substitutions), so an average figure can obscure the real repeated-sprint, phosphagen-
dominant-per-play structure while also underweighting the role of aerobic recovery between
bursts.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's stated conditioning priority for
football is alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp and game demands, with
glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" absorbed incidentally rather
than programmed as a primary target (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39`); the baseline also states the aerobic
system's main value for speed-power athletes is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP
between bouts), not distance capacity (citing `2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md
p.9`). **Inference:** this table's 90/10/0 split for football (near-zero credited to the
long-term/aerobic system) looks, at first read, to be in tension with the baseline's
explicit inclusion of aerobic capacity as a Goal-1 priority for football — but the tension
likely resolves once "aerobic system" is understood functionally: the baseline treats
aerobic fitness as enabling faster ATP/phosphagen regeneration between the very
phosphagen-dominant plays this table describes, not as a source of in-play energy. Read
together, not as contradictory: this table describes what fuels a single play; the
baseline describes what determines how well that fuel regenerates for the next one.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky's own caution applies directly here: **Inference**
do not use the 90/10/0 football figure as a precise or current number; it is a decades-old
average estimate for the sport as a whole, not a modern, position-specific or play-by-play
breakdown, and the source text itself flags the whole table's accuracy as needing
re-examination. This entry is rated `contested` because it is presented as a classic,
already-questioned scheme rather than an established modern reference.

**Example** — **Inference:** a single football play (a few seconds of maximal effort)
draws almost entirely on the phosphagen system, consistent with the table; but the
athlete's ability to repeat that near-maximal output play after play, series after series,
depends heavily on aerobic capacity for recovery between plays — the quality the baseline
prioritizes.

**Related** — None in this ingest yet; candidate future link to a conditioning synthesis
note once Phase 4 of the Flint project reaches conditioning and energy systems.

# The Classic "Slow-Fibres-First-by-Force-Magnitude" Recruitment Model Fails for Ballistic Movement

**What it is** — The standard recruitment scheme (slow-twitch fibres recruited first up to
roughly 20% of maximum force, then progressively more fast-twitch fibres as force rises)
holds for graded, progressive loading, but Bosco (1982, cited PDF pp. 74-75, printed pp.
63-64) shows it breaks down for ballistic motion. Walking at moderate speed produces over
700 N of vertical ground reaction force yet, by contact time and movement pattern, relies
almost entirely on slow-twitch action; a maximal, high-velocity knee extension against a
leg-press plate produces less force than walking despite being nearly pure fast-twitch
action. The force-velocity curve itself differs by jump type: squat jumps and isokinetic
testing reflect mainly the muscle's contractile component and follow the traditional
hyperbolic F-V curve, while countermovement (dip) jumps and depth jumps are strongly
shaped by elastic energy released from the Series Elastic Component during the preceding
rapid stretch, producing an entirely different curve shape that does not fit the
traditional model. Sprinting, high jump, and long jump coordinates also fall far from the
traditional F-V curve. Bosco specifically cautions that isokinetic training is not
advisable for athletes in predominantly ballistic sports.

**Why it works** — Force magnitude alone does not determine which fibres are recruited or
how force is produced; movement pattern, contact duration, and whether elastic energy
storage/release is involved (SSC-mediated ballistic actions vs. purely contractile,
non-ballistic actions) change both the recruitment pattern and the resulting force-time and
force-velocity relationships.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] and
[[claim--fiber-recruitment-not-simply-graded-by-force|this entry's]] own caution: SJ, CMJ,
and depth-jump testing are not interchangeable measures of the same underlying quality,
because they load the contractile component and the SEC to very different degrees. Also
reinforces caution about isokinetic testing/training for ballistic-sport athletes already
raised in [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` rather than `supported` because it
directly overturns a simpler, still widely-taught recruitment model (force-graded,
slow-then-fast) using a small number of illustrative examples (walking, car-pushing,
seated knee extension) rather than a systematic dataset; **Inference:** treat the classic
graded model as a reasonable first approximation for slow, controlled movement, and this
critique as the more accurate account specifically for ballistic/SSC-involved movement.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach should not assume a squat-jump-based force
measurement predicts depth-jump or sprint ground-reaction performance; the elastic
contribution present in the latter two is largely absent from the former.

**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].
######## claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence.md
---
type: library-entry

# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops

**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), Verkhoshansky states biochemical adaptation to
training follows a definite sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first, oxidative ATP
resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle protein (myosin)
and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase; only after that
does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining or detraining, these
adaptations are lost in the reverse order they were gained. The longer the training period,
the more thorough the adaptation and the longer those biochemical changes persist after
training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels). This gain/loss asymmetry across
different systems is termed heterochronic (different tissues and processes change on
different timelines). Overtraining specifically shows a distinct pattern: reduced
glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/glycogen, blood plasma
dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to disrupted acid-base
balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)

**Why it works** — Different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity, structural protein
synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular mechanisms with
different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts, then de-adapts"
model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while others are gained
late and lost early.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** this converges directionally with
Platonov's heterochronic principle (different systems have different adaptation/de-
adaptation timelines) but the two are not a stated one-to-one match — the baseline's
build-easy/lose-fast claim is about energy-system categories (aerobic vs. alactic), while
Platonov's sequence is about biochemical sub-processes within training generally (oxidative
capacity, structural protein, glycolysis, CP). Treat them as parallel instances of the same
underlying heterochronicity concept, not as the same specific claim restated.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
four-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use
it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than
a specific testing checklist.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete returning from a multi-week layoff might show
CP-system/power qualities holding up relatively better than the earlier-gained oxidative
and glycogen-storage qualities, or vice versa, depending on the specific loss sequence;
either way, "detraining" is not a single uniform decline and re-testing across qualities
(not just one) gives a more accurate readiness picture.

**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].
######## claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths.md

type: library-entry

# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept

**What it is** — Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
older term "anaerobic threshold" has similarly been replaced by "blood lactate threshold"
or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation) since lactate does not require an absence of
oxygen to form. (PDF pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)

**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise

16	
17	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (via Siff) argues "adaptive reconstruction" is a more
18	accurate term than "supercompensation" for the body's response to training load, for two
19	specific reasons stated in the text: (1) enhanced performance is not simply the result of
20	increased stores of bioenergetic substances (the energy-overshoot picture supercompensation
21	implies), but also of structural changes in muscle and connective tissue and enhanced
22	efficiency of bioenergetic and neuromuscular processing; (2) no supercompensation has been
23	observed for any bioenergetic substance except glycogen — other biochemicals deplete under
24	strenuous exercise but do not overshoot their baseline afterward, and each returns to
25	baseline on its own timeline, making the timing of a "supercompensation window" for
26	non-glycogen substances indeterminate. Russian sources use "Current Adaptation Reserves"
27	(CAR) for the readily-available (superficial) and emergency (deep) energy sources drawn on

34	pattern is essentially unique to glycogen undercuts that precision and supports treating
35	"the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general heuristic, not a substance-by-
36	substance timing rule.

131	# Collagenous Tissue's Four-Region Loading Curve, and Why Loading Rate Changes What Fails First
132	
133	**What it is** — Collagenous tissue (e.g. the ACL, studied by Frankel & Nordin 1980)
134	loaded to failure shows four regions: Region I, the "toe region," where the crimped
135	tissue straightens with little force and mild stretching here produces no long-term
136	flexibility change; Region II, a near-linear region where fibres are fully uncrimped and
137	parallel; Region III, where sequential microfailure of overstretched fibres begins; Region
138	IV, complete failure. Loading rate changes the outcome: increasing loading rate roughly
139	fourfold raised knee ligament failure load by almost 50% (Kennedy et al., 1976), and which
140	structure fails first flips with rate — at slow loading rates the ligament's bony
141	insertion is the weakest link, while at fast loading rates the ligament itself is the
142	weakest link (bone's strength rises faster with rate than the ligament's). Healthy tendon's
143	tensile strength can be more than twice that of its associated muscle, which is why
144	ruptures are more common in muscle than tendon. (PDF pp. 54-56, printed pp. 43-45.)
145	
146	**Why it works** — Collagen is viscoelastic: it behaves more elastically under rapid
147	loading and more plastically (creeping, deforming) under slow, sustained loading, so both
148	the loading speed and the tissue's own rate-dependent stiffness change determine where in
149	the body an excessive load actually causes failure.
150	
151	**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant background for understanding why static
152	stretching held gently (Region I) does not meaningfully change tissue length or
153	flexibility over time, and why ballistic or rapid loading, once past Region II, carries
154	real microfailure risk; also relevant context for why the pattern of injury (bone
155	avulsion vs. mid-ligament tear vs. muscle strain) can differ by the speed of the loading
156	event, which matters for how Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance jointly interpret
157	an injury mechanism.
158	
159	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is basic tissue mechanics from cited
160	1970s-1980s cadaveric/animal ligament research (ACL specifically), not a live-tissue,
161	in-vivo human athlete dataset; do not use the specific numbers (50% failure-load increase,
162	the fourfold rate figure) as applicable outside the original ACL loading-rate study cited.
163	This is background science, not a clinical decision rule, and should not substitute for
164	Athletic Medicine's own injury assessment framework.
165	
166	**Example** — **Inference:** a sudden high-rate valgus load to the knee is more likely to
167	produce mid-ligament ACL failure, while a slower, sustained load is more likely to fail at
168	the bony insertion first; this pattern helps explain, but does not replace, imaging and
169	clinical exam in determining actual injury location.
170	
171	**Related** — [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
172	[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

187	# Continuous Circuit Training Does Not Simultaneously Build Strength and Endurance; Interval Circuit Training Is a Better Fit
188	
189	**What it is** — Research does not support the claim (made by some instructors and machine
190	manufacturers) that continuous circuit training (CCT) simultaneously develops
191	cardiovascular endurance and strength. Interval circuit training (ICT: high-intensity
192	loading with regular rest intervals) is described as more suitable for developing strength
193	and strength-endurance together. Supporting evidence cited: prolonged low-intensity
194	endurance training performed alongside strength training in the same phase seriously
195	compromises strength/power development, partly because fast-twitch fibres can start
196	behaving like slow-twitch fibres under prolonged low-intensity load; muscle biopsy studies
197	of distance runners' gastrocnemius after a marathon show necrosis and inflammation
198	detectable at least 7 days later, an abnormality not seen in comparable biopsies from
199	weightlifters, sprinters, or rowers after strenuous sessions. (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59.)
200	
201	**Why it works** — Continuous, moderate-intensity circuit work trains the aerobic/oxidative
202	system and biases fibre behavior toward slow-twitch characteristics, which is a different
203	and partly conflicting neuromuscular target from the high-force, high-velocity, largely
204	fast-twitch demands of strength and power work; ICT's rest intervals let each work bout
205	stay in a higher-intensity, more strength/power-specific zone instead of drifting toward
206	an endurance stimulus.
207	
208	**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when designing off-season/GPP programming
209	that needs to develop both conditioning and strength: the text's recommendation is to
210	prescribe cardiovascular training separately, in limited amounts, early in the off-season,
211	with higher-intensity resistance training emphasized later, and to use interval-style
212	(work/rest) circuits rather than continuous circuits when the goal includes
213	strength-endurance. **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own
214	conditioning priority stack for football (alactic and aerobic capacity/power first, with
215	glycolytic conditioning absorbed incidentally rather than programmed as a primary target;
216	`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34,
217	39`), though the baseline material does not itself cite this fibre-type mechanism.
218	
219	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is evidence against combining continuous,
220	prolonged low-intensity work with concurrent strength training in the same block, not an
221	argument against all conditioning; short, high-intensity interval conditioning is treated
222	as more compatible with strength/power goals. The gastrocnemius necrosis finding is
223	specific to marathon-distance running, not necessarily to all forms of aerobic
224	conditioning used in team-sport contexts.
225	
226	**Example** — **Inference:** programming continuous, moderate-pace circuit stations as a
227	"two birds, one stone" strength-and-conditioning solution is not well supported by this
228	evidence; separating a short conditioning block from resistance training, or using
229	interval-format circuits with real rest between high-intensity efforts, is the better-
230	supported approach.
231

247	# Muscle Adapts in Days; Tendon, Ligament, and Bone Take Weeks to Months
248	
249	**What it is** — Muscle tissue adapts to increased loading within several days, whereas
250	connective tissues (tendon, ligament, joint capsule) and tissue systems with a high
251	connective-tissue content (bone, cartilage) only show significant adaptation and
252	hypertrophy after several weeks to months of progressive loading (McDonagh & Davies,
253	1984). Verkhoshansky states training prescription must account for the different
254	adaptation rates of all involved systems and avoid overtraining whichever system adapts
255	slowest; he recommends gradual load increases and avoiding impulsive/explosive methods
256	particularly during General Physical Preparation (GPP) and for relative novices to
257	strength training. (PDF p. 46, printed p. 35.)
258	
259	**Why it works** — Muscle's adaptive machinery (protein synthesis, neural recruitment)
260	responds faster than the slower turnover and remodeling of collagenous tissue; a program
261	that progresses load at the muscle's adaptation rate can outpace what tendon, ligament,
262	and bone can structurally tolerate, which is a well-established mechanism in tendon and
263	connective-tissue injury research independent of this text.
264	
265	**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly supports conservative, gradual load
266	progression in GPP/early training blocks and for novice athletes specifically, and argues
267	against introducing high-impulse plyometric or explosive work before a base period of
268	progressive loading has given connective tissue time to adapt. This is a mechanistic
269	rationale for why "the athlete feels ready for more" (muscle-level readiness) is not
270	sufficient justification for a rapid load jump (tendon/bone-level readiness lags behind).
271	
272	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this passage gives no specific timeline (only
273	"several days" vs. "several weeks or months") and no athlete-population-specific data; do
274	not treat it as a precise dosing table. **Inference:** this is a general injury-risk
275	mechanism, not a substitute for clinical input from Athletic Medicine on a specific
276	athlete's tissue status or injury history.
277	
278	**Example** — **Inference:** a novice athlete whose squat strength (muscle-level) is
279	progressing quickly should still have their loading ramp paced by a longer timeline
280	(weeks to months) appropriate to tendon and bone adaptation, not by how fast their 1RM is
281	climbing.
282

298	# Classic Energy-System Percentage Tables by Sport (Fox & Mathews, 1974) — Football Listed at ~90% Phosphagen
299	
300	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky reproduces Fox & Mathews' (1974) classic tables estimating
301	the percentage contribution of the short-term (phosphagen/ATP-CP), intermediate
302	(non-oxidative glycolytic), and long-term (oxidative/aerobic) energy systems to different
303	training modes and sports. American football is listed at 90% short-term, 10%
304	intermediate, 0% long-term — among the most phosphagen-dominant sports in the table,
305	comparable to golf (95/5/0) and volleyball (90/10/0), and far more phosphagen-dominant
306	than field hockey or soccer half-backs (60/20/20). Verkhoshansky himself cautions that
307	this "highly determinate" scheme, compiled decades earlier, has been questioned, that
308	figures for some events (he names the 1500m specifically) have since been revised, and
309	that it should not be used casually because it disguises moment-to-moment metabolic
310	demand shifts within a single sport. (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81.)
311	
312	**Why it works** — The table estimates an average, whole-game contribution, whereas actual
313	play consists of short high-intensity bursts (plays) separated by long rest (huddles,
314	substitutions), so an average figure can obscure the real repeated-sprint, phosphagen-
315	dominant-per-play structure while also underweighting the role of aerobic recovery between
316	bursts.

319	football is alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp and game demands, with

328	likely resolves once "aerobic system" is understood functionally: the baseline treats
329	aerobic fitness as enabling faster ATP/phosphagen regeneration between the very

363	# The Classic "Slow-Fibres-First-by-Force-Magnitude" Recruitment Model Fails for Ballistic Movement
364	
365	**What it is** — The standard recruitment scheme (slow-twitch fibres recruited first up to
366	roughly 20% of maximum force, then progressively more fast-twitch fibres as force rises)
367	holds for graded, progressive loading, but Bosco (1982, cited PDF pp. 74-75, printed pp.
368	63-64) shows it breaks down for ballistic motion. Walking at moderate speed produces over
369	700 N of vertical ground reaction force yet, by contact time and movement pattern, relies
370	almost entirely on slow-twitch action; a maximal, high-velocity knee extension against a
371	leg-press plate produces less force than walking despite being nearly pure fast-twitch
372	action. The force-velocity curve itself differs by jump type: squat jumps and isokinetic
373	testing reflect mainly the muscle's contractile component and follow the traditional
374	hyperbolic F-V curve, while countermovement (dip) jumps and depth jumps are strongly
375	shaped by elastic energy released from the Series Elastic Component during the preceding
376	rapid stretch, producing an entirely different curve shape that does not fit the
377	traditional model. Sprinting, high jump, and long jump coordinates also fall far from the
378	traditional F-V curve. Bosco specifically cautions that isokinetic training is not
379	advisable for athletes in predominantly ballistic sports.
380	
381	**Why it works** — Force magnitude alone does not determine which fibres are recruited or
382	how force is produced; movement pattern, contact duration, and whether elastic energy
383	storage/release is involved (SSC-mediated ballistic actions vs. purely contractile,
384	non-ballistic actions) change both the recruitment pattern and the resulting force-time and
385	force-velocity relationships.
386	
387	**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces
388	[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] and
389	[[claim--fiber-recruitment-not-simply-graded-by-force|this entry's]] own caution: SJ, CMJ,
390	and depth-jump testing are not interchangeable measures of the same underlying quality,
391	because they load the contractile component and the SEC to very different degrees. Also
392	reinforces caution about isokinetic testing/training for ballistic-sport athletes already
393	raised in [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]].
394	
395	**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` rather than `supported` because it
396	directly overturns a simpler, still widely-taught recruitment model (force-graded,
397	slow-then-fast) using a small number of illustrative examples (walking, car-pushing,
398	seated knee extension) rather than a systematic dataset; **Inference:** treat the classic
399	graded model as a reasonable first approximation for slow, controlled movement, and this
400	critique as the more accurate account specifically for ballistic/SSC-involved movement.
401	
402	**Example** — **Inference:** a coach should not assume a squat-jump-based force
403	measurement predicts depth-jump or sprint ground-reaction performance; the elastic
404	contribution present in the latter two is largely absent from the former.
405	
406	**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]],
407	[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

421	
422	# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops
423	
424	**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), Verkhoshansky states biochemical adaptation to
425	training follows a definite sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first, oxidative ATP
426	resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle protein (myosin)
427	and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase; only after that
428	does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining or detraining, these
429	adaptations are lost in the reverse order they were gained. The longer the training period,
430	the more thorough the adaptation and the longer those biochemical changes persist after
431	training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels). This gain/loss asymmetry across
432	different systems is termed heterochronic (different tissues and processes change on
433	different timelines). Overtraining specifically shows a distinct pattern: reduced
434	glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/glycogen, blood plasma
435	dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to disrupted acid-base
436	balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)
437	
438	**Why it works** — Different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity, structural protein
439	synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular mechanisms with
440	different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts, then de-adapts"
441	model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while others are gained
442	late and lost early.
443	
444	**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
445	that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
446	hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
447	often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
448	systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** this converges directionally with
449	Platonov's heterochronic principle (different systems have different adaptation/de-
450	adaptation timelines) but the two are not a stated one-to-one match — the baseline's
451	build-easy/lose-fast claim is about energy-system categories (aerobic vs. alactic), while
452	Platonov's sequence is about biochemical sub-processes within training generally (oxidative
453	capacity, structural protein, glycolysis, CP). Treat them as parallel instances of the same
454	underlying heterochronicity concept, not as the same specific claim restated.
455	
456	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
457	structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
458	without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
459	four-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use
460	it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than
461	a specific testing checklist.
462	
463	**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete returning from a multi-week layoff might show
464	CP-system/power qualities holding up relatively better than the earlier-gained oxidative
465	and glycogen-storage qualities, or vice versa, depending on the specific loss sequence;
466	either way, "detraining" is not a single uniform decline and re-testing across qualities
467	(not just one) gives a more accurate readiness picture.
468

483	
484	# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept
485	
486	**What it is** — Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
487	to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
488	acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
489	the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
490	strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
491	peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
492	below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
493	cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
494	(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
495	anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
496	recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
497	circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
498	older term "anaerobic threshold" has similarly been replaced by "blood lactate threshold"
499	or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation) since lactate does not require an absence of
500	oxygen to form. (PDF pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)
501	
502	**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
503	physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
504	product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
505	rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
506	dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).
507	
508	**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
509	classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
510	next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
511	framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.
512	
513	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
514	irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
515	marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
516	"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
517	corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.
518	
519	**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
520	more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
521	would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
522	"flushing out lactic acid."
523	
524	**Related** — [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].

597	# A Minimum Load Threshold Drives Strength Gains, and It Rises as the Athlete Adapts
598	
599	**What it is** — Hettinger & Muller (1953) are cited for a threshold training stimulus of
600	roughly one-third of maximal strength needed to produce a strength increase in an average
601	person; as strength rises, the required stimulus intensity rises too, eventually reaching
602	80-95% of the athlete's maximum, sometimes matching or exceeding actual competition
603	intensity (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Each stimulus level has its own "strengthening
604	threshold," a ceiling beyond which no further gain occurs at that intensity, and this
605	ceiling is described as further from the untrained state the less trained the athlete is.
606	Separately, Korobkov, Gerasimov & Vasiliev (via Verkhoshansky, 1977) are cited for the
607	finding that in the initial stages of training, strength increases roughly uniformly
608	regardless of load, with approximately equivalent gains reported at 20%, 40%, 60% and 80%
609	of 1RM; raising training intensity early (heavier load, faster tempo, less rest) does not
610	reliably improve on this until strength has already progressed some way. (PDF pp. 33-34,
611	printed pp. 22-23.)
612	
613	**Why it works** — Early neuromuscular adaptation (see
614	[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]) responds to almost
615	any sufficiently repeated stimulus above a low floor; once that easy adaptive window
616	closes, further progress requires a stimulus that approaches the athlete's current
617	ceiling, because there is less slack left in recruitment and coordination to exploit.
618	
619	**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports keeping early-phase (novice) load prescription
620	simple and consistency-focused rather than chasing high intensities, and supports
621	progressively raising relative intensity toward 80-95% of max as an athlete's training age
622	increases, consistent with this book's own training-age-scaling heuristic
623	([[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]]).
624	
625	**When NOT to apply** — These are single-source, decades-old figures cited without a
626	stated sample or modern replication in this text (Hettinger 1961; Korobkov, Gerasimov &
627	Vasiliev via Verkhoshansky 1977; PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 22-23). **Inference:** do not
628	treat "one-third of max" or the specific 20/40/60/80% equivalence as precise, universal
629	cutoffs for a current athlete population; use them as a directional argument for why novice
630	programming can be simple, not as exact percentages to program from.
631	
632	**Example** — **Inference:** A true beginner's program built around consistent submaximal loading (e.g.
633	50-60% 1RM) can produce comparable early strength gains to a heavier protocol, so there is
634	little value in front-loading high intensity before the athlete has trained long enough to
635	need it.
636	
637	**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]].
638	######## claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer.md
639	---
640	type: library-entry
641	kind: claim
642	domain: strength-and-conditioning
643	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
644	chapter: "1.4"
645	topic: velocity and contraction-mode specificity
646	category: [specificity, velocity, exercise-selection]
647	confidence: supported
648	ingest-tier: full-text
649	created: 2026-09-26
650	---
651	
652	# High-Velocity Training Transfers to Low Velocity Better Than the Reverse; Contraction Modes Barely Cross Over
653	
654	**What it is** — Two specific, cited findings under the specificity umbrella: (1)
655	low-velocity isokinetic training improves low-velocity strength but has minimal effect on
656	high-velocity strength; high-velocity isokinetic training improves high-velocity strength
657	and transfers somewhat better to low-velocity strength than the reverse direction
658	(Moffroid & Whipple 1970; Perrine & Edgerton 1981; Kanehisa & Miyashita 1983b). (2)
659	Contraction-mode adaptations are narrow: concentric-eccentric (weightlifting-style)
660	training raises competitive strength but produces only small isometric or concentric
661	isokinetic gains; isometric training raises isometric strength but not concentric
662	isokinetic strength; elbow-extension training with weights increases triceps strength and
663	girth without a matching isokinetic-strength change. Static and dynamic training even
664	produce different microscopic structural changes in the muscle. (PDF pp. 38-40, printed
665	pp. 27-29.)
666	
667	**Why it works** — Force-velocity curve position (see
668	[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]) and contraction-mode
669	recruitment patterns are trained narrowly because different neural drive strategies and
670	structural adaptations underlie each; high-velocity training likely also recruits fast-
671	twitch units that contribute somewhat at slower speeds, which is the proposed reason the
672	transfer is asymmetric rather than symmetric.
673	
674	**When to apply** — **Inference:** when selecting exercise velocity and contraction mode,
675	match both to the sport action being targeted, and consider biasing toward higher-velocity
676	work when in doubt, since the text's cited data shows it transfers in both directions
677	somewhat, whereas slow, heavy work transfers poorly to fast actions. **Eric's baseline:**
678	the isometric seated calf raise and other isometric testing are run on the ForceDecks
679	"Mid-Thigh Pull" setting as part of the department's standard protocol
680	(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
681	`protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`). **Inference:**
682	this claim's contraction-mode specificity finding supports treating isometric testing as
683	its own distinct quality rather than a proxy for dynamic 1RM strength; neither source states
684	this connection directly.
685	
686	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** these are 1970s-1980s isokinetic-dynamometer
687	studies (PDF pp. 38-40, printed pp. 27-29); isokinetic machine training is a narrow,
688	lab-style modality rarely used in current collegiate S&C practice, and this specific
689	transfer asymmetry has not been independently re-verified here for free-weight or
690	plyometric training modes. **Inference:** do not assume the same asymmetric-transfer ratio
691	applies to, say, barbell velocity-based training without separate evidence; this extension
692	is not addressed in the text.
693	
694	**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete tested for isometric mid-thigh pull strength should not be assumed
695	to have an equivalent dynamic 1RM or sprint force capability; each needs its own
696	assessment and, if targeted, its own specific training exposure.
697	
698	**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]].
699	######## claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes.md
700	---
701	type: library-entry
702	kind: claim
703	domain: strength-and-conditioning
704	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
705	chapter: "1"
706	topic: voluntary strength reserve size
707	category: [strength, testing, neural]
708	confidence: supported
709	ingest-tier: full-text
710	created: 2026-09-26
711	---
712	
713	# The Voluntary-Involuntary Strength Reserve Has a Measured Size
714	
715	**What it is** — Two cited figures quantify how much force voluntary effort leaves
716	unused relative to the athlete's true ceiling. (1) In experienced weightlifters, the mean
717	gap between training maximum (TFmax) and competitive maximum (CFmax) is about 12.5 ± 2.5%,
718	larger in heavier weight classes (Zatsiorsky, 1995; PDF p. 13, printed p. 2). (2) Under
719	involuntary or hypnotic conditions, strength output can rise by up to 35% in untrained
720	people, but by less than 10% in trained athletes (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2, no primary
721	citation given in text for this figure).
722	
723	**Why it works** — Both numbers describe the same phenomenon from different angles: a
724	protective neural inhibition normally holds voluntary output below the muscle's true
725	contractile ceiling, and anything that reduces that inhibition (competitive arousal,
726	hypnosis, involuntary reflex recruitment) exposes more of it. Training narrows the
727	untapped reserve because part of the strength-training adaptation is learning to
728	recruit and inhibit less, not just growing tissue.
729	
730	**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is best used as a coaching narrative for why
731	max-effort numbers move around by context (weigh-in day nerves, meet atmosphere, testing
732	environment), and as a rough expectation that a smaller gap between training and
733	competitive/testing efforts is itself a marker of higher training status. Neither the
734	book nor Eric's baseline states this as an applied rule; it is this entry's own synthesis
735	of the two cited numbers.
736	
737	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky gives no primary citation for the hypnosis figure
738	(PDF p. 13, printed p. 2); treat it as a single, unverified secondary claim, not a number
739	to plan around. The 12.5 ± 2.5% figure is stated specifically for experienced Olympic
740	weightlifters under meet conditions (Zatsiorsky, 1995; PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
741	**Inference:** it should not be assumed to transfer directly to Baylor's team-sport
742	athletes tested on a force plate (ForceDecks CMJ/IMTP) rather than in a weightlifting
743	competition, and neither number should be used as a correction factor applied to that data
744	without independent verification; this caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in
745	`method-baseline.md`.
746	
747	**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete who tests near-identically on a submaximal VBT-estimated 1RM and
748	a rare true max attempt is showing a small reserve gap; a large, inconsistent gap between
749	estimated and tested max may point to arousal/readiness on test day rather than a change
750	in underlying capacity.
751	
752	**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]].

######## claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation.md
---

# "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (via Siff) argues "adaptive reconstruction" is a more
accurate term than "supercompensation" for the body's response to training load, for two
specific reasons stated in the text: (1) enhanced performance is not simply the result of
increased stores of bioenergetic substances (the energy-overshoot picture supercompensation
implies), but also of structural changes in muscle and connective tissue and enhanced
efficiency of bioenergetic and neuromuscular processing; (2) no supercompensation has been
observed for any bioenergetic substance except glycogen — other biochemicals deplete under
strenuous exercise but do not overshoot their baseline afterward, and each returns to
baseline on its own timeline, making the timing of a "supercompensation window" for
non-glycogen substances indeterminate. Russian sources use "Current Adaptation Reserves"
(CAR) for the readily-available (superficial) and emergency (deep) energy sources drawn on
during Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome resistance phase. (PDF pp. 94-96, printed pp.
83-85.)

**Why it works** — If supercompensation literally meant every adaptation-relevant substance
or structure overshoots baseline on a predictable clock, timing the next training stimulus
to "catch the peak" would be a precise science; the empirical finding that this overshoot
pattern is essentially unique to glycogen undercuts that precision and supports treating
"the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general heuristic, not a substance-by-
substance timing rule.

**When to apply** — This library already carries the supercompensation model in
[[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], which itself notes
"contemporary sport science largely prefers the fitness-fatigue (two-factor) model over
literal supercompensation" and recommends treating supercompensation "as a useful mental
model, not a measured prescription." **Inference:** this entry adds the specific mechanism
for that caution (structural/efficiency changes beyond energy stores, and the
glycogen-only overshoot finding) and the CAR terminology, which the Bompa entry does not
include; use both together rather than duplicating either.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` because it is itself a critique of
a still widely-taught model (supercompensation), argued from a mix of established fact
(structural adaptation beyond energy stores) and an absence-of-evidence claim (no
overshoot observed for other biochemicals) that could be revised by newer measurement
techniques. **Inference:** don't treat "adaptive reconstruction" as a rejection of
periodization practice built on supercompensation timing; the text itself notes
supercompensation theory, despite its shortcomings, had a profound and still-useful impact
on periodization design.

**Example** — **Inference:** glycogen loading before an endurance event is a legitimate
application of true supercompensation; assuming a similarly precise "peak window" exists
for, say, connective tissue remodeling or neuromuscular efficiency gains is not supported
by the same evidence.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (reciprocal link
recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.16 sharpens the "useful mental model, not a
measured prescription" caution with the specific glycogen-only-overshoot finding and the
CAR/adaptive-reconstruction terminology).
######## claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.4"
topic: bilateral deficit
category: [specificity, testing, exercise-selection]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26

# The Bilateral Deficit: Two Limbs Together Produce Less Force Than the Sum of Each Alone

**What it is** — Force produced during a bilateral (two-limb, e.g. barbell) contraction is
usually less than the sum of the forces each limb produces individually (e.g. dumbbells),
a phenomenon called the bilateral deficit, accompanied by reduced integrated EMG
suggesting the prime movers are less activated bilaterally (Coyle et al. 1981;
Vandervoort et al. 1984). The deficit is reported as insignificant in athletes who always
use their limbs simultaneously in their sport (e.g. weightlifters), and the text
recommends athletes whose sport involves bilateral action of the same muscle groups train
bilaterally to minimize the deficit (Secher, 1975). (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28.)

**Why it works** — The deficit is attributed to a neural, not mechanical, limitation:
reduced activation of the prime movers during simultaneous bilateral effort, which
training the specific bilateral pattern appears to reduce over time — another instance of
narrow, mode-specific neuromuscular adaptation.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** when deciding whether to prioritize bilateral (back
squat, bench, clean) or unilateral (split squat, single-leg press, lunge) exercise
variants, match the training mode to how the sport actually loads the limbs. For sports
with genuinely unilateral force production (sprinting, most cutting and
change-of-direction actions), this text's finding argues for meaningful unilateral training
exposure, not exclusively bilateral lifts, since bilateral-only training may under-develop
the single-limb activation football and track actions require. This football-specific
application is this entry's own extension, not stated in the text.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not use this to argue against bilateral lifts
altogether; compound bilateral lifts remain valuable for maximal strength and are
appropriate where the sport itself uses bilateral effort (e.g. some blocking or lifting
actions). Verkhoshansky gives no specific deficit magnitude for team-sport athletes in
this section (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28); **Inference:** the deficit's size and
trainability likely vary by athlete and lift, which is this entry's own caution.

**Example** — **Inference:** A sprinter's single-leg force production during ground contact is not fully
predicted by their bilateral back squat strength alone; programming that includes
single-leg strength work targets the bilateral deficit gap directly relevant to sprint and
change-of-direction performance.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]].
######## claim--collagen-loading-curve-and-injury-risk.md
---
type: library-entry

domain: strength-and-conditioning

category: [injury-risk, connective-tissue, flexibility]
confidence: supported
