# Collagenous Tissue's Four-Region Loading Curve, and Why Loading Rate Changes What Fails First

**What it is** — Collagenous tissue (e.g. the ACL, studied by Frankel & Nordin 1980)
loaded to failure shows four regions: Region I, the "toe region," where the crimped
tissue straightens with little force and mild stretching here produces no long-term
flexibility change; Region II, a near-linear region where fibres are fully uncrimped and
parallel; Region III, where sequential microfailure of overstretched fibres begins; Region
IV, complete failure. Loading rate changes the outcome: increasing loading rate roughly
fourfold raised knee ligament failure load by almost 50% (Kennedy et al., 1976), and which
structure fails first flips with rate — at slow loading rates the ligament's bony
insertion is the weakest link, while at fast loading rates the ligament itself is the
weakest link (bone's strength rises faster with rate than the ligament's). Healthy tendon's
tensile strength can be more than twice that of its associated muscle, which is why
ruptures are more common in muscle than tendon. (PDF pp. 54-56, printed pp. 43-45.)

**Why it works** — Collagen is viscoelastic: it behaves more elastically under rapid
loading and more plastically (creeping, deforming) under slow, sustained loading, so both
the loading speed and the tissue's own rate-dependent stiffness change determine where in
the body an excessive load actually causes failure.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant background for understanding why static
stretching held gently (Region I) does not meaningfully change tissue length or
flexibility over time, and why ballistic or rapid loading, once past Region II, carries
real microfailure risk; also relevant context for why the pattern of injury (bone
avulsion vs. mid-ligament tear vs. muscle strain) can differ by the speed of the loading
event, which matters for how Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance jointly interpret
an injury mechanism.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is basic tissue mechanics from cited
1970s-1980s cadaveric/animal ligament research (ACL specifically), not a live-tissue,
in-vivo human athlete dataset; do not use the specific numbers (50% failure-load increase,
the fourfold rate figure) as applicable outside the original ACL loading-rate study cited.
This is background science, not a clinical decision rule, and should not substitute for
Athletic Medicine's own injury assessment framework.

**Example** — **Inference:** a sudden high-rate valgus load to the knee is more likely to
produce mid-ligament ACL failure, while a slower, sustained load is more likely to fail at
the bony insertion first; this pattern helps explain, but does not replace, imaging and
clinical exam in determining actual injury location.

**Related** — [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].
######## claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.12"
topic: concurrent strength and endurance training
category: [concurrent-training, programming, fiber-type]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Continuous Circuit Training Does Not Simultaneously Build Strength and Endurance; Interval Circuit Training Is a Better Fit

**What it is** — Research does not support the claim (made by some instructors and machine
manufacturers) that continuous circuit training (CCT) simultaneously develops
cardiovascular endurance and strength. Interval circuit training (ICT: high-intensity
loading with regular rest intervals) is described as more suitable for developing strength
and strength-endurance together. Supporting evidence cited: prolonged low-intensity
endurance training performed alongside strength training in the same phase seriously
compromises strength/power development, partly because fast-twitch fibres can start
behaving like slow-twitch fibres under prolonged low-intensity load; muscle biopsy studies
of distance runners' gastrocnemius after a marathon show necrosis and inflammation
detectable at least 7 days later, an abnormality not seen in comparable biopsies from
weightlifters, sprinters, or rowers after strenuous sessions. (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59.)

**Why it works** — Continuous, moderate-intensity circuit work trains the aerobic/oxidative
system and biases fibre behavior toward slow-twitch characteristics, which is a different
and partly conflicting neuromuscular target from the high-force, high-velocity, largely
fast-twitch demands of strength and power work; ICT's rest intervals let each work bout
stay in a higher-intensity, more strength/power-specific zone instead of drifting toward
an endurance stimulus.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when designing off-season/GPP programming
that needs to develop both conditioning and strength: the text's recommendation is to
prescribe cardiovascular training separately, in limited amounts, early in the off-season,
with higher-intensity resistance training emphasized later, and to use interval-style
(work/rest) circuits rather than continuous circuits when the goal includes
strength-endurance. **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own
conditioning priority stack for football (alactic and aerobic capacity/power first, with
glycolytic conditioning absorbed incidentally rather than programmed as a primary target;
`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34,
39`), though the baseline material does not itself cite this fibre-type mechanism.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is evidence against combining continuous,
prolonged low-intensity work with concurrent strength training in the same block, not an
argument against all conditioning; short, high-intensity interval conditioning is treated
as more compatible with strength/power goals. The gastrocnemius necrosis finding is
specific to marathon-distance running, not necessarily to all forms of aerobic
conditioning used in team-sport contexts.

**Example** — **Inference:** programming continuous, moderate-pace circuit stations as a
"two birds, one stone" strength-and-conditioning solution is not well supported by this
evidence; separating a short conditioning block from resistance training, or using
interval-format circuits with real rest between high-intensity efforts, is the better-
supported approach.

**Related** — [[claim--fiber-recruitment-not-simply-graded-by-force]].
######## claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.6"
topic: tissue adaptation timelines
category: [injury-risk, connective-tissue, programming]
confidence: proven
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Muscle Adapts in Days; Tendon, Ligament, and Bone Take Weeks to Months

**What it is** — Muscle tissue adapts to increased loading within several days, whereas
connective tissues (tendon, ligament, joint capsule) and tissue systems with a high
connective-tissue content (bone, cartilage) only show significant adaptation and
hypertrophy after several weeks to months of progressive loading (McDonagh & Davies,
1984). Verkhoshansky states training prescription must account for the different
adaptation rates of all involved systems and avoid overtraining whichever system adapts
slowest; he recommends gradual load increases and avoiding impulsive/explosive methods
particularly during General Physical Preparation (GPP) and for relative novices to
strength training. (PDF p. 46, printed p. 35.)

**Why it works** — Muscle's adaptive machinery (protein synthesis, neural recruitment)
responds faster than the slower turnover and remodeling of collagenous tissue; a program
that progresses load at the muscle's adaptation rate can outpace what tendon, ligament,
and bone can structurally tolerate, which is a well-established mechanism in tendon and
connective-tissue injury research independent of this text.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly supports conservative, gradual load
progression in GPP/early training blocks and for novice athletes specifically, and argues
against introducing high-impulse plyometric or explosive work before a base period of
progressive loading has given connective tissue time to adapt. This is a mechanistic
rationale for why "the athlete feels ready for more" (muscle-level readiness) is not
sufficient justification for a rapid load jump (tendon/bone-level readiness lags behind).

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this passage gives no specific timeline (only
"several days" vs. "several weeks or months") and no athlete-population-specific data; do
not treat it as a precise dosing table. **Inference:** this is a general injury-risk
mechanism, not a substitute for clinical input from Athletic Medicine on a specific
athlete's tissue status or injury history.

**Example** — **Inference:** a novice athlete whose squat strength (muscle-level) is
progressing quickly should still have their loading ramp paced by a longer timeline
(weeks to months) appropriate to tendon and bone adaptation, not by how fast their 1RM is
climbing.

**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].
######## claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.15"
topic: energy system contribution by sport
category: [energy-systems, conditioning, football]
confidence: contested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Classic Energy-System Percentage Tables by Sport (Fox & Mathews, 1974) — Football Listed at ~90% Phosphagen

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky reproduces Fox & Mathews' (1974) classic tables estimating
the percentage contribution of the short-term (phosphagen/ATP-CP), intermediate
(non-oxidative glycolytic), and long-term (oxidative/aerobic) energy systems to different
training modes and sports. American football is listed at 90% short-term, 10%
intermediate, 0% long-term — among the most phosphagen-dominant sports in the table,
comparable to golf (95/5/0) and volleyball (90/10/0), and far more phosphagen-dominant
than field hockey or soccer half-backs (60/20/20). Verkhoshansky himself cautions that
this "highly determinate" scheme, compiled decades earlier, has been questioned, that
figures for some events (he names the 1500m specifically) have since been revised, and
that it should not be used casually because it disguises moment-to-moment metabolic
demand shifts within a single sport. (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81.)

**Why it works** — The table estimates an average, whole-game contribution, whereas actual
play consists of short high-intensity bursts (plays) separated by long rest (huddles,
substitutions), so an average figure can obscure the real repeated-sprint, phosphagen-
dominant-per-play structure while also underweighting the role of aerobic recovery between
bursts.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's stated conditioning priority for
football is alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp and game demands, with
glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" absorbed incidentally rather
than programmed as a primary target (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39`); the baseline also states the aerobic
system's main value for speed-power athletes is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP
between bouts), not distance capacity (citing `2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md
p.9`). **Inference:** this table's 90/10/0 split for football (near-zero credited to the
long-term/aerobic system) looks, at first read, to be in tension with the baseline's
explicit inclusion of aerobic capacity as a Goal-1 priority for football — but the tension
likely resolves once "aerobic system" is understood functionally: the baseline treats
aerobic fitness as enabling faster ATP/phosphagen regeneration between the very
phosphagen-dominant plays this table describes, not as a source of in-play energy. Read
together, not as contradictory: this table describes what fuels a single play; the
baseline describes what determines how well that fuel regenerates for the next one.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky's own caution applies directly here: **Inference**
do not use the 90/10/0 football figure as a precise or current number; it is a decades-old
average estimate for the sport as a whole, not a modern, position-specific or play-by-play
breakdown, and the source text itself flags the whole table's accuracy as needing
re-examination. This entry is rated `contested` because it is presented as a classic,
already-questioned scheme rather than an established modern reference.

**Example** — **Inference:** a single football play (a few seconds of maximal effort)
draws almost entirely on the phosphagen system, consistent with the table; but the
athlete's ability to repeat that near-maximal output play after play, series after series,
depends heavily on aerobic capacity for recovery between plays — the quality the baseline
prioritizes.

**Related** — None in this ingest yet; candidate future link to a conditioning synthesis
note once Phase 4 of the Flint project reaches conditioning and energy systems.
######## claim--fiber-recruitment-not-simply-graded-by-force.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.12"
topic: fibre recruitment in ballistic movement
category: [fiber-type, plyometrics, testing]
confidence: contested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# The Classic "Slow-Fibres-First-by-Force-Magnitude" Recruitment Model Fails for Ballistic Movement

**What it is** — The standard recruitment scheme (slow-twitch fibres recruited first up to
roughly 20% of maximum force, then progressively more fast-twitch fibres as force rises)
holds for graded, progressive loading, but Bosco (1982, cited PDF pp. 74-75, printed pp.
63-64) shows it breaks down for ballistic motion. Walking at moderate speed produces over
700 N of vertical ground reaction force yet, by contact time and movement pattern, relies
almost entirely on slow-twitch action; a maximal, high-velocity knee extension against a
leg-press plate produces less force than walking despite being nearly pure fast-twitch
action. The force-velocity curve itself differs by jump type: squat jumps and isokinetic
testing reflect mainly the muscle's contractile component and follow the traditional
hyperbolic F-V curve, while countermovement (dip) jumps and depth jumps are strongly
shaped by elastic energy released from the Series Elastic Component during the preceding
rapid stretch, producing an entirely different curve shape that does not fit the
traditional model. Sprinting, high jump, and long jump coordinates also fall far from the
traditional F-V curve. Bosco specifically cautions that isokinetic training is not
advisable for athletes in predominantly ballistic sports.

**Why it works** — Force magnitude alone does not determine which fibres are recruited or
how force is produced; movement pattern, contact duration, and whether elastic energy
storage/release is involved (SSC-mediated ballistic actions vs. purely contractile,
non-ballistic actions) change both the recruitment pattern and the resulting force-time and
force-velocity relationships.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] and
[[claim--fiber-recruitment-not-simply-graded-by-force|this entry's]] own caution: SJ, CMJ,
and depth-jump testing are not interchangeable measures of the same underlying quality,
because they load the contractile component and the SEC to very different degrees. Also
reinforces caution about isokinetic testing/training for ballistic-sport athletes already
raised in [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` rather than `supported` because it
directly overturns a simpler, still widely-taught recruitment model (force-graded,
slow-then-fast) using a small number of illustrative examples (walking, car-pushing,
seated knee extension) rather than a systematic dataset; **Inference:** treat the classic
graded model as a reasonable first approximation for slow, controlled movement, and this
critique as the more accurate account specifically for ballistic/SSC-involved movement.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach should not assume a squat-jump-based force
measurement predicts depth-jump or sprint ground-reaction performance; the elastic
contribution present in the latter two is largely absent from the former.

**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].
######## claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.16"
topic: sequence of biochemical adaptation
category: [adaptation, detraining, overtraining]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops

**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), Verkhoshansky states biochemical adaptation to
training follows a definite sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first, oxidative ATP
resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle protein (myosin)
and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase; only after that
does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining or detraining, these
adaptations are lost in the reverse order they were gained. The longer the training period,
the more thorough the adaptation and the longer those biochemical changes persist after
training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels). This gain/loss asymmetry across
different systems is termed heterochronic (different tissues and processes change on
different timelines). Overtraining specifically shows a distinct pattern: reduced
glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/glycogen, blood plasma
dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to disrupted acid-base
balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)

**Why it works** — Different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity, structural protein
synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular mechanisms with
different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts, then de-adapts"
model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while others are gained
late and lost early.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** this converges directionally with
Platonov's heterochronic principle (different systems have different adaptation/de-
adaptation timelines) but the two are not a stated one-to-one match — the baseline's
build-easy/lose-fast claim is about energy-system categories (aerobic vs. alactic), while
Platonov's sequence is about biochemical sub-processes within training generally (oxidative
capacity, structural protein, glycolysis, CP). Treat them as parallel instances of the same
underlying heterochronicity concept, not as the same specific claim restated.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
four-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use
it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than
a specific testing checklist.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete returning from a multi-week layoff might show
CP-system/power qualities holding up relatively better than the earlier-gained oxidative
and glycogen-storage qualities, or vice versa, depending on the specific loss sequence;
either way, "detraining" is not a single uniform decline and re-testing across qualities
(not just one) gives a more accurate readiness picture.

**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].
######## claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.15"
topic: lactate and fatigue misconceptions
category: [energy-systems, education, myth-busting]
confidence: proven
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept

**What it is** — Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
older term "anaerobic threshold" has similarly been replaced by "blood lactate threshold"
or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation) since lactate does not require an absence of
oxygen to form. (PDF pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)

**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
"flushing out lactic acid."

**Related** — [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].

# Soviet Sport-School Guideline Ages by Sport (Start, Specialize, Peak)

**What it is** — A per-sport table (Table 1.2) of recommended ages to begin a sport,
begin specialization, and expect high performance, drawn from the Soviet sports-school
system. Examples: basketball 7-8 / 10-12 / 20-25; gymnastics (women) 4-5 / 10-11 / 14-18;
gymnastics (men) 5-6 / 12-14 / 18-24; swimming 3-7 / 10-12 / 16-18; track-and-field 6-7 /
13-14 / 18-23; weightlifting 10-11 / 17-18 / 21-28; wrestling 10-11 / 15-16 / 24-28 (17
sports listed in total). Early, intense specialization is explicitly discouraged in
strength and endurance sports for children; the average age of Soviet Olympians in the
era cited was about 24, with fewer than 10% under age 20. (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp.
24-25.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the likely underlying rationale matches this library's
existing long-term athletic development material — early specialization in
strength/endurance sports produces faster short-term progress but a lower ultimate ceiling
and more attrition, because the young athlete has not built the broad physical base
specialization later draws on. Verkhoshansky's text does not itself restate this mechanism
in this passage; it presents the table and the age-of-Olympians statistic as its supporting
evidence (PDF p. 36, printed p. 25).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a more granular, sport-by-sport reference
table alongside this library's existing LTAD guidance. It converges with, and adds numeric
detail beyond, the Bompa library's
[[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model|Long-Term Sequential Development
Model]], which states a general "not before ~14-15" specialization guideline but does not
break it out by individual sport; this convergence is this entry's own comparison, not
stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a 20th-century Soviet sports-school table,
not a modern, population-representative dataset; individual biological maturation varies
(see [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological vs Training
Age]]), and American collegiate sport pathways (e.g. football, not listed in Table 1.2 at
all) do not map cleanly onto these Soviet age bands. Treat the specific ages as
illustrative, not prescriptive, for a Baylor Athletics context; this caution is this
entry's own judgment.

**Example** — **Inference:** The table's general caution against early strength/endurance specialization
supports keeping a young multi-sport athlete on broad physical preparation rather than
early single-sport strength specialization, consistent with existing LTAD guidance already
in this library.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]] (reciprocal link
recommended there: add a line noting Supertraining Table 1.2 gives per-sport numeric ages
that concretize this framework's general specialization-age guidance).
######## claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky

topic: minimum effective training load
category: [strength, programming, training-age]
confidence: supported

---

# A Minimum Load Threshold Drives Strength Gains, and It Rises as the Athlete Adapts

**What it is** — Hettinger & Muller (1953) are cited for a threshold training stimulus of
roughly one-third of maximal strength needed to produce a strength increase in an average
person; as strength rises, the required stimulus intensity rises too, eventually reaching
80-95% of the athlete's maximum, sometimes matching or exceeding actual competition
intensity (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Each stimulus level has its own "strengthening
threshold," a ceiling beyond which no further gain occurs at that intensity, and this
ceiling is described as further from the untrained state the less trained the athlete is.
Separately, Korobkov, Gerasimov & Vasiliev (via Verkhoshansky, 1977) are cited for the
finding that in the initial stages of training, strength increases roughly uniformly
regardless of load, with approximately equivalent gains reported at 20%, 40%, 60% and 80%
of 1RM; raising training intensity early (heavier load, faster tempo, less rest) does not
reliably improve on this until strength has already progressed some way. (PDF pp. 33-34,
printed pp. 22-23.)

**Why it works** — Early neuromuscular adaptation (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]) responds to almost
any sufficiently repeated stimulus above a low floor; once that easy adaptive window
closes, further progress requires a stimulus that approaches the athlete's current
ceiling, because there is less slack left in recruitment and coordination to exploit.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports keeping early-phase (novice) load prescription
simple and consistency-focused rather than chasing high intensities, and supports
progressively raising relative intensity toward 80-95% of max as an athlete's training age
increases, consistent with this book's own training-age-scaling heuristic
([[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]]).

**When NOT to apply** — These are single-source, decades-old figures cited without a
stated sample or modern replication in this text (Hettinger 1961; Korobkov, Gerasimov &
Vasiliev via Verkhoshansky 1977; PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 22-23). **Inference:** do not
treat "one-third of max" or the specific 20/40/60/80% equivalence as precise, universal
cutoffs for a current athlete population; use them as a directional argument for why novice
programming can be simple, not as exact percentages to program from.

**Example** — **Inference:** A true beginner's program built around consistent submaximal loading (e.g.
50-60% 1RM) can produce comparable early strength gains to a heavier protocol, so there is
little value in front-loading high intensity before the athlete has trained long enough to
need it.

**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]].
######## claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim

category: [specificity, velocity, exercise-selection]

ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# High-Velocity Training Transfers to Low Velocity Better Than the Reverse; Contraction Modes Barely Cross Over

**What it is** — Two specific, cited findings under the specificity umbrella: (1)
low-velocity isokinetic training improves low-velocity strength but has minimal effect on
high-velocity strength; high-velocity isokinetic training improves high-velocity strength
and transfers somewhat better to low-velocity strength than the reverse direction
(Moffroid & Whipple 1970; Perrine & Edgerton 1981; Kanehisa & Miyashita 1983b). (2)
Contraction-mode adaptations are narrow: concentric-eccentric (weightlifting-style)
training raises competitive strength but produces only small isometric or concentric
isokinetic gains; isometric training raises isometric strength but not concentric
isokinetic strength; elbow-extension training with weights increases triceps strength and
girth without a matching isokinetic-strength change. Static and dynamic training even
produce different microscopic structural changes in the muscle. (PDF pp. 38-40, printed
pp. 27-29.)

**Why it works** — Force-velocity curve position (see
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]) and contraction-mode
recruitment patterns are trained narrowly because different neural drive strategies and
structural adaptations underlie each; high-velocity training likely also recruits fast-
twitch units that contribute somewhat at slower speeds, which is the proposed reason the
transfer is asymmetric rather than symmetric.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** when selecting exercise velocity and contraction mode,
match both to the sport action being targeted, and consider biasing toward higher-velocity
work when in doubt, since the text's cited data shows it transfers in both directions
somewhat, whereas slow, heavy work transfers poorly to fast actions. **Eric's baseline:**
the isometric seated calf raise and other isometric testing are run on the ForceDecks
"Mid-Thigh Pull" setting as part of the department's standard protocol
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`). **Inference:**
this claim's contraction-mode specificity finding supports treating isometric testing as
its own distinct quality rather than a proxy for dynamic 1RM strength; neither source states
this connection directly.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** these are 1970s-1980s isokinetic-dynamometer
studies (PDF pp. 38-40, printed pp. 27-29); isokinetic machine training is a narrow,
lab-style modality rarely used in current collegiate S&C practice, and this specific
transfer asymmetry has not been independently re-verified here for free-weight or
plyometric training modes. **Inference:** do not assume the same asymmetric-transfer ratio
applies to, say, barbell velocity-based training without separate evidence; this extension
is not addressed in the text.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete tested for isometric mid-thigh pull strength should not be assumed
to have an equivalent dynamic 1RM or sprint force capability; each needs its own
assessment and, if targeted, its own specific training exposure.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]].

type: library-entry

category: [strength, testing, neural]

# The Voluntary-Involuntary Strength Reserve Has a Measured Size

**What it is** — Two cited figures quantify how much force voluntary effort leaves
unused relative to the athlete's true ceiling. (1) In experienced weightlifters, the mean
gap between training maximum (TFmax) and competitive maximum (CFmax) is about 12.5 ± 2.5%,
larger in heavier weight classes (Zatsiorsky, 1995; PDF p. 13, printed p. 2). (2) Under
involuntary or hypnotic conditions, strength output can rise by up to 35% in untrained
people, but by less than 10% in trained athletes (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2, no primary
citation given in text for this figure).

**Why it works** — Both numbers describe the same phenomenon from different angles: a
protective neural inhibition normally holds voluntary output below the muscle's true
contractile ceiling, and anything that reduces that inhibition (competitive arousal,
hypnosis, involuntary reflex recruitment) exposes more of it. Training narrows the
untapped reserve because part of the strength-training adaptation is learning to
recruit and inhibit less, not just growing tissue.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is best used as a coaching narrative for why
max-effort numbers move around by context (weigh-in day nerves, meet atmosphere, testing
environment), and as a rough expectation that a smaller gap between training and
competitive/testing efforts is itself a marker of higher training status. Neither the
book nor Eric's baseline states this as an applied rule; it is this entry's own synthesis
of the two cited numbers.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky gives no primary citation for the hypnosis figure
(PDF p. 13, printed p. 2); treat it as a single, unverified secondary claim, not a number
to plan around. The 12.5 ± 2.5% figure is stated specifically for experienced Olympic
weightlifters under meet conditions (Zatsiorsky, 1995; PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
**Inference:** it should not be assumed to transfer directly to Baylor's team-sport
athletes tested on a force plate (ForceDecks CMJ/IMTP) rather than in a weightlifting
competition, and neither number should be used as a correction factor applied to that data
without independent verification; this caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in
`method-baseline.md`.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete who tests near-identically on a submaximal VBT-estimated 1RM and
a rare true max attempt is showing a small reserve gap; a large, inconsistent gap between
estimated and tested max may point to arousal/readiness on test day rather than a change
in underlying capacity.

**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]].

2	---
3	type: library-entry

14	
15	# Central vs. Peripheral Fatigue, and Low- vs. High-Frequency Fatigue
16	
17	**What it is** — Fatigue during short-duration strength/power work is split into
18	**central fatigue** (reduced motivation, impaired spinal nerve transmission, reduced motor
19	neuron recruitment and firing rate — a CNS-level phenomenon) and **peripheral fatigue**
20	(failure somewhere in the excitation-contraction chain at the muscle cell itself: motor
21	end-plate, sarcolemma, T-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, contractile proteins).
22	Peripheral fatigue further splits into **low-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at <20 Hz
23	stimulation, from depressed calcium release, recovering slowly over up to 48 hours) and
24	**high-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at >50 Hz, recovering faster). "Muscle wisdom"
25	names the CNS's own down-regulation of motor neuron discharge rate during a sustained
26	maximal contraction, believed to protect against electrical failure and possibly to
27	postpone central fatigue. Exercise-induced ammonia accumulation is cited as a possible
28	contributor to central fatigue at high intensities/durations. Intensive CNS activation
29	(max weights, max power, plyometrics) is stated to need at least 48 hours of recovery if
30	no restorative methods are used. (PDF pp. 24-27, printed pp. 13-16.)
31	
32	**Why it works** — Fatigue is not a single process with one cause; the central/peripheral
33	split and the frequency-dependent split reflect genuinely different physiological
34	bottlenecks (nervous drive vs. contractile-machinery failure vs. calcium-handling
35	kinetics), which is why they have different time courses and respond to different
36	recovery strategies.
37	
38	**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states intensive CNS activation (max weights, max power,
39	plyometrics) needs at least 48 hours of recovery if no restorative methods are used (PDF p.
40	25, printed p. 14). **Inference:** this supports spacing high-CNS-cost sessions (max
41	strength, high-velocity work) at least two days apart within a microcycle, and treating
42	"still feels flat two days after a max-effort day" as plausible central fatigue rather than
43	assuming poor effort or motivation; this specific practical framing is not stated in the
44	text.
45	
46	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a mechanistic taxonomy from exercise
47	physiology, not a monitoring protocol. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength
48	index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen daily readiness marker
49	(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
50	`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); **Inference:** mRSI is a downstream readiness proxy,
51	not a direct central/peripheral fatigue assay, so a flat CMJ day should not be
52	over-attributed to a specific named mechanism (e.g., "low-frequency fatigue") without EMG
53	or stimulation data — neither source states this equivalence, and this caution is this
54	entry's own judgment.
55	
56	**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete who trained max-effort squats yesterday and shows reduced CMJ
57	output today is more likely showing central/low-frequency fatigue still resolving than a
58	loss of underlying strength; retesting 48 hours later is more informative than reacting to
59	the single depressed value.
60	
61	**Related** — [[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]].

75	
76	# Compensatory (Acceleration/Action) Training — Using Proprioceptive Feedback to Actively Manage Bar Speed
77	
78	**What it is** — Free weights (unlike some variable-resistance machines) let the lifter
79	feel changing leverage through the range of motion via proprioceptive feedback and respond
80	by voluntarily accelerating or decelerating the bar to raise or lower the force produced.
81	This is termed Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT), most obviously used
82	concentrically, but the text argues it applies just as much eccentrically (muscles
83	actively resist gravity's acceleration to control the descent) and even isometrically
84	(the lifter must continuously compensate for fatigue-driven declines in neural drive to
85	hold a constant position), leading the author to prefer "Compensatory Action Training" as
86	the fuller name. (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21; Ch 7.1 develops it further.)
87	
88	**Why it works** — Because force is not fixed by the weight alone (F = ma; a lighter bar
89	accelerated hard can still produce meaningful force), an athlete who actively drives bar
90	speed rather than passively moving a fixed load is directly manipulating the training
91	stimulus at every point in the range of motion, not just at the load's nominal percentage
92	of 1RM.
93	
94	**When to apply** — **Inference:** this reads as a conceptual ancestor of today's
95	velocity-based training (VBT) cueing — "move the bar as fast as possible" instructions on
96	submaximal sets are a modern implementation of the same idea. **Eric's baseline:** Perch
97	camera-based velocity-based training is part of the department's current technology stack
98	(`method-baseline.md`, "Data, technology and reporting," citing
99	`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7`). **Inference:** CAT's proprioceptive-feedback
100	logic maps onto that existing Perch capability, though neither the book nor the baseline
101	draws this connection directly. **Inference:** also useful as coaching language for
102	eccentric-phase control (actively resisting the descent) and isometric holds (actively
103	maintaining tension); this extension beyond the text's own concentric framing is this
104	entry's own reading of Verkhoshansky's eccentric/isometric CAT discussion (PDF p. 32,
105	printed p. 21).
106	
107	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a technique/cueing concept, not a
108	load-prescription protocol; it doesn't specify a percentage, velocity target, or rep scheme
109	on its own in the text. **Inference:** cueing maximal intended acceleration on every rep is
110	not appropriate for all training goals (e.g., controlled-tempo hypertrophy work
111	deliberately avoids this); this caveat is not addressed in this section of the text.
112	
113	**Example** — **Inference:** Coaching "explode the bar up" on a submaximal front squat set is applying
114	CAT: the athlete voluntarily increases bar acceleration beyond what the load alone would
115	produce, raising the true training force above the load's nominal value.
116

131	
132	# Structural and Functional Determinants of Strength
133	
134	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky lists the factors that determine how much strength a
135	muscle group can produce. Structural factors: cross-sectional area of the muscle, density
136	of fibres per unit cross-section, and mechanical leverage efficiency across the joint.
137	Functional (neural) factors: number of fibres contracting simultaneously, rate of fibre
138	contraction, efficiency of firing synchronization, nerve conduction velocity, degree of
139	inhibition of non-contributing fibres, proportion of large-diameter (fast-twitch) fibres
140	active, efficiency of cooperation between fibre types, efficiency of stretch reflexes,
141	excitation threshold of the nerve fibres, and initial muscle length before contraction.
142	Maximum strength is produced at an optimum, not a maximum, frequency of nerve firing
143	(Vredensky, via Vorobyev 1978), and that optimal frequency itself shifts with fatigue
144	level (Kernell & Monster, 1982). Synchronization of motor unit firing across fibres does
145	not appear to meaningfully increase the rate of strength production; sequencing
146	(efficient timing) may matter more than simultaneity, especially where stored elastic
147	energy must be released at the right moment (Miller et al., 1981). (PDF pp. 44-45,
148	printed pp. 33-34.)
149	
150	**Why it works** — This is a fuller inventory of why two athletes with the same
151	cross-sectional muscle area can produce very different force: most of the list is neural
152	(recruitment, timing, inhibition, reflex efficiency), consistent with this chapter's
153	overall theme that strength is a neuromuscular, not purely structural, phenomenon.
154	
155	**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a longer checklist than
156	[[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] when explaining to students
157	or staff (e.g. in HHPR 5355) why hypertrophy alone does not fully predict strength, and
158	for generating hypotheses about why an athlete with good muscle mass underperforms on
159	force output (check firing rate, synchronization, initial muscle length/joint angle,
160	rather than assuming a training-volume problem).
161	
162	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky notes more research is needed before drawing a
163	firm conclusion about strength gains from increased motor-unit synchronization (PDF p.
164	45, printed p. 34); **Inference:** do not treat "improve synchronization" as an
165	established, targetable training goal on its own — none of these functional factors
166	listed have a stated field-testable metric in this section.
167	
168	**Example** — **Inference:** two athletes with similar squat cross-sectional muscle
169	estimates (e.g. via anthropometrics) but different 1RM outputs are most likely differing
170	on the functional/neural list (recruitment, firing rate, inhibition), not on structural
171	factors alone.
172	
173	**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]],
174	[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

188	
189	# Seven Factors That Limit Strength Production
190	
191	**What it is** — Strength output in the short and long term is limited by seven
192	interacting factors: **trainability** (genetic ceiling for hypertrophy, fibre-type
193	distribution, leverage, and pre-training status); **neuromuscular efficiency** (skill in
194	recruiting the right muscles accurately and powerfully); **biomechanical efficiency**
195	(leverage and relative muscle-group strength, trainable unlike raw genetic trainability);
196	**psychological factors** (motivation, focus, pain tolerance, perceived exertion, coach
197	influence); **pain and fear of pain** (distinguishing injury pain, a protective signal to
198	act on, from effort pain, a subjective load-intensity signal usable via an RPE-style
199	scale); **injury and fear of injury** (reflex inhibition of contraction around a damaged
200	joint is well documented; return to top performance depends on the athlete's own
201	perception that rehab is complete, not just medical clearance); and **fatigue** (central
202	vs. peripheral, discussed further in
203	[[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]]). (PDF pp. 23-24, printed pp.
204	12-13.)
205	
206	**Why it works** — Strength testing and training programs typically control for load,
207	volume, and technique, but this list makes explicit that psychological state, injury
208	history, and perceived pain/fear operate as real physiological limiters on force output,
209	not just "mental" factors layered on top of a physical ceiling — reflex inhibition around
210	an injured joint is a measurable neuromuscular effect, not a motivation problem.
211	
212	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a checklist when an athlete's force output
213	underperforms their apparent physical capacity: before assuming a physical/programming
214	cause, rule out fear of re-injury, unaddressed effort-pain tolerance, or psychological
215	state. Verkhoshansky states "return to top level performance will occur only if the
216	athlete perceives rehabilitation to be complete" and the fear of pain or re-injury being
217	minimal (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13). **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role
218	in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and
219	Athletic Medicine's RTP decisions, a support/advisory role rather than a final-decision
220	role (`method-baseline.md`, "Rehab and return to play," citing
221	`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6`); that same baseline section is flagged as
222	"the thinnest discipline in the corpus" with no stated RTP criteria or battery.
223	**Inference:** Verkhoshansky's fear-of-injury/pain framing is a plausible partial fill for
224	that documented gap, though neither source states this connection directly.
225	
226	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive taxonomy, not a measurement
227	protocol; none of these seven factors have a given cutoff or test threshold in this section
228	of the text (PDF pp. 23-24, printed pp. 12-13). **Inference:** do not use "fear of injury"
229	as a catch-all explanation without other supporting evidence (movement quality, self-report,
230	clinical input from Athletic Medicine); reflex inhibition and psychological guarding can
231	look similar from the outside. This caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in the
232	text.
233	
234	**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete cleared medically after an ACL reconstruction who still shows
235	reduced force output on the operated leg during testing may be exhibiting reflex inhibition
236	and/or fear of re-injury, not a residual physical deficit alone; that changes what the
237	next intervention should target.
238	
239	**Related** — [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]].

253	
254	# The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition
255	
256	**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
257	initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
258	faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
259	(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
260	Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
261	swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
262	same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
263	research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
264	found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
265	and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
266	that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
267	high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
268	performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
269	restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
270	every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
271	pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)
272	
273	**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
274	after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure
275	(not just a qualitative "wave" description), which is what allows taper researchers to ask
276	a specific, testable question: how much and how recently loaded should training be before
277	competition to maximize the fitness-minus-fatigue difference at competition time.
278	
279	**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the more technical, equation-based underpinning
280	of this library's already-captured practical rule
281	([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]); cite this entry when a
282	more rigorous or quantitative framing is needed (e.g. explaining the model to a sport
283	scientist or in a research-facing document), and cite the Bompa heuristic for the everyday
284	coaching rule of thumb. The taper-volume finding directly supports reducing training
285	volume, not just intensity, in the days immediately before a competition or key testing
286	date.
287	
288	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific mathematical constants (A, B, T1, T2)
289	must be fit per individual and per training phase, and the text notes they require
290	periodic re-estimation; do not treat this as a plug-and-play formula without that
291	fitting process. The taper studies cited are from the early-to-mid 1990s and largely from
292	swimming; **Inference:** don't assume the exact taper-volume findings transfer unchanged to
293	football or other team sports without independent verification.
294	
295	**Example** — **Inference:** rather than assuming a flat "taper week" cuts intensity but
296	keeps volume similar, this model's logic and the cited taper research both point toward
297	deliberately reducing volume (not just easing intensity) in the final days before a key
298	competition or test date, to let the longer-lasting fitness effect show through as the
299	shorter fatigue effect clears.
300	
301	**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]],
302	[[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

316	
317	# Functional vs. Structural Resistance Training
318	
319	**What it is** — Two basic categories of resistance training effect: structural training
320	targets muscle hypertrophy (and some tissue flexibility); functional training targets
321	performance qualities (static strength, speed-strength, muscular endurance, reactive
322	ability) through four neural mechanisms: (1) intermuscular coordination — sequencing and
323	synchronizing action between different muscle groups; (2) intramuscular coordination —
324	control within one muscle via number encoding (how many fibres are recruited), rate
325	encoding (firing frequency), and pattern encoding (sequencing of fibre types); (3)
326	facilitatory/inhibitory reflex processes; (4) motor learning, programming the CNS to
327	execute a specific task. No training is purely structural; all training is functional to
328	some degree and may also elicit structural change. (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7.)
329	
330	**Why it works** — Force output for a given movement is the product of both how much
331	contractile tissue exists (structural) and how effectively the nervous system recruits,
332	times, and sequences that tissue (functional). Early or stagnation-phase training gets
333	more return from the functional side because coordination has more room to improve;
334	structural change is slower and more load-dependent.
335	
336	**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states functional stages should precede structural
337	stages both for beginners and during a plateau at an advanced level (PDF p. 19, printed p.
338	8, cross-referenced to 1.2 and Ch2). **Inference:** this supports using the split as a
339	diagnostic lens when an athlete's strength stalls: ask whether the limiter is likely
340	structural (needs more hypertrophy-phase volume) or functional (needs improved
341	coordination, rate coding, or motor learning of the specific lift/skill); this diagnostic
342	framing is this entry's own extension, not stated as a test procedure in the text.
343	
344	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a conceptual split, not a measured
345	diagnostic; number, rate, and pattern encoding are not directly observable from a force
346	plate or barbell velocity alone, so inferring which mechanism is limiting a given athlete
347	is coach judgment, not a test result. Verkhoshansky's use of "functional training" here
348	means neural coordination and recruitment specifically (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7);
349	**Inference:** don't confuse it with the modern commercial-gym use of the same term
350	(balance boards, unstable surfaces), which is a different, later usage the text does not
351	address.
352	
353	**Example** — **Inference:** A lifter whose 1RM is stagnant despite visible muscle gain may be limited by
354	intermuscular coordination (poor bracing/synchronization under heavy load) rather than by
355	insufficient muscle; technique and coordination work, not more volume, is the higher-value
356	fix.
357	
358	**Related** — [[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]].

372	
373	# Skilled Movement Depends on the Kinaesthetic System, and Is Shaped by Mental Rehearsal Before It Starts
374	
375	**What it is** — Skilled movement relies on the kinaesthetic sense, built from four
376	subsystems: joint receptors (joint angle and rate of change), muscle spindles (muscle
377	length and tension), the Golgi tendon apparatus (tension monitoring, protects against
378	excessive loading by reducing tension past a critical value), and the vestibular apparatus
379	(head/body position, velocity, acceleration), plus touch and pain receptors.
380	Proprioception is described as second only to pain in producing the most intense and
381	widespread brain electrical activity. Separately, research (Evarts 1973, 1979; Siff 1977)
382	found that the motor cortex, cerebellum, and basal ganglia all become active before a
383	movement begins, not merely in response to it as classically assumed; a specific 9 Hz "mu
384	rhythm" brain pattern is blocked in advance of movement. The cerebellum corrects and
385	reorganizes motor commands before they reach the muscles (feedforward control) and can
386	coordinate movement even without peripheral feedback; the motor cortex governs the amount
387	and pattern of muscular contraction. Russian training practice uses visualization (watching
388	film of top athletes/coaches, mental rehearsal) and autogenic training (imagining the full
389	sensory and emotional experience of competition, sometimes monitored with ECG/EMG/GSR) to
390	exploit this pre-movement brain activity. (PDF pp. 81-83, printed pp. 70-72.)
391	
392	**Why it works** — Because motor planning measurably begins before the muscles act,
393	rehearsing a movement mentally (with vivid sensory and emotional detail) engages some of
394	the same preparatory neural circuitry as physically performing it, giving visualization a
395	plausible mechanism beyond simple relaxation or confidence-building.
396	
397	**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports including structured visualization/mental
398	rehearsal as a real training tool, not just a "soft skill," for technical rehearsal (e.g.
399	before a max-effort lift or a technical skill) and pre-competition routines. Also useful
400	teaching framework for explaining to athletes and students (e.g. HHPR 5355) why
401	proprioceptive/joint-position training (balance, landing mechanics, reactive drills) is
402	foundational to skill, not a separate "prehab" category.
403	
404	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** visualization/autogenic training is presented here
405	as a supplement integrated with physical practice, not a substitute for it; the text does
406	not claim mental rehearsal alone produces motor learning without physical repetition. The
407	detailed neuroanatomical claims (specific roles of basal ganglia vs. cerebellum, the mu
408	rhythm) are cited to 1970s research and should be treated as illustrative of the general
409	feedforward principle rather than as current, precise neuroscience.
410	
411	**Example** — **Inference:** having an athlete mentally rehearse a technical lift or a
412	competition scenario in vivid sensory detail before attempting it live is a direct,
413	practical application of this feedforward research, not just a motivational exercise.
414	
415	**Related** — [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]].

429	
430	# Precise Muscle-Action Terminology: Why "Isotonic" and "Isokinetic" Are Usually Wrong
431	
432	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky argues most everyday strength-training terms are
433	technically imprecise. Concentric: proximal and distal muscle attachments move toward one
434	another. Eccentric: they move apart (not literally a "contraction," despite the common
435	name — the muscle is returning toward resting length under load). Isometric: attachments
436	don't move relative to each other (joint angle constant); more accurately called "static."
437	"Isotonic" (constant tension) is argued to be almost never actually true during real joint
438	movement, since tension changes with acceleration, deceleration, and reflex activation
439	throughout a range; European and Russian scientists prefer "auxotonic" (changing tension
440	and length) or "allodynamic" instead. "Isokinetic" (constant velocity) is also argued to
441	be physically impossible over a full range, since starting from and returning to rest
442	requires acceleration; isokinetic devices are more accurately "quasi-isokinetic," and
443	isokinetic-machine torque output is typically much lower than isometric torque at the same
444	joint angle. "Quasi-isometric" action is defined separately: the slow, near-static muscle
445	action seen in heavy, near-maximal resistance training performed anywhere across a joint's
446	range (not fixed at one angle like true isometrics), relevant to maximal strength,
447	hypertrophy, and active flexibility training rather than power or speed. (PDF pp. 60-64,
448	printed pp. 49-53.)
449	
450	**Why it works** — Real joint movement always involves changing acceleration
451	(Newton's laws), so any term implying a truly constant mechanical variable throughout a
452	full range is describing an idealization, not the actual muscle physics; the more precise
453	terms track what is actually held constant and where.
454	
455	**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when interpreting or reporting isokinetic
456	dynamometer data (if used by Athletic Medicine or research collaborators): understand that
457	the constant-velocity claim applies only to the device's controlled range, not to the
458	underlying muscle action, and that isokinetic torque values are not directly comparable to
459	isometric (e.g. IMTP) values at the same joint angle. Also useful coaching-language
460	precision: heavy squat/bench-style lifting performed slowly is "quasi-isometric," a
461	distinct quality from true fixed-angle isometrics like the IMTP.
462	
463	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a terminology-precision argument, not a
464	claim that isokinetic or isotonic training methods are ineffective; the critique is about
465	what the words accurately describe, not about training value. Don't over-correct common
466	usage in casual coaching communication where the imprecise terms are well understood by
467	convention.
468	
469	**Example** — **Inference:** describing an IMTP as "isometric" (fixed joint angle) versus
470	a slow, heavy back squat as "quasi-isometric" (near-static but occurring across a range)
471	keeps clear which type of force-plate or barbell data is actually comparable to which.
472	
473	**Related** — [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]].

488	# Table 1.1 — Resistance Training Prescription by Goal (Strength, Power, Hypertrophy, Endurance)
489	
490	**What it is** — A dynamic (non-isometric) resistance-training prescription chart by
491	goal (PDF p. 22, printed p. 11):
492	
493	| Variable | Strength | Power | Hypertrophy | Endurance |
494	|---|---|---|---|---|
495	| Load (% 1RM) | 80-100 | 70-100 | 60-80 | 40-60 |
496	| Reps/set | 1-5 | 1-5 | 8-15 | 25-60 |
497	| Sets/exercise | 4-7 | 3-5 | 4-8 | 2-4 |
498	| Rest between sets | 2-6 min | 2-6 min | 2-5 min | 1-2 min |
499	| Duration/set | 5-10 s | 4-8 s | 20-60 s | 80-150 s |
500	| Speed/rep (% max) | 60-100 | 90-100 | 60-90 | 60-80 |
501	| Sessions/week | 3-6 | 3-6 | 5-7 | 8-14 |
502	
503	High-volume, low-resistance work is called an **extensive** method (an
504	**extensification/accumulation** phase); low-volume, high-intensity work is an
505	**intensive** method (an **intensification** phase). Early training typically opens with
506	an extensive phase before progressing to an intensive one; periodization is described as
507	cyclically alternating these two phase types.
508	
509	**Why it works** — Each goal loads the neuromuscular and metabolic systems differently:
510	near-maximal loads at low reps bias neural recruitment and force capacity (strength);
511	high-velocity submaximal loads bias rate of force development (power); moderate loads at
512	moderate-to-high volume bias metabolic and mechanical stress for hypertrophy; light loads
513	at very high reps bias oxidative/metabolic endurance.
514	
515	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a first-pass, generic reference when scoping a
516	new program's load/volume targets by goal, and as shared vocabulary for extensive/intensive
517	phase naming. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches undulating/non-linear
518	periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week, stated as the
519	personally preferred model over strict linear progression (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength
520	and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26`). **Inference:** that
521	undulating model and this text's extensive/intensive phase language describe related but
522	not identical ideas (wave-to-wave volume change vs. phase-to-phase intensity change); the
523	baseline material does not cite Verkhoshansky's specific terminology.
524	
525	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states this chart is "adequate for the average
526	personal trainer or coach dealing with the average client or lower level athlete" but
527	incomplete for advanced athletes: it ignores strength-speed, explosive strength,
528	flexibility-strength, and strength-endurance as separate qualities (PDF p. 22, printed p.
529	11), and ignores the other prescription variables covered in
530	[[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]] and later chapters. **Inference:** do
531	not use this table as a complete program design tool for a well-trained collegiate
532	athlete; treat it as a starting reference, not an endpoint.
533	
534	**Example** — **Inference:** Blocking out approximate set/rep/load ranges for a new hypertrophy-emphasis
535	mesocycle (60-80% 1RM, 8-15 reps, 4-8 sets) before layering in the athlete-specific
536	adjustments the text says this table omits.
537

553	# The S-Factors Pyramidal Model of Fitness (Strength, Speed, Stamina, Suppleness, Skill, Structure, Spirit)
554	
555	**What it is** — A comprehensive model of fitness built from seven "S-factors": Strength,
556	Speed, Stamina (systemic or local muscular endurance), Suppleness (flexibility), Skill
557	(neuromuscular efficiency, including a "Style" sub-quality — an individual's manner of
558	expressing a skill), Structure (somatotype, size, shape), and Spirit (psychological
559	preparedness). The model is built in two stages: a triangular base relating strength,
560	stamina, speed, and suppleness, then a pyramid adding skill/neuromuscular control as the
561	process that makes all movement possible, with flexibility placed at the center of the
562	base because range of movement underlies expression of every other quality. From the
563	pairwise relationships between factors, an extended list of compound fitness qualities is
564	derived: static/dynamic strength and strength-endurance, strength-speed, speed-strength,
565	strength-speed endurance, speed, endurance, flexibility-strength, flexibility-endurance,
566	flexibility-speed, skill, strength-skill, flexibility-skill, speed-skill, and
567	skill-endurance. Relative versions of these qualities (per unit bodymass) matter
568	separately in sports where bodymass is constrained (e.g. weight-class sports). (PDF pp.
569	102-103, printed pp. 91-92.)
570	
571	**Why it works** — Rather than treating strength, speed, endurance, and flexibility as
572	four independent boxes, this model treats them as vertices whose pairwise and triple
573	combinations describe most of the specific fitness qualities that actually appear in
574	sport (e.g. "speed-strength" and "strength-speed" as two distinct qualities depending on
575	which end of the force-velocity spectrum dominates, already discussed in
576	[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]), with skill/
577	neuromuscular control cutting across all of them.
578	
579	**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a master vocabulary/reference when precisely
580	naming which quality a given test or exercise targets (e.g. distinguishing
581	"strength-speed" training from "speed-strength" training, or "flexibility-strength" from
582	plain flexibility), and as a teaching framework (e.g. HHPR 5355) for showing students why
583	"fitness" is not one thing to test or train, but a structured set of specific,
584	combinable qualities.
585	
586	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky himself calls this model "representational or
587	descriptive rather than scientifically analytical" and notes it is complicated by other
588	factors such as quasi-isometric states at very slow speeds (PDF p. 102, printed p. 91);
589	**Inference:** don't treat it as a validated measurement taxonomy with defined tests for
590	each named compound quality — most of these terms (e.g. "flexibility-skill") have no
591	standard test attached in this text.
592	
593	**Example** — **Inference:** describing an athlete's need as "relative strength-speed"
594	(power per unit bodymass) rather than just "power" gives a program design target that is
595	precise about both the force-velocity region and the bodymass constraint, useful for a
596	weight-class or position-limited athlete.
597	
598	**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]],
599	[[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]].

613	
614	# Sarcomere Hypertrophy (Functional) vs. Sarcoplasmic Hypertrophy (Non-Functional)
615	
616	**What it is** — Two distinct types of muscle hypertrophy are described. Sarcomere
617	hypertrophy: an increase in the size and number of sarcomeres within myofibrils; when
618	added in parallel (not just in series) this increases the muscle's cross-sectional density
619	of contractile tissue and produces a real increase in strength. Sarcoplasmic hypertrophy:
620	an increase in the volume of non-contractile protein and semifluid plasma between fibres;
621	cross-sectional area increases, but the density of contractile tissue per unit area
622	decreases, with no corresponding strength increase. Except in sports where added bodymass
623	itself matters (bodybuilding, sumo), sarcomere hypertrophy is described as far more
624	important for athletic performance. Longer, more strenuous submaximal loading (not rapid,
625	near-maximal, low-repetition loading like Olympic weightlifting) is associated with more
626	sarcoplasmic and less sarcomere hypertrophy; high-repetition, moderate-resistance training
627	(bodybuilding/circuit-style) can also make fast-twitch fibres behave more like slow-twitch
628	fibres. (PDF pp. 77-78, printed pp. 66-67.)
629	
630	**Why it works** — The two hypertrophy types build different cellular components (more
631	contractile machinery per fibre vs. more non-contractile fluid/protein volume around
632	existing machinery), so they produce different ratios of size gain to strength gain
633	depending on the loading style that stimulated them.
634	
635	**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant to explaining why an athlete can add
636	measurable muscle mass/girth from high-volume, moderate-load training without a
637	proportionate strength increase, and why weightlifting-style low-rep, high-intensity work
638	is more strength-efficient per unit of added mass than bodybuilding-style volume training.
639	Useful framing for a strength coach deciding whether a hypertrophy block should be
640	biased toward heavier, lower-rep work (sarcomere-biased) or higher-volume work
641	(sarcoplasm-biased), depending on whether the goal is functional strength or added bodymass
642	for a specific position.
643	
644	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the exact biochemical trigger for hypertrophy is
645	stated in the text as not fully known, and this sarcomere/sarcoplasm distinction, while
646	still commonly discussed, has not been definitively confirmed by direct human
647	biopsy/histology consensus in the broader literature since; treat it as a useful coaching
648	model, not a settled biochemical fact, and don't claim a specific training protocol
649	produces "only" one type of hypertrophy in isolation.
650	
651	**Example** — **Inference:** a lineman training for added mass and positional strength
652	might justifiably include both rep ranges, but should not assume high-rep hypertrophy
653	volume alone will translate proportionally into functional strength gains without
654	lower-rep, higher-intensity work also present in the program.
655	
656	**Related** — [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]].

670	
671	# The Muscle Model: Series Elastic Component (SEC) vs. Parallel Elastic Component (PEC)
672	
673	**What it is** — A mechanical model of muscle (Levin & Wyman, 1927) treats it as a
674	contractile component in series with a Series Elastic Component (SEC: tendon,
675	cross-bridges, myofilaments, titin, Z-discs) and in parallel with a Parallel Elastic
676	Component (PEC: sarcolemma, rest-state cross-bridging, surrounding sheaths). The PEC
677	carries the force of a relaxed muscle stretched beyond resting length, and stores little
678	usable energy; the SEC is tensioned by an actively contracting muscle resisting a rapid
679	stretch, and stores considerable elastic energy — this is the mechanism plyometric/shock
680	training exploits. Slow-twitch (ST) dominant muscle shows smaller mechanical strain when
681	stretched while contracted but has a stiffer, more elastic SEC than fast-twitch
682	(FT)-dominant muscle, largely due to higher collagen concentration in slow muscle; FT
683	fibres store more elastic energy overall. Static/relaxed/passive stretching mainly loads
684	the PEC; tensed/active stretching (and PNF techniques) load both the SEC and PEC. (PDF
685	pp. 51-52, printed pp. 40-41.)
686	
687	**Why it works** — Distinguishing which structure (PEC vs. SEC) is under tension during a
688	given stretch or contraction condition explains why different stretching methods (static
689	passive vs. active/PNF) target different tissue, and why fast, elastic-energy-storing
690	tissue (SEC-dominant, FT-rich muscle) behaves differently under rapid loading than slow,
691	postural (ST-rich, PEC/collagen-dominant) muscle.
692	
693	**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for explaining why plyometric/reactive-strength
694	training targets the SEC specifically (rapid stretch under active contraction) rather than
695	simple static flexibility work (which mostly loads the PEC), and for choosing PNF-style
696	active stretching when the goal is to influence both components rather than the PEC alone.
697	
698	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the anatomical location of SEC/PEC elements is
699	explicitly stated as not precisely identified (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41); treat this as a
700	functional/mechanical model for reasoning about elastic energy, not a literal anatomical
701	map to test or measure directly in an athlete.
702	
703	**Example** — **Inference:** a sprinter's calf (fast, elastic, SEC-dominant) and a
704	postural trunk muscle (slower, stiffer, PEC/collagen-dominant) would, by this model, be
705	expected to respond differently to the same static-stretch dose, supporting muscle-specific
706	rather than uniform flexibility prescription.
707	
708	**Related** — [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
709	[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].
