723	
724	# The Shock Method (Original Russian "Udarnyi Metod"), and Why "Plyometrics" Is a Loose Translation
725	
726	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky developed the "shock method" (udarnyi metod) as a special
727	speed-strength training method exploiting connective and elastic tissue's ability to
728	store and release elastic energy during stretch-shortening of the muscle complex (running,
729	jumping, throwing, rapid lifting). The rise in concentric strength after rapid "shock"
730	loading comes from two sources: increased muscle tension from the myotatic (stretch)
731	reflex, and explosive release of elastic energy stored in connective/elastic tissue during
732	the eccentric phase. Historically, in the original Russian nomenclature, "pliometric"
733	referred specifically to eccentric (lengthening) contraction, distinct from "isometric"
734	(static) and "miometric" (concentric, shortening); the term "plyometrics," as adopted in
735	the West, has drifted to describe a broader category of jumping drills, many of which do
736	not reproduce true shock-method characteristics. Verkhoshansky's preferred precise
737	definition: an eccentric contraction suddenly terminated in an explosive isometric
738	contraction, producing a powerful myotatic reflex and a rapid extension of the muscle's
739	passive components, followed by an explosive concentric contraction. (PDF p. 45, printed
740	p. 34.)
741	
742	**Why it works** — The stretch-shortening cycle mechanism (reflex potentiation plus
743	elastic energy return) is well established in modern SSC/plyometric research
744	independent of this text; this entry's contribution is the terminology history and the
745	precise mechanical definition, which distinguishes genuine shock-method work from
746	ordinary jumping drills marketed under the same name.
747	
748	**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when auditing whether a program's "plyometric"
749	exercises actually meet Verkhoshansky's precise definition (a sudden eccentric-to-isometric-
750	to-concentric sequence) versus being ordinary jump training relabeled; this matters for
751	predicting whether the intended reactive-strength adaptation is actually being trained.
752	This library already traces Verkhoshansky's shock-method lineage at a higher level in
753	[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas|The
754	Soviet Lineage Behind Modern Sprint-Training Ideas]]; that entry credits him with "shock
755	method (plyometrics)" but does not cover the terminology history or mechanism given here,
756	so this entry adds a genuinely new angle rather than duplicating it.
757	
758	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not assume every drill called "plyometric" in
759	current commercial or popular usage (e.g. step-aerobics-style jumping) reproduces the
760	shock-method mechanism; Verkhoshansky himself notes this drift and recommends "shock
761	method" or "depth jumps" as the more precise Russian-tradition terms (PDF p. 45, printed
762	p. 34). This terminology distinction does not itself tell a coach which drills are safe or
763	appropriate for a given athlete; that is a separate training-age and readiness question.
764	
765	**Example** — **Inference:** a coach programming "plyometrics" for a novice athlete should
766	check whether the intended exercise involves a true rapid eccentric-to-concentric shock
767	transition (a depth jump) or is really just a submaximal hop/jump drill; the two carry very
768	different neuromuscular demands despite sharing the popular label.
769	
770	**Related** — [[framework--determinants-of-strength-structural-functional]],
771	[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas]]
772	(reciprocal link recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.6 gives the original
773	Russian terminology split — isometric/miometric/pliometric — and the precise mechanical
774	definition of the shock method that this lineage table only names in passing).

788	
789	# Estimating Strength Deficit by Comparing a Static-Start Jump to a Dip/Countermovement Jump
790	
791	**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
792	voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
793	ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]). True Fmm
794	requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and risky to test directly. As a
795	field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from a static, knees-flexed start
796	(no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a sudden dip (a countermovement
797	that recruits the stretch reflex and involuntary/reactive contribution). A small
798	difference between the two jumps suggests the athlete is already recruiting most of their
799	available force voluntarily, i.e. training should emphasize raw force/strength capacity;
800	a large difference suggests a bigger untapped reactive/neural reserve, i.e. training
801	should emphasize "shock" and ballistic (reactive) methods instead. (PDF p. 20, printed
802	p. 9; the explosive-strength-deficit formalism, Fmax vs. Fmm, is credited to Zatsiorsky,
803	1995, discussed further via the force-time curve in Ch3.)
804	
805	**Why it works** — A countermovement recruits the stretch-shortening cycle and a degree
806	of involuntary reflex potentiation that a static start cannot access; the size of the
807	resulting performance gap is a rough behavioral index of how much of the athlete's
808	reactive/neural potential is already expressed voluntarily versus still latent.
809	
810	**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks
811	includes the squat jump (quarter-squat start, static, 3s hold) and the countermovement
812	jump (x3), among other variants (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
813	monitoring," citing `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`); mRSI from daily CMJ testing is
814	the department's chosen daily readiness marker (same section, citing
815	`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). **Inference:** comparing SJ height/output to CMJ
816	height/output for the same athlete is effectively running this framework's proposed
817	1993-2009-era proxy with instrumented, repeatable data instead of a stopwatch-and-tape
818	comparison; neither the book nor the baseline states this equivalence directly. **Inference:**
819	a small SJ-CMJ gap (or a low CMJ-to-SJ ratio) would, by this framework's logic, suggest
820	programming should lean toward raw strength/force development, while a large gap would
821	suggest more reactive-strength/shock-method work (depth jumps, plyometrics); this specific
822	programming inference is not stated in either source and would need independent
823	validation before use.
824	
825	**When NOT to apply** — This is a directional heuristic from Verkhoshansky's text (PDF p.
826	20, printed p. 9), not a validated cutoff; no threshold percentage is given there for
827	"small" versus "large" gap. **Inference:** the modern jump-testing literature uses more
828	specific derived metrics (RSI, mRSI, eccentric utilization ratio) developed independently
829	of this 1990s framework, and those should be the primary interpretive tool; treat this
830	entry as a conceptual ancestor, not a replacement. **Inference:** do not use a single
831	SJ/CMJ comparison on one test day to make a training-emphasis decision; use trended data.
832	This trending caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in the source text.
833	
834	**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete with SJ and CMJ heights within 1-2 cm of each other is a candidate
835	for a strength-emphasis block; an athlete with a large CMJ advantage over SJ (a high
836	eccentric utilization ratio) is more likely to respond to reactive/plyometric emphasis.
837	
838	**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]].
839	######## framework--types-of-maximal-strength.md
840	---
841	type: library-entry
842	kind: framework

852	
853	# Types of Maximal Strength (CFmax, TFmax, Fmm, Relative Strength)
854	
855	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) separates "maximum strength" into a
856	ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
857	1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
858	competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
859	and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
860	only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
861	or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
862	Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
863	isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)
864	
865	**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
866	mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
867	structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
868	than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
869	reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.
870	
871	**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states the competitive maximum, not the daily training
872	maximum, should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
873	comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
874	**Inference:** this ladder is a useful lens for deciding which measured maximum should
875	anchor programmed intensity for a given athlete. **Eric's baseline:** the department
876	prefers VBT-estimated 1RM (Perch) over live 1RM attempts, estimating toward a target mean
877	velocity rather than forcing a true competitive-maximum attempt in the weight room
878	(`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`).
879	**Inference:** that preference is consistent with this framework's logic of anchoring
880	intensity to a stable maximum rather than a noisy daily one, though the baseline document
881	does not itself cite Zatsiorsky's TFmax/CFmax terminology.
882	
883	**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology and reasoning framework, not a measured
884	protocol; Fmm requires electrical stimulation or reflex loading, which Verkhoshansky
885	himself calls impractical (PDF p. 12, printed p. 1). **Inference:** none of these four
886	maxima are named as routinely and directly measured in Baylor's own documented protocols
887	(`method-baseline.md`), so this should be treated as a mental model for why training-day
888	and competition-day 1RMs diverge, not as a set of numbers to test for. Verkhoshansky states
889	the eccentric > isometric > concentric ordering is a general tendency, not a fixed ratio,
890	varying by joint angle, velocity, and muscle group (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2, cross-referenced
891	to 1.2).
892	
893	**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete's best training-day squat (TFmax) is consistently lower than
894	what they hit in a max-out competition or meet (CFmax); programming off the meet number
895	rather than a re-tested gym max avoids under-loading the athlete for weeks after a strong
896	competitive performance.
897	
898	**Related** — [[claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes]] (the numeric
899	gaps between these maxima); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
900	(a practical field proxy for the same voluntary/involuntary gap).
901	######## framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness.md
902	---
903	type: library-entry
904	kind: framework
905	domain: strength-and-conditioning
906	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
907	chapter: "1.5"
908	topic: work capacity, fitness, preparedness
909	category: [testing, readiness, terminology]
910	confidence: supported
911	ingest-tier: full-text
912	created: 2026-09-26
913	---
914	
915	# Work Capacity, Fitness, and Preparedness Are Three Different Things
916	
917	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) defines three related but distinct
918	terms. Work capacity is the general ability of the body to produce work of different
919	intensity and duration using its energy systems. Fitness is the specific ability to use
920	that work capacity to execute a given task efficiently and safely; it is a slow-changing
921	state that does not vary meaningfully over a period of days. Preparedness is not stable:
922	it is the resultant, at any given instant, of the interaction between the slow-changing
923	fitness component and the fast-changing, opposing effect of exercise-induced fatigue.
924	"Instantaneous preparedness" can be pushed down by transient factors (mental state,
925	sickness, fatigue, sleepiness) without any change in underlying fitness. (PDF pp. 43-44,
926	printed pp. 32-33; developed further at 1.16.3.)
927	
928	**Why it works** — Separating a slow, structural capacity (fitness) from a fast,
929	state-dependent expression of it (preparedness) explains why an athlete's fitness can be
930	objectively unchanged from one day to the next while their measured or perceived output
931	still swings substantially, because the fatigue component is riding on top of a stable
932	base.
933	
934	**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical
935	capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness
936	(day-to-day fluctuation) in the department's own testing philosophy, with both tracked
937	because they answer different questions (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment,"
938	citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7`). **Inference:** that distinction maps
939	closely onto this framework's fitness/preparedness split (fitness ~ the baseline's
940	"preparedness," Verkhoshansky's "preparedness" ~ the baseline's "readiness"), though the
941	two sources use the words differently and neither cites the other; a reader moving between
942	them should track the underlying concept, not the label.
943	
944	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the terminology mismatch matters — do not assume
945	"preparedness" means the same thing in both sources without checking which sense is
946	meant, since Verkhoshansky's "preparedness" is the department's "readiness," not its
947	"preparedness." This entry's own definitions above use Verkhoshansky's terms throughout.
948	
949	**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete whose long-term strength and conditioning markers
950	(fitness/base preparedness) have been stable for weeks can still show a depressed CMJ
951	reading (Verkhoshansky's "instantaneous preparedness," the baseline's "readiness") after
952	poor sleep or travel, without any real loss of underlying capacity.
953	
954	**Related** — [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]].

# Central vs. Peripheral Fatigue, and Low- vs. High-Frequency Fatigue

**What it is** — Fatigue during short-duration strength/power work is split into
**central fatigue** (reduced motivation, impaired spinal nerve transmission, reduced motor
neuron recruitment and firing rate — a CNS-level phenomenon) and **peripheral fatigue**
(failure somewhere in the excitation-contraction chain at the muscle cell itself: motor
end-plate, sarcolemma, T-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, contractile proteins).
Peripheral fatigue further splits into **low-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at <20 Hz
stimulation, from depressed calcium release, recovering slowly over up to 48 hours) and
**high-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at >50 Hz, recovering faster). "Muscle wisdom"
names the CNS's own down-regulation of motor neuron discharge rate during a sustained
maximal contraction, believed to protect against electrical failure and possibly to
postpone central fatigue. Exercise-induced ammonia accumulation is cited as a possible
contributor to central fatigue at high intensities/durations. Intensive CNS activation
(max weights, max power, plyometrics) is stated to need at least 48 hours of recovery if
no restorative methods are used. (PDF pp. 24-27, printed pp. 13-16.)

**Why it works** — Fatigue is not a single process with one cause; the central/peripheral
split and the frequency-dependent split reflect genuinely different physiological
bottlenecks (nervous drive vs. contractile-machinery failure vs. calcium-handling
kinetics), which is why they have different time courses and respond to different
recovery strategies.

**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states intensive CNS activation (max weights, max power,
plyometrics) needs at least 48 hours of recovery if no restorative methods are used (PDF p.
25, printed p. 14). **Inference:** this supports spacing high-CNS-cost sessions (max
strength, high-velocity work) at least two days apart within a microcycle, and treating
"still feels flat two days after a max-effort day" as plausible central fatigue rather than
assuming poor effort or motivation; this specific practical framing is not stated in the
text.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a mechanistic taxonomy from exercise
physiology, not a monitoring protocol. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength
index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen daily readiness marker
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); **Inference:** mRSI is a downstream readiness proxy,
not a direct central/peripheral fatigue assay, so a flat CMJ day should not be
over-attributed to a specific named mechanism (e.g., "low-frequency fatigue") without EMG
or stimulation data — neither source states this equivalence, and this caution is this
entry's own judgment.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete who trained max-effort squats yesterday and shows reduced CMJ
output today is more likely showing central/low-frequency fatigue still resolving than a
loss of underlying strength; retesting 48 hours later is more informative than reacting to
the single depressed value.

**Related** — [[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]].

# Compensatory (Acceleration/Action) Training — Using Proprioceptive Feedback to Actively Manage Bar Speed

**What it is** — Free weights (unlike some variable-resistance machines) let the lifter
feel changing leverage through the range of motion via proprioceptive feedback and respond
by voluntarily accelerating or decelerating the bar to raise or lower the force produced.
This is termed Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT), most obviously used
concentrically, but the text argues it applies just as much eccentrically (muscles
actively resist gravity's acceleration to control the descent) and even isometrically
(the lifter must continuously compensate for fatigue-driven declines in neural drive to
hold a constant position), leading the author to prefer "Compensatory Action Training" as
the fuller name. (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21; Ch 7.1 develops it further.)

**Why it works** — Because force is not fixed by the weight alone (F = ma; a lighter bar
accelerated hard can still produce meaningful force), an athlete who actively drives bar
speed rather than passively moving a fixed load is directly manipulating the training
stimulus at every point in the range of motion, not just at the load's nominal percentage
of 1RM.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this reads as a conceptual ancestor of today's
velocity-based training (VBT) cueing — "move the bar as fast as possible" instructions on
submaximal sets are a modern implementation of the same idea. **Eric's baseline:** Perch
camera-based velocity-based training is part of the department's current technology stack
(`method-baseline.md`, "Data, technology and reporting," citing
`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7`). **Inference:** CAT's proprioceptive-feedback
logic maps onto that existing Perch capability, though neither the book nor the baseline
draws this connection directly. **Inference:** also useful as coaching language for
eccentric-phase control (actively resisting the descent) and isometric holds (actively
maintaining tension); this extension beyond the text's own concentric framing is this
entry's own reading of Verkhoshansky's eccentric/isometric CAT discussion (PDF p. 32,
printed p. 21).

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a technique/cueing concept, not a
load-prescription protocol; it doesn't specify a percentage, velocity target, or rep scheme
on its own in the text. **Inference:** cueing maximal intended acceleration on every rep is
not appropriate for all training goals (e.g., controlled-tempo hypertrophy work
deliberately avoids this); this caveat is not addressed in this section of the text.

**Example** — **Inference:** Coaching "explode the bar up" on a submaximal front squat set is applying
CAT: the athlete voluntarily increases bar acceleration beyond what the load alone would
produce, raising the true training force above the load's nominal value.

# Structural and Functional Determinants of Strength

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky lists the factors that determine how much strength a
muscle group can produce. Structural factors: cross-sectional area of the muscle, density
of fibres per unit cross-section, and mechanical leverage efficiency across the joint.
Functional (neural) factors: number of fibres contracting simultaneously, rate of fibre
contraction, efficiency of firing synchronization, nerve conduction velocity, degree of
inhibition of non-contributing fibres, proportion of large-diameter (fast-twitch) fibres
active, efficiency of cooperation between fibre types, efficiency of stretch reflexes,
excitation threshold of the nerve fibres, and initial muscle length before contraction.
Maximum strength is produced at an optimum, not a maximum, frequency of nerve firing
(Vredensky, via Vorobyev 1978), and that optimal frequency itself shifts with fatigue
level (Kernell & Monster, 1982). Synchronization of motor unit firing across fibres does
not appear to meaningfully increase the rate of strength production; sequencing
(efficient timing) may matter more than simultaneity, especially where stored elastic
energy must be released at the right moment (Miller et al., 1981). (PDF pp. 44-45,
printed pp. 33-34.)

**Why it works** — This is a fuller inventory of why two athletes with the same
cross-sectional muscle area can produce very different force: most of the list is neural
(recruitment, timing, inhibition, reflex efficiency), consistent with this chapter's
overall theme that strength is a neuromuscular, not purely structural, phenomenon.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a longer checklist than
[[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] when explaining to students
or staff (e.g. in HHPR 5355) why hypertrophy alone does not fully predict strength, and
for generating hypotheses about why an athlete with good muscle mass underperforms on
force output (check firing rate, synchronization, initial muscle length/joint angle,
rather than assuming a training-volume problem).

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky notes more research is needed before drawing a
firm conclusion about strength gains from increased motor-unit synchronization (PDF p.
45, printed p. 34); **Inference:** do not treat "improve synchronization" as an
established, targetable training goal on its own — none of these functional factors
listed have a stated field-testable metric in this section.

**Example** — **Inference:** two athletes with similar squat cross-sectional muscle
estimates (e.g. via anthropometrics) but different 1RM outputs are most likely differing
on the functional/neural list (recruitment, firing rate, inhibition), not on structural
factors alone.

[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

# Seven Factors That Limit Strength Production

**What it is** — Strength output in the short and long term is limited by seven
interacting factors: **trainability** (genetic ceiling for hypertrophy, fibre-type
distribution, leverage, and pre-training status); **neuromuscular efficiency** (skill in
recruiting the right muscles accurately and powerfully); **biomechanical efficiency**
(leverage and relative muscle-group strength, trainable unlike raw genetic trainability);
**psychological factors** (motivation, focus, pain tolerance, perceived exertion, coach
influence); **pain and fear of pain** (distinguishing injury pain, a protective signal to
act on, from effort pain, a subjective load-intensity signal usable via an RPE-style
scale); **injury and fear of injury** (reflex inhibition of contraction around a damaged
joint is well documented; return to top performance depends on the athlete's own
perception that rehab is complete, not just medical clearance); and **fatigue** (central
vs. peripheral, discussed further in
[[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]]). (PDF pp. 23-24, printed pp.
12-13.)

**Why it works** — Strength testing and training programs typically control for load,
volume, and technique, but this list makes explicit that psychological state, injury
history, and perceived pain/fear operate as real physiological limiters on force output,
not just "mental" factors layered on top of a physical ceiling — reflex inhibition around
an injured joint is a measurable neuromuscular effect, not a motivation problem.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a checklist when an athlete's force output
underperforms their apparent physical capacity: before assuming a physical/programming
cause, rule out fear of re-injury, unaddressed effort-pain tolerance, or psychological
state. Verkhoshansky states "return to top level performance will occur only if the
athlete perceives rehabilitation to be complete" and the fear of pain or re-injury being
minimal (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13). **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role
in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and
Athletic Medicine's RTP decisions, a support/advisory role rather than a final-decision
role (`method-baseline.md`, "Rehab and return to play," citing
`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6`); that same baseline section is flagged as
"the thinnest discipline in the corpus" with no stated RTP criteria or battery.
**Inference:** Verkhoshansky's fear-of-injury/pain framing is a plausible partial fill for
that documented gap, though neither source states this connection directly.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive taxonomy, not a measurement
protocol; none of these seven factors have a given cutoff or test threshold in this section
of the text (PDF pp. 23-24, printed pp. 12-13). **Inference:** do not use "fear of injury"
as a catch-all explanation without other supporting evidence (movement quality, self-report,
clinical input from Athletic Medicine); reflex inhibition and psychological guarding can
look similar from the outside. This caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in the
text.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete cleared medically after an ACL reconstruction who still shows
reduced force output on the operated leg during testing may be exhibiting reflex inhibition
and/or fear of re-injury, not a residual physical deficit alone; that changes what the
next intervention should target.

**Related** — [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]].

# The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition

**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)

**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure
(not just a qualitative "wave" description), which is what allows taper researchers to ask
a specific, testable question: how much and how recently loaded should training be before
competition to maximize the fitness-minus-fatigue difference at competition time.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the more technical, equation-based underpinning
of this library's already-captured practical rule
([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]); cite this entry when a
more rigorous or quantitative framing is needed (e.g. explaining the model to a sport
scientist or in a research-facing document), and cite the Bompa heuristic for the everyday
coaching rule of thumb. The taper-volume finding directly supports reducing training
volume, not just intensity, in the days immediately before a competition or key testing
date.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific mathematical constants (A, B, T1, T2)
must be fit per individual and per training phase, and the text notes they require
periodic re-estimation; do not treat this as a plug-and-play formula without that
fitting process. The taper studies cited are from the early-to-mid 1990s and largely from
swimming; **Inference:** don't assume the exact taper-volume findings transfer unchanged to
football or other team sports without independent verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** rather than assuming a flat "taper week" cuts intensity but
keeps volume similar, this model's logic and the cited taper research both point toward
deliberately reducing volume (not just easing intensity) in the final days before a key
competition or test date, to let the longer-lasting fitness effect show through as the
shorter fatigue effect clears.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]],
[[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

# Functional vs. Structural Resistance Training

**What it is** — Two basic categories of resistance training effect: structural training
targets muscle hypertrophy (and some tissue flexibility); functional training targets
performance qualities (static strength, speed-strength, muscular endurance, reactive
ability) through four neural mechanisms: (1) intermuscular coordination — sequencing and
synchronizing action between different muscle groups; (2) intramuscular coordination —
control within one muscle via number encoding (how many fibres are recruited), rate
encoding (firing frequency), and pattern encoding (sequencing of fibre types); (3)
facilitatory/inhibitory reflex processes; (4) motor learning, programming the CNS to
execute a specific task. No training is purely structural; all training is functional to
some degree and may also elicit structural change. (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7.)

**Why it works** — Force output for a given movement is the product of both how much
contractile tissue exists (structural) and how effectively the nervous system recruits,
times, and sequences that tissue (functional). Early or stagnation-phase training gets
more return from the functional side because coordination has more room to improve;
structural change is slower and more load-dependent.

**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states functional stages should precede structural
stages both for beginners and during a plateau at an advanced level (PDF p. 19, printed p.
8, cross-referenced to 1.2 and Ch2). **Inference:** this supports using the split as a
diagnostic lens when an athlete's strength stalls: ask whether the limiter is likely
structural (needs more hypertrophy-phase volume) or functional (needs improved
coordination, rate coding, or motor learning of the specific lift/skill); this diagnostic
framing is this entry's own extension, not stated as a test procedure in the text.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a conceptual split, not a measured
diagnostic; number, rate, and pattern encoding are not directly observable from a force
plate or barbell velocity alone, so inferring which mechanism is limiting a given athlete
is coach judgment, not a test result. Verkhoshansky's use of "functional training" here
means neural coordination and recruitment specifically (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7);
**Inference:** don't confuse it with the modern commercial-gym use of the same term
(balance boards, unstable surfaces), which is a different, later usage the text does not
address.

**Example** — **Inference:** A lifter whose 1RM is stagnant despite visible muscle gain may be limited by
intermuscular coordination (poor bracing/synchronization under heavy load) rather than by
insufficient muscle; technique and coordination work, not more volume, is the higher-value
fix.

**Related** — [[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]].

# Skilled Movement Depends on the Kinaesthetic System, and Is Shaped by Mental Rehearsal Before It Starts

**What it is** — Skilled movement relies on the kinaesthetic sense, built from four
subsystems: joint receptors (joint angle and rate of change), muscle spindles (muscle
length and tension), the Golgi tendon apparatus (tension monitoring, protects against
excessive loading by reducing tension past a critical value), and the vestibular apparatus
(head/body position, velocity, acceleration), plus touch and pain receptors.
Proprioception is described as second only to pain in producing the most intense and
widespread brain electrical activity. Separately, research (Evarts 1973, 1979; Siff 1977)
found that the motor cortex, cerebellum, and basal ganglia all become active before a
movement begins, not merely in response to it as classically assumed; a specific 9 Hz "mu
rhythm" brain pattern is blocked in advance of movement. The cerebellum corrects and
reorganizes motor commands before they reach the muscles (feedforward control) and can
coordinate movement even without peripheral feedback; the motor cortex governs the amount
and pattern of muscular contraction. Russian training practice uses visualization (watching
film of top athletes/coaches, mental rehearsal) and autogenic training (imagining the full
sensory and emotional experience of competition, sometimes monitored with ECG/EMG/GSR) to
exploit this pre-movement brain activity. (PDF pp. 81-83, printed pp. 70-72.)

**Why it works** — Because motor planning measurably begins before the muscles act,
rehearsing a movement mentally (with vivid sensory and emotional detail) engages some of
the same preparatory neural circuitry as physically performing it, giving visualization a
plausible mechanism beyond simple relaxation or confidence-building.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports including structured visualization/mental
rehearsal as a real training tool, not just a "soft skill," for technical rehearsal (e.g.
before a max-effort lift or a technical skill) and pre-competition routines. Also useful
teaching framework for explaining to athletes and students (e.g. HHPR 5355) why
proprioceptive/joint-position training (balance, landing mechanics, reactive drills) is
foundational to skill, not a separate "prehab" category.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** visualization/autogenic training is presented here
as a supplement integrated with physical practice, not a substitute for it; the text does
not claim mental rehearsal alone produces motor learning without physical repetition. The
detailed neuroanatomical claims (specific roles of basal ganglia vs. cerebellum, the mu
rhythm) are cited to 1970s research and should be treated as illustrative of the general
feedforward principle rather than as current, precise neuroscience.

**Example** — **Inference:** having an athlete mentally rehearse a technical lift or a
competition scenario in vivid sensory detail before attempting it live is a direct,
practical application of this feedforward research, not just a motivational exercise.

**Related** — [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]].

# Precise Muscle-Action Terminology: Why "Isotonic" and "Isokinetic" Are Usually Wrong

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky argues most everyday strength-training terms are
technically imprecise. Concentric: proximal and distal muscle attachments move toward one
another. Eccentric: they move apart (not literally a "contraction," despite the common
name — the muscle is returning toward resting length under load). Isometric: attachments
don't move relative to each other (joint angle constant); more accurately called "static."
"Isotonic" (constant tension) is argued to be almost never actually true during real joint
movement, since tension changes with acceleration, deceleration, and reflex activation
throughout a range; European and Russian scientists prefer "auxotonic" (changing tension
and length) or "allodynamic" instead. "Isokinetic" (constant velocity) is also argued to
be physically impossible over a full range, since starting from and returning to rest
requires acceleration; isokinetic devices are more accurately "quasi-isokinetic," and
isokinetic-machine torque output is typically much lower than isometric torque at the same
joint angle. "Quasi-isometric" action is defined separately: the slow, near-static muscle
action seen in heavy, near-maximal resistance training performed anywhere across a joint's
range (not fixed at one angle like true isometrics), relevant to maximal strength,
hypertrophy, and active flexibility training rather than power or speed. (PDF pp. 60-64,
printed pp. 49-53.)

**Why it works** — Real joint movement always involves changing acceleration
(Newton's laws), so any term implying a truly constant mechanical variable throughout a
full range is describing an idealization, not the actual muscle physics; the more precise
terms track what is actually held constant and where.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when interpreting or reporting isokinetic
dynamometer data (if used by Athletic Medicine or research collaborators): understand that
the constant-velocity claim applies only to the device's controlled range, not to the
underlying muscle action, and that isokinetic torque values are not directly comparable to
isometric (e.g. IMTP) values at the same joint angle. Also useful coaching-language
precision: heavy squat/bench-style lifting performed slowly is "quasi-isometric," a
distinct quality from true fixed-angle isometrics like the IMTP.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a terminology-precision argument, not a
claim that isokinetic or isotonic training methods are ineffective; the critique is about
what the words accurately describe, not about training value. Don't over-correct common
usage in casual coaching communication where the imprecise terms are well understood by
convention.

**Example** — **Inference:** describing an IMTP as "isometric" (fixed joint angle) versus
a slow, heavy back squat as "quasi-isometric" (near-static but occurring across a range)
keeps clear which type of force-plate or barbell data is actually comparable to which.

**Related** — [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]].

# Table 1.1 — Resistance Training Prescription by Goal (Strength, Power, Hypertrophy, Endurance)

**What it is** — A dynamic (non-isometric) resistance-training prescription chart by
goal (PDF p. 22, printed p. 11):

| Variable | Strength | Power | Hypertrophy | Endurance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Load (% 1RM) | 80-100 | 70-100 | 60-80 | 40-60 |
| Reps/set | 1-5 | 1-5 | 8-15 | 25-60 |
| Sets/exercise | 4-7 | 3-5 | 4-8 | 2-4 |
| Rest between sets | 2-6 min | 2-6 min | 2-5 min | 1-2 min |
| Duration/set | 5-10 s | 4-8 s | 20-60 s | 80-150 s |
| Speed/rep (% max) | 60-100 | 90-100 | 60-90 | 60-80 |
| Sessions/week | 3-6 | 3-6 | 5-7 | 8-14 |

High-volume, low-resistance work is called an **extensive** method (an
**extensification/accumulation** phase); low-volume, high-intensity work is an
**intensive** method (an **intensification** phase). Early training typically opens with
an extensive phase before progressing to an intensive one; periodization is described as
cyclically alternating these two phase types.

**Why it works** — Each goal loads the neuromuscular and metabolic systems differently:
near-maximal loads at low reps bias neural recruitment and force capacity (strength);
high-velocity submaximal loads bias rate of force development (power); moderate loads at
moderate-to-high volume bias metabolic and mechanical stress for hypertrophy; light loads
at very high reps bias oxidative/metabolic endurance.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a first-pass, generic reference when scoping a
new program's load/volume targets by goal, and as shared vocabulary for extensive/intensive
phase naming. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches undulating/non-linear
periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week, stated as the
personally preferred model over strict linear progression (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength
and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26`). **Inference:** that
undulating model and this text's extensive/intensive phase language describe related but
not identical ideas (wave-to-wave volume change vs. phase-to-phase intensity change); the
baseline material does not cite Verkhoshansky's specific terminology.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states this chart is "adequate for the average
personal trainer or coach dealing with the average client or lower level athlete" but
incomplete for advanced athletes: it ignores strength-speed, explosive strength,
flexibility-strength, and strength-endurance as separate qualities (PDF p. 22, printed p.
11), and ignores the other prescription variables covered in
[[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]] and later chapters. **Inference:** do
not use this table as a complete program design tool for a well-trained collegiate
athlete; treat it as a starting reference, not an endpoint.

**Example** — **Inference:** Blocking out approximate set/rep/load ranges for a new hypertrophy-emphasis
mesocycle (60-80% 1RM, 8-15 reps, 4-8 sets) before layering in the athlete-specific
adjustments the text says this table omits.

# The S-Factors Pyramidal Model of Fitness (Strength, Speed, Stamina, Suppleness, Skill, Structure, Spirit)

**What it is** — A comprehensive model of fitness built from seven "S-factors": Strength,
Speed, Stamina (systemic or local muscular endurance), Suppleness (flexibility), Skill
(neuromuscular efficiency, including a "Style" sub-quality — an individual's manner of
expressing a skill), Structure (somatotype, size, shape), and Spirit (psychological
preparedness). The model is built in two stages: a triangular base relating strength,
stamina, speed, and suppleness, then a pyramid adding skill/neuromuscular control as the
process that makes all movement possible, with flexibility placed at the center of the
base because range of movement underlies expression of every other quality. From the
pairwise relationships between factors, an extended list of compound fitness qualities is
derived: static/dynamic strength and strength-endurance, strength-speed, speed-strength,
strength-speed endurance, speed, endurance, flexibility-strength, flexibility-endurance,
flexibility-speed, skill, strength-skill, flexibility-skill, speed-skill, and
skill-endurance. Relative versions of these qualities (per unit bodymass) matter
separately in sports where bodymass is constrained (e.g. weight-class sports). (PDF pp.
102-103, printed pp. 91-92.)

**Why it works** — Rather than treating strength, speed, endurance, and flexibility as
four independent boxes, this model treats them as vertices whose pairwise and triple
combinations describe most of the specific fitness qualities that actually appear in
sport (e.g. "speed-strength" and "strength-speed" as two distinct qualities depending on
which end of the force-velocity spectrum dominates, already discussed in
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]), with skill/
neuromuscular control cutting across all of them.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a master vocabulary/reference when precisely
naming which quality a given test or exercise targets (e.g. distinguishing
"strength-speed" training from "speed-strength" training, or "flexibility-strength" from
plain flexibility), and as a teaching framework (e.g. HHPR 5355) for showing students why
"fitness" is not one thing to test or train, but a structured set of specific,
combinable qualities.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky himself calls this model "representational or
descriptive rather than scientifically analytical" and notes it is complicated by other
factors such as quasi-isometric states at very slow speeds (PDF p. 102, printed p. 91);
**Inference:** don't treat it as a validated measurement taxonomy with defined tests for
each named compound quality — most of these terms (e.g. "flexibility-skill") have no
standard test attached in this text.

**Example** — **Inference:** describing an athlete's need as "relative strength-speed"
(power per unit bodymass) rather than just "power" gives a program design target that is
precise about both the force-velocity region and the bodymass constraint, useful for a
weight-class or position-limited athlete.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]],
[[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]].

# Sarcomere Hypertrophy (Functional) vs. Sarcoplasmic Hypertrophy (Non-Functional)

**What it is** — Two distinct types of muscle hypertrophy are described. Sarcomere
hypertrophy: an increase in the size and number of sarcomeres within myofibrils; when
added in parallel (not just in series) this increases the muscle's cross-sectional density
of contractile tissue and produces a real increase in strength. Sarcoplasmic hypertrophy:
an increase in the volume of non-contractile protein and semifluid plasma between fibres;
cross-sectional area increases, but the density of contractile tissue per unit area
decreases, with no corresponding strength increase. Except in sports where added bodymass
itself matters (bodybuilding, sumo), sarcomere hypertrophy is described as far more
important for athletic performance. Longer, more strenuous submaximal loading (not rapid,
near-maximal, low-repetition loading like Olympic weightlifting) is associated with more
sarcoplasmic and less sarcomere hypertrophy; high-repetition, moderate-resistance training
(bodybuilding/circuit-style) can also make fast-twitch fibres behave more like slow-twitch
fibres. (PDF pp. 77-78, printed pp. 66-67.)

**Why it works** — The two hypertrophy types build different cellular components (more
contractile machinery per fibre vs. more non-contractile fluid/protein volume around
existing machinery), so they produce different ratios of size gain to strength gain
depending on the loading style that stimulated them.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant to explaining why an athlete can add
measurable muscle mass/girth from high-volume, moderate-load training without a
proportionate strength increase, and why weightlifting-style low-rep, high-intensity work
is more strength-efficient per unit of added mass than bodybuilding-style volume training.
Useful framing for a strength coach deciding whether a hypertrophy block should be
biased toward heavier, lower-rep work (sarcomere-biased) or higher-volume work
(sarcoplasm-biased), depending on whether the goal is functional strength or added bodymass
for a specific position.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the exact biochemical trigger for hypertrophy is
stated in the text as not fully known, and this sarcomere/sarcoplasm distinction, while
still commonly discussed, has not been definitively confirmed by direct human
biopsy/histology consensus in the broader literature since; treat it as a useful coaching
model, not a settled biochemical fact, and don't claim a specific training protocol
produces "only" one type of hypertrophy in isolation.

**Example** — **Inference:** a lineman training for added mass and positional strength
might justifiably include both rep ranges, but should not assume high-rep hypertrophy
volume alone will translate proportionally into functional strength gains without
lower-rep, higher-intensity work also present in the program.

**Related** — [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]].

# The Muscle Model: Series Elastic Component (SEC) vs. Parallel Elastic Component (PEC)

**What it is** — A mechanical model of muscle (Levin & Wyman, 1927) treats it as a
contractile component in series with a Series Elastic Component (SEC: tendon,
cross-bridges, myofilaments, titin, Z-discs) and in parallel with a Parallel Elastic
Component (PEC: sarcolemma, rest-state cross-bridging, surrounding sheaths). The PEC
carries the force of a relaxed muscle stretched beyond resting length, and stores little
usable energy; the SEC is tensioned by an actively contracting muscle resisting a rapid
stretch, and stores considerable elastic energy — this is the mechanism plyometric/shock
training exploits. Slow-twitch (ST) dominant muscle shows smaller mechanical strain when
stretched while contracted but has a stiffer, more elastic SEC than fast-twitch
(FT)-dominant muscle, largely due to higher collagen concentration in slow muscle; FT
fibres store more elastic energy overall. Static/relaxed/passive stretching mainly loads
the PEC; tensed/active stretching (and PNF techniques) load both the SEC and PEC. (PDF
pp. 51-52, printed pp. 40-41.)

**Why it works** — Distinguishing which structure (PEC vs. SEC) is under tension during a
given stretch or contraction condition explains why different stretching methods (static
passive vs. active/PNF) target different tissue, and why fast, elastic-energy-storing
tissue (SEC-dominant, FT-rich muscle) behaves differently under rapid loading than slow,
postural (ST-rich, PEC/collagen-dominant) muscle.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for explaining why plyometric/reactive-strength
training targets the SEC specifically (rapid stretch under active contraction) rather than
simple static flexibility work (which mostly loads the PEC), and for choosing PNF-style
active stretching when the goal is to influence both components rather than the PEC alone.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the anatomical location of SEC/PEC elements is
explicitly stated as not precisely identified (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41); treat this as a
functional/mechanical model for reasoning about elastic energy, not a literal anatomical
map to test or measure directly in an athlete.

**Example** — **Inference:** a sprinter's calf (fast, elastic, SEC-dominant) and a
postural trunk muscle (slower, stiffer, PEC/collagen-dominant) would, by this model, be
expected to respond differently to the same static-stretch dose, supporting muscle-specific
rather than uniform flexibility prescription.

**Related** — [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

# The Shock Method (Original Russian "Udarnyi Metod"), and Why "Plyometrics" Is a Loose Translation

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky developed the "shock method" (udarnyi metod) as a special
speed-strength training method exploiting connective and elastic tissue's ability to
store and release elastic energy during stretch-shortening of the muscle complex (running,
jumping, throwing, rapid lifting). The rise in concentric strength after rapid "shock"
loading comes from two sources: increased muscle tension from the myotatic (stretch)
reflex, and explosive release of elastic energy stored in connective/elastic tissue during
the eccentric phase. Historically, in the original Russian nomenclature, "pliometric"
referred specifically to eccentric (lengthening) contraction, distinct from "isometric"
(static) and "miometric" (concentric, shortening); the term "plyometrics," as adopted in
the West, has drifted to describe a broader category of jumping drills, many of which do
not reproduce true shock-method characteristics. Verkhoshansky's preferred precise
definition: an eccentric contraction suddenly terminated in an explosive isometric
contraction, producing a powerful myotatic reflex and a rapid extension of the muscle's
passive components, followed by an explosive concentric contraction. (PDF p. 45, printed
p. 34.)

**Why it works** — The stretch-shortening cycle mechanism (reflex potentiation plus
elastic energy return) is well established in modern SSC/plyometric research
independent of this text; this entry's contribution is the terminology history and the
precise mechanical definition, which distinguishes genuine shock-method work from
ordinary jumping drills marketed under the same name.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when auditing whether a program's "plyometric"
exercises actually meet Verkhoshansky's precise definition (a sudden eccentric-to-isometric-
to-concentric sequence) versus being ordinary jump training relabeled; this matters for
predicting whether the intended reactive-strength adaptation is actually being trained.
This library already traces Verkhoshansky's shock-method lineage at a higher level in
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas|The
Soviet Lineage Behind Modern Sprint-Training Ideas]]; that entry credits him with "shock
method (plyometrics)" but does not cover the terminology history or mechanism given here,
so this entry adds a genuinely new angle rather than duplicating it.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not assume every drill called "plyometric" in
current commercial or popular usage (e.g. step-aerobics-style jumping) reproduces the
shock-method mechanism; Verkhoshansky himself notes this drift and recommends "shock
method" or "depth jumps" as the more precise Russian-tradition terms (PDF p. 45, printed
p. 34). This terminology distinction does not itself tell a coach which drills are safe or
appropriate for a given athlete; that is a separate training-age and readiness question.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach programming "plyometrics" for a novice athlete should
check whether the intended exercise involves a true rapid eccentric-to-concentric shock
transition (a depth jump) or is really just a submaximal hop/jump drill; the two carry very
different neuromuscular demands despite sharing the popular label.

**Related** — [[framework--determinants-of-strength-structural-functional]],
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas]]
(reciprocal link recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.6 gives the original
Russian terminology split — isometric/miometric/pliometric — and the precise mechanical
definition of the shock method that this lineage table only names in passing).

# Estimating Strength Deficit by Comparing a Static-Start Jump to a Dip/Countermovement Jump

**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]). True Fmm
requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and risky to test directly. As a
field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from a static, knees-flexed start
(no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a sudden dip (a countermovement
that recruits the stretch reflex and involuntary/reactive contribution). A small
difference between the two jumps suggests the athlete is already recruiting most of their
available force voluntarily, i.e. training should emphasize raw force/strength capacity;
a large difference suggests a bigger untapped reactive/neural reserve, i.e. training
should emphasize "shock" and ballistic (reactive) methods instead. (PDF p. 20, printed
p. 9; the explosive-strength-deficit formalism, Fmax vs. Fmm, is credited to Zatsiorsky,
1995, discussed further via the force-time curve in Ch3.)

**Why it works** — A countermovement recruits the stretch-shortening cycle and a degree
of involuntary reflex potentiation that a static start cannot access; the size of the
resulting performance gap is a rough behavioral index of how much of the athlete's
reactive/neural potential is already expressed voluntarily versus still latent.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks
includes the squat jump (quarter-squat start, static, 3s hold) and the countermovement
jump (x3), among other variants (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`); mRSI from daily CMJ testing is
the department's chosen daily readiness marker (same section, citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). **Inference:** comparing SJ height/output to CMJ
height/output for the same athlete is effectively running this framework's proposed
1993-2009-era proxy with instrumented, repeatable data instead of a stopwatch-and-tape
comparison; neither the book nor the baseline states this equivalence directly. **Inference:**
a small SJ-CMJ gap (or a low CMJ-to-SJ ratio) would, by this framework's logic, suggest
programming should lean toward raw strength/force development, while a large gap would
suggest more reactive-strength/shock-method work (depth jumps, plyometrics); this specific
programming inference is not stated in either source and would need independent
validation before use.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a directional heuristic from Verkhoshansky's text (PDF p.
20, printed p. 9), not a validated cutoff; no threshold percentage is given there for
"small" versus "large" gap. **Inference:** the modern jump-testing literature uses more
specific derived metrics (RSI, mRSI, eccentric utilization ratio) developed independently
of this 1990s framework, and those should be the primary interpretive tool; treat this
entry as a conceptual ancestor, not a replacement. **Inference:** do not use a single
SJ/CMJ comparison on one test day to make a training-emphasis decision; use trended data.
This trending caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in the source text.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete with SJ and CMJ heights within 1-2 cm of each other is a candidate
for a strength-emphasis block; an athlete with a large CMJ advantage over SJ (a high
eccentric utilization ratio) is more likely to respond to reactive/plyometric emphasis.

**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]].

# Types of Maximal Strength (CFmax, TFmax, Fmm, Relative Strength)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) separates "maximum strength" into a
ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)

**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.

**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states the competitive maximum, not the daily training
maximum, should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
**Inference:** this ladder is a useful lens for deciding which measured maximum should
anchor programmed intensity for a given athlete. **Eric's baseline:** the department
prefers VBT-estimated 1RM (Perch) over live 1RM attempts, estimating toward a target mean
velocity rather than forcing a true competitive-maximum attempt in the weight room
(`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`).
**Inference:** that preference is consistent with this framework's logic of anchoring
intensity to a stable maximum rather than a noisy daily one, though the baseline document
does not itself cite Zatsiorsky's TFmax/CFmax terminology.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology and reasoning framework, not a measured
protocol; Fmm requires electrical stimulation or reflex loading, which Verkhoshansky
himself calls impractical (PDF p. 12, printed p. 1). **Inference:** none of these four
maxima are named as routinely and directly measured in Baylor's own documented protocols
(`method-baseline.md`), so this should be treated as a mental model for why training-day
and competition-day 1RMs diverge, not as a set of numbers to test for. Verkhoshansky states
the eccentric > isometric > concentric ordering is a general tendency, not a fixed ratio,
varying by joint angle, velocity, and muscle group (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2, cross-referenced
to 1.2).

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete's best training-day squat (TFmax) is consistently lower than
what they hit in a max-out competition or meet (CFmax); programming off the meet number
rather than a re-tested gym max avoids under-loading the athlete for weeks after a strong
competitive performance.

**Related** — [[claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes]] (the numeric
gaps between these maxima); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
(a practical field proxy for the same voluntary/involuntary gap).

# Work Capacity, Fitness, and Preparedness Are Three Different Things

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) defines three related but distinct
terms. Work capacity is the general ability of the body to produce work of different
intensity and duration using its energy systems. Fitness is the specific ability to use
that work capacity to execute a given task efficiently and safely; it is a slow-changing
state that does not vary meaningfully over a period of days. Preparedness is not stable:
it is the resultant, at any given instant, of the interaction between the slow-changing
fitness component and the fast-changing, opposing effect of exercise-induced fatigue.
"Instantaneous preparedness" can be pushed down by transient factors (mental state,
sickness, fatigue, sleepiness) without any change in underlying fitness. (PDF pp. 43-44,
printed pp. 32-33; developed further at 1.16.3.)

**Why it works** — Separating a slow, structural capacity (fitness) from a fast,
state-dependent expression of it (preparedness) explains why an athlete's fitness can be
objectively unchanged from one day to the next while their measured or perceived output
still swings substantially, because the fatigue component is riding on top of a stable
base.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical
capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness
(day-to-day fluctuation) in the department's own testing philosophy, with both tracked
because they answer different questions (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7`). **Inference:** that distinction maps
closely onto this framework's fitness/preparedness split (fitness ~ the baseline's
"preparedness," Verkhoshansky's "preparedness" ~ the baseline's "readiness"), though the
two sources use the words differently and neither cites the other; a reader moving between
them should track the underlying concept, not the label.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the terminology mismatch matters — do not assume
"preparedness" means the same thing in both sources without checking which sense is
meant, since Verkhoshansky's "preparedness" is the department's "readiness," not its
"preparedness." This entry's own definitions above use Verkhoshansky's terms throughout.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete whose long-term strength and conditioning markers
(fitness/base preparedness) have been stable for weeks can still show a depressed CMJ
reading (Verkhoshansky's "instantaneous preparedness," the baseline's "readiness") after
poor sleep or travel, without any real loss of underlying capacity.

**Related** — [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]].

185	
186	# Strength Deficit Size Points to a Different Training Method
187	
188	**What it is** — If an athlete's strength deficit (see
189	[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]) is large for a given muscle
190	group, the text recommends near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (weightlifting or
191	plyometric methods) or, if very large, Compensatory Activation Training (CAT) with 5-8RM
192	loads. If the deficit is small, it recommends submaximal hypertrophy work (bodybuilding-
193	style loading) followed by maximal efforts against heavy loads. Verkhoshansky's own
194	research is cited as finding the strength deficit increases as external resistance and
195	movement time decrease, meaning it matters most for fast, low-resistance actions such as
196	running, jumping, and throwing, and matters less for slow, high-resistance actions. (PDF
197	p. 21, printed p. 10.)
198	
199	**Why it works** — A large deficit means there is untapped voluntary/neural capacity
200	still available, so training that improves recruitment and rate of activation (max effort
201	or reactive/plyometric methods) has the most room to produce gains. A small deficit means
202	the athlete is already recruiting close to their ceiling voluntarily, so further gains
203	require growing the tissue itself (hypertrophy) before neural methods can express more
204	force.
205	
206	**When to apply** — **Inference:** as a screening question for method selection in
207	explosive/team-sport athletes: for actions with little time to produce force (change of
208	direction, sprint push-off, jump takeoff), a large SJ/CMJ-style deficit would, by this
209	heuristic's logic, point toward reactive-strength and max-effort work over added
210	hypertrophy volume, and a small deficit toward a hypertrophy or general-strength emphasis
211	instead. This specific application to team-sport screening is not stated in the text.
212	
213	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky's Compensatory Activation Training (CAT) with 5-8RM
214	loads (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10) is not a validated modern method name; **Inference:**
215	treat it as historical terminology for near-maximal effort training, not a specific
216	protocol to prescribe as written. **Inference:** do not use this rule to skip hypertrophy
217	work in an athlete simply because their sport is "fast" — the size of the individual's own
218	measured deficit, not the sport category alone, should drive the decision, and no deficit
219	was actually measured with a validated modern tool in this text; this caution is this
220	entry's own judgment.
221	
222	**Example** — **Inference:** A running back with a large gap between static-start and countermovement
223	jump height is a better fit for added reactive/plyometric work in that block; a running
224	back with almost no gap between the two jumps, but comparatively low absolute strength, is
225	a better fit for a strength/hypertrophy emphasis first.
226	
227	**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]],
228	[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]].

242	
243	# The Same Force (F = ma) Produced Different Ways Trains Differently
244	
245	**What it is** — Newton's second law (F = ma) means the same force can be produced with a
246	large mass and small acceleration (powerlifting-style, heavy load), a small mass and large
247	acceleration (many track and field actions), a moderate mass and moderate acceleration
248	(bodybuilding-style hypertrophy training, roughly 8-12 reps), or near-zero acceleration
249	under isometric/isokinetic conditions. Despite equal force output, these methods are
250	argued and shown in practice not to produce the same training effect, because different
251	neural, muscular, and metabolic processes are engaged in each case. (PDF pp. 32-33,
252	printed pp. 21-22.)
253	
254	**Why it works** — Force alone does not specify the movement's velocity, duration, muscle
255	action type, or motor unit recruitment/firing pattern, all of which independently affect
256	the training stimulus; two efforts that reach the same peak force via different mass-
257	acceleration combinations are mechanically equal on that one variable but different on
258	several others that matter physiologically. This is the mechanistic backbone of the
259	general specificity-of-training principle, which is well established independent of this
260	text.
261	
262	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a reasoning check against choosing exercises
263	solely by "how much force does this produce," when the intended adaptation (max strength
264	vs. explosive power vs. hypertrophy vs. isometric endurance) requires matching the
265	mass-acceleration profile, not just the force magnitude, to the target quality. This
266	generalized application is this entry's own extension of the four loading-option
267	comparison (PDF pp. 32-33, printed pp. 21-22).
268	
269	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states isokinetic training (option d, F = k.R)
270	correlates poorly with actual sporting performance despite producing meaningful
271	non-specific strength gains in a lab setting (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22, citing Rosentzweig
272	& Hinson 1972, Ostemig 1986). **Inference:** don't treat isokinetic results as a proxy for
273	how an athlete will perform in ballistic, free-loading sport actions; this specific
274	caution is this entry's own restatement of that finding's practical implication.
275	
276	**Example** — **Inference:** A powerlifting-style heavy squat and an Olympic-style ballistic
277	clean pull can both produce a similar peak force at the bar, but the clean pull's high
278	acceleration under a lighter relative load trains rate of force development and ballistic
279	coordination that the heavy, slow squat does not, and vice versa for maximal-tension
280	adaptation.
281	
282	**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].

296	
297	# The Force-Velocity Relationship, and Why Strength Doesn't Guarantee Speed
298	
299	**What it is** — Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve: velocity of contraction is
300	inversely related to load; large force cannot be produced at very high velocities under
301	constant conditions; heavy strength training shifts the curve upward, particularly in
302	beginners (raising force at all velocities, called training for "strength-speed"); light,
303	high-velocity training shifts the curve's velocity maximum rightward (called training for
304	"speed-strength"). Because power = force x velocity, both shifts raise power, just at
305	different points on the curve. Critically, there is no correlation between an athlete's
306	maximal strength and their maximal velocity — they are described as different motor
307	abilities. (PDF pp. 30-31, printed pp. 19-20; Zatsiorsky & Matveev 1964, Komi 1979,
308	Zatsiorsky 1995.)
309	
310	**Why it works** — The F-V relationship reflects the cross-bridge cycling and motor unit
311	recruitment limits of muscle contraction; it has been confirmed for whole-body sporting
312	movement as well as isolated muscle, and is the direct ancestor of the force-velocity
313	profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others) used in modern sprint and jump testing.
314	
315	**When to apply** — **Inference:** justifies programming that targets a specific region of
316	the force-velocity spectrum rather than assuming "more strength" automatically transfers to
317	speed: heavy-load, low-velocity work develops the force end; light-load, high-velocity
318	(including ballistic/plyometric) work develops the velocity end. **Inference:** usable as
319	the conceptual basis for choosing between a strength-speed or speed-strength emphasis block
320	for an athlete whose limiter has been identified (e.g., via jump testing or sprint
321	force-velocity profiling); this specific screening application is not stated in the text.
322	
323	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't treat "no correlation between max strength and
324	max velocity" (PDF p. 31, printed p. 20) as license to ignore strength training for a
325	speed-limited athlete; a certain strength floor is plausibly still necessary before
326	speed-specific training pays off. **Eric's baseline:** the Vermeil hierarchy of athletic
327	development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill) is
328	repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass" (`method-baseline.md`,
329	"Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10,18-19`).
330	**Inference:** that sequencing is broadly consistent with treating a strength floor as a
331	prerequisite, though neither this text's cited section nor the baseline states the two
332	frameworks are equivalent. Verkhoshansky himself flags the classic hyperbolic F-V curve as
333	not universally accurate: research on the lumbar erector spinae shows a "yielding" drop in
334	force during constant-velocity eccentric stretching that the standard curve doesn't predict
335	(Sutamo & McGill, 1995; PDF p. 30, printed p. 19) — the model is a strong generalization,
336	not a universal law for every muscle group.
337	
338	**Example** — **Inference:** Two athletes with equal back squat 1RM (similar max force) can have very
339	different unloaded sprint speeds; that gap is F-V curve position, not raw strength, and
340	argues for velocity-end training (sprint work, light-load ballistics) rather than more
341	heavy squatting to close it.
342	
343	**Related** — [[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]],
344	[[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]].

358	
359	# Strength Increase Is Initiated by Neuromuscular Stimulation, Not Muscle Size
360	
361	**What it is** — "The fundamental principle of strength training... is that all strength
362	increase is initiated by neuromuscular stimulation." Strength is framed as a function of
363	how powerfully and efficiently muscle is activated by the nervous system first, with
364	hypertrophy as a downstream, longer-term structural consequence of a given stimulus
365	regime, not the driver of early gains. (PDF pp. 17-18, printed pp. 6-7.)
366	
367	**Why it works** — Hypertrophy is a slow structural adaptation; force output can rise
368	well before meaningful cross-sectional area change through improved recruitment,
369	firing rate, and coordination of the muscle already present. This is one of the more
370	independently replicated findings in strength physiology outside this text (early-phase
371	strength gains preceding measurable hypertrophy is a standard finding in resistance
372	training research), which is why this entry is rated `proven` rather than `supported`
373	despite the book being the citation vehicle here.
374	
375	**When to apply** — **Inference:** this principle explains early-training-block strength
376	gains in novice athletes that outpace any visible muscle growth. **Eric's baseline:**
377	Tracy Fober's "use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer" standard prioritizes
378	movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM
379	numbers, especially early in a training cycle (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power,"
380	citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21`; `week1-lecture.md p.46`).
381	**Inference:** that coaching standard is consistent with this principle's emphasis on
382	coordination before load, though the baseline material does not itself cite the
383	neuromuscular-primacy mechanism. **Inference:** the same logic likely explains why
384	detraining strength loss can outpace measurable muscle loss (neural efficiency degrading
385	faster than tissue), though this text does not state that extension explicitly.
386	
387	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states maximal strength "depends to a great extent"
388	on adequate muscle cross-section (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7), so hypertrophy is not
389	unimportant at higher training ages. **Inference:** this principle should not be used to
390	justify skipping hypertrophy-phase work for athletes past the early-adaptation window,
391	where structural gains matter more for continued strength progress; this caution is not
392	stated in the text itself.
393	
394	**Example** — **Inference:** A freshman who has never lifted seriously often adds meaningful strength in
395	the first 4-6 weeks of a program with little visible size change; that gain is
396	predominantly neural (coordination, recruitment, reduced antagonist co-contraction), not
397	tissue growth.
398	
399	**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] (the
400	mechanisms by which this happens).
