414	
415	# Rate of Force (or Tension) Development Is a Separate Limiter from Maximal Force
416	
417	**What it is** — Sporting performance does not depend simply on the ability to produce
418	maximum force, because many sporting actions happen too fast to recruit an adequate
419	number of muscle fibres in the available time. Rate of Force Development (RFD) / Rate of
420	Tension Development (RTD) — how quickly force rises, not just its ceiling — is named as an
421	independently important limiter, worth assessing on its own alongside maximal-force
422	deficits. (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10; cross-referenced to 2.2.1 for more detail.)
423	
424	**Why it works** — Many athletic actions (sprint ground contact, jump takeoff, change of
425	direction) last far less time than it takes to reach true maximal voluntary force. An
426	athlete can have high 1RM strength but a slow force-time curve, and still underperform in
427	short-duration actions, because the task ends before peak force is reached. This
428	distinction (peak force vs. rate of rise to a sub-maximal time point) is well established
429	in modern force-time curve analysis, independent of this text.
430	
431	**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** force-plate metric selection follows the
432	Output/Driver/Strategy/Fluffy (ODSF) framework, picking 1-2 output metrics, 1-3 driver
433	metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force), and 1-3 strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations)
434	rather than reporting peak values alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
435	neuromuscular monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`, credited to Hawkin Dynamics, not
436	Eric's own framework). **Inference:** this principle's force-vs-rate distinction supports
437	that driver-metric emphasis and argues for testing and reporting RFD-type variables
438	separately from 1RM or peak-force values, especially for athletes in short-ground-contact
439	positions; this specific link between the ODSF framework and Verkhoshansky's RFD argument
440	is not stated in either source.
441	
442	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states RFD/RTD deficits are developed further in
443	later chapters on strength-speed and explosive strength (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10,
444	cross-referenced to Ch3, Ch5), implying the two qualities are trainable somewhat
445	independently. **Inference:** don't substitute a single RFD number for the full force-time
446	curve when the movement or time window matters (RFD at 0-50ms is a different quality than
447	RFD at 100-200ms); this time-window caution is this entry's own addition, not stated in
448	this section of the text.
449	
450	**Example** — **Inference:** Two athletes with the same back squat 1RM can produce very different sprint
451	starts if one reaches a given force threshold in 100ms and the other takes 200ms; testing
452	and training that difference requires RFD-sensitive measures, not another max-strength
453	test.
454	
455	**Related** — [[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]].

469	
470	# A Short Transition (Amortization) Between Stretch and Shortening Preserves Stored Elastic Energy
471	
472	**What it is** — Actin-myosin cross-bridges have a limited lifetime, 15-120 milliseconds
473	(Edman et al., 1978). For stored elastic energy from a stretch to be used in the
474	following concentric contraction, the transition period between the end of the eccentric
475	(stretch) phase and the start of the concentric (shortening) phase must be brief; a longer
476	delay lets cross-bridges detach and the elastic potential dissipates as slippage rather
477	than being used for work. A greater velocity of stretch during the eccentric phase also
478	increases elastic energy storage (Rack & Westbury, 1974). Much of the extra positive work
479	seen in rapid eccentric-concentric (plyometric) actions is attributed to this stored
480	elastic energy plus a separate pre-loading/pre-stretch effect (tension at the start of the
481	concentric phase is already elevated by the preceding stretch). Tendon-based elastic energy
482	storage during locomotion largely happens via near-isometric muscle contraction with
483	minimal muscle fibre length change, which is also more metabolically efficient than
484	dynamic contraction. (PDF pp. 55-56, printed pp. 44-45.)
485	
486	**Why it works** — The cross-bridge attachment window is a hard physiological time
487	constraint; the mechanics of elastic energy return depend on catching that window, which
488	is why a fast stretch-to-shorten transition (a short "amortization phase," in later
489	plyometrics terminology) is functionally different from a slow, paused transition even if
490	the stretch magnitude is identical.
491	
492	**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the underlying mechanism behind coaching cues
493	for minimizing ground-contact/amortization time in plyometric and reactive-strength work
494	(depth jumps, bounds, sprint ground contacts), and behind why reactive strength index
495	(RSI/mRSI, already the department's chosen daily readiness marker) is sensitive to contact
496	time as well as jump height — a longer amortization phase indicates the athlete is not
497	capturing the SSC benefit this mechanism describes.
498	
499	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the cited cross-bridge lifetime range (15-120ms) is
500	a cellular-level parameter, not a directly coachable or measurable field variable; do not
501	try to cue an athlete toward a specific millisecond target. Use it as the "why" behind a
502	qualitative cue (minimize ground contact time, avoid pausing at the bottom of a jump), not
503	as a number to program.
504	
505	**Example** — **Inference:** cueing an athlete to "spend as little time on the ground as
506	possible" during a depth jump, rather than pausing briefly before jumping, is a practical
507	application of keeping the stretch-to-shorten transition inside the cross-bridge
508	attachment window.
509	
510	**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]],
511	[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]].

525	
526	# Strength Training Adapts Along (at Least) Ten Independent, Narrow Dimensions
527	
528	**What it is** — Strength gains transfer narrowly, not generally, across at least ten
529	independent dimensions: type of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region/range of
530	movement, velocity of movement, force of contraction, muscle fibre recruitment,
531	metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility, and fatigue. Training that improves one
532	dimension often produces little or no improvement on the others, even when the same
533	muscle groups are involved. Specificity is explicitly distinguished from simulation:
534	mimicking a sport movement with added resistance is not the same as training the specific
535	factors above, and can actually distort the neuromuscular programming needed for the real
536	skill because of changes in center of gravity, moment of inertia, and mechanical
537	stiffness introduced by the resistance. (PDF pp. 38-39, printed pp. 27-28.)
538	
539	**Why it works** — Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
540	muscular systems together (see
541	[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
542	demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
543	recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
544	any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
545	adaptation. This is one of the more broadly replicated findings in strength and
546	conditioning research, independent of this text.
547	
548	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a master reasoning check before assuming an
549	exercise "transfers" to a sport skill: ask which of the ten dimensions the exercise
550	actually matches, not just whether it uses similar muscles. **Eric's baseline:** the
551	Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of
552	movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production,
553	and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise transfers, and
554	is taught in HHPR 5355 (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
555	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`, `week1-lecture.md p.34`). **Inference:**
556	Dynamic Correspondence (this book's Ch4.3, not yet ingested) is plausibly the applied
557	extension of this same ten-dimension specificity logic to exercise selection, though this
558	chapter does not itself state that link.
559	
560	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't use "specificity" as an argument against any
561	general preparation work; this book's own 1.1 material and this library's Bompa
562	multilateral/LTAD entries support building a general base before narrowing to sport-specific
563	work. This principle governs which dimensions transfer, not whether general work has value
564	at an earlier training age; that distinction is this entry's own reading, not stated as
565	such in this passage of the text.
566	
567	**Example** — **Inference:** Heavy squat strength does not automatically transfer to high-velocity sprint
568	force production (different point on the velocity dimension) even though both use similar
569	musculature; each needs its own specific training exposure.
570	
571	**Related** — [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]],
572	[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]].

586	
587	# Strength Expression Depends on Torque Management, Not Just Load
588	
589	**What it is** — Torque (force times the perpendicular distance from the force's line of
590	action to the joint fulcrum) determines effective loading on a joint, independent of the
591	absolute weight lifted. Bringing a load closer to a joint reduces the torque at that
592	joint for the same weight: flexing the elbows reduces shoulder torque during dumbbell
593	raises/flyes/bench press; keeping a bar close to the body during the clean or deadlift
594	reduces torque at the lumbar spine and hips, allowing a heavier load to be lifted more
595	safely. Swinging the bar away from the body during a snatch pull, or a javelin away from
596	the shoulder during wind-up, are cited as inefficient uses of torque. (PDF pp. 28-29,
597	printed pp. 17-18.)
598	
599	**Why it works** — Torque = force x moment arm; for a fixed external force (a given
600	weight), shortening the moment arm directly lowers the rotational demand on the joint,
601	which is standard, independently-established biomechanics, not specific to this text.
602	
603	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a coaching cue and technical-fault-diagnosis
604	tool for any lift where the bar or load can drift away from the body's midline (clean,
605	snatch, deadlift, overhead press) or away from a joint (dumbbell raises, flyes); keeping
606	the load's path close to the relevant joint is both a safety cue and a load-capacity cue.
607	This general coaching application is this entry's own extension of Verkhoshansky's
608	worked examples (PDF pp. 28-29, printed pp. 17-18).
609	
610	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a mechanical principle about joint
611	loading, not a complete safety framework; it does not account for tissue tolerance,
612	technique proficiency, or fatigue-related form breakdown on its own, and the text does
613	not claim that it does. **Inference:** reducing joint torque is not always desirable if
614	the goal is specifically to overload that joint's musculature for rehabilitation purposes
615	(e.g., some hip- or shoulder-isolation rehab work intentionally increases moment arm at a
616	target joint under controlled load); this rehab caveat is not addressed in this section of
617	the text.
618	
619	**Example** — **Inference:** Cueing an athlete to keep the bar against the shins and thighs during a
620	clean pull, rather than swinging it forward, reduces lumbar torque for the same bar
621	weight and is both a technique and a load-management fix.
622	
623	**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].

637	
638	# All Dynamic Movement Is Triphasic: Isometric, Then Concentric/Eccentric, Then Isometric Again
639	
640	**What it is** — Classifying muscle action as simply "static" (isometric) or "dynamic"
641	(concentric/eccentric) is described as an oversimplification. Every dynamic action must
642	begin from an isometric phase (the muscle must first develop enough tension to
643	counterbalance the load before any movement starts: concentric if tension exceeds the
644	load, eccentric if it doesn't), and every movement ends in another isometric phase before
645	reversing or stopping, because Newton's laws require the system to momentarily come to
646	rest at a direction change. In ballistic/ fast movement, the transition isometric phase is
647	very brief; in slow maximal efforts (e.g. a powerlifting squat or bench), it can be much
648	longer. The brief isometric phase in a plyometric movement is specifically termed
649	"explosive isometric" action and is central to speed-strength training and movements like
650	the weightlifting jerk, shot put, and high jump. Movement termination/reversal can also
651	involve any combination of agonist eccentric or isometric action, antagonist concentric or
652	isometric action, stabilizer action at the joint or nearby joints, and passive connective-
653	tissue damping — not simply "antagonist opposes agonist" as popular descriptions suggest.
654	(PDF pp. 65-66, printed pp. 54-55.)
655	
656	**Why it works** — This follows directly from Newtonian mechanics (a moving system must
657	have zero velocity at the instant it reverses direction) combined with the physiological
658	fact that muscle tension must build before it can move a load; the "explosive isometric"
659	phase is the same brief coupling window discussed in
660	[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]], described here from the
661	whole-joint-action perspective rather than the cross-bridge perspective.
662	
663	**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces that "isometric strength" is not a separate,
664	niche quality but a phase present in every dynamic lift and sprint/jump action, which
665	supports including isometric testing (IMTP) and isometric-emphasis training as directly
666	relevant to dynamic performance, not a side quality. Also a caution for kinesiology
667	teaching (e.g. HHPR 5355): movement termination is not simply "antagonist stops agonist";
668	several structures can share that role, so a simplistic agonist/antagonist explanation for
669	a given movement's braking phase may be incomplete.
670	
671	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky himself notes inappropriate antagonist activation
672	opposing a strongly contracting agonist is a recognized injury mechanism (e.g. hamstrings
673	rupturing when they fire to oppose the quadriceps during sprinting or kicking, PDF p. 60,
674	printed p. 49); **Inference:** this triphasic framework describes normal, coordinated
675	movement termination, and should not be conflated with that pathological
676	premature-antagonist-activation injury pattern, which is a distinct, unwanted phenomenon
677	rather than part of the normal triphasic sequence.
678	
679	**Example** — **Inference:** a sprinter's ground-contact phase is not purely
680	"eccentric-then-concentric"; it necessarily includes the brief isometric coupling phase
681	this principle describes, which is the same window where the reactive-strength/elastic
682	mechanism in [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]] operates.
683	
684	**Related** — [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]],
685	[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]].

# Deeper Knee Flexion Reduces "Shock" Loading; Fibre-Type Mix Should Guide Jump Tempo

**What it is** — Two related findings on individualizing plyometric prescription.
(1) Soft-tissue spring stiffness around the knee drops sharply with flexion angle
(Greene & McMahon, cited PDF p. 58, printed p. 47: roughly 120 kN/m at 0 degrees down to
30 kN/m at 75 degrees), so the Series Elastic Component's contribution falls as knee
flexion increases, meaning deeper-flexion landings reduce the "shock" character of a
plyometric exercise. (2) Vertical jump testing found rapid, short-range stretch phases
were most beneficial for the vastus medialis (fast-twitch-rich), while knee extensors of
athletes with more slow-twitch fibres (e.g. distance runners) benefited more from slower,
larger-amplitude jumps with a longer transition between stretch and shortening (Bosco et
al., 1982), attributed to differing cross-bridge lifetimes between fibre types. (PDF pp.
57-58, printed pp. 46-47.)

**Why it works** — Both findings trace back to the same underlying mechanics: SEC
contribution and cross-bridge dynamics vary with joint angle and fibre-type composition,
so a jump protocol that is optimal for one joint angle or one athlete's fibre profile is
not automatically optimal for another.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports limiting knee flexion depth in depth-jump and
shock-method work specifically when the goal is maximal elastic/reactive loading (deeper
flexion shifts the exercise toward general strength/power rather than true "shock"
stimulus), and supports considering an athlete's likely fibre-type profile (position,
event, or direct biopsy/proxy data if available) when choosing fast-short vs.
slow-larger-amplitude jump variants.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** fibre-type composition is rarely measured directly
in a collegiate athletics setting; do not treat sport or position alone as a reliable proxy
without other supporting evidence (this entry's application to specific positions is its
own inference, not stated in the text). The specific stiffness values (120 kN/m to 30
kN/m) come from one biomechanics study on a flexible-board bouncing task, not from a
depth-jump or standard field-testing setup, so treat them as illustrative of the trend
rather than as target numbers.

**Example** — **Inference:** a shallow-knee-flexion, low-amplitude rebound drill better
targets true reactive/shock adaptation than a deep-squat-style jump, which behaves more
like a general power exercise; a distance-oriented athlete may respond better to a slightly
slower, larger-amplitude jump variant than a power-position athlete.

**Related** — [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]],
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].
######## heuristic--plan-variation-to-avoid-restrictive-neural-patterns.md
---
type: library-entry

confidence: contested

# Restrictive, Repetitive Patterns May Overspecialize the Nervous System

**What it is** — Drawing on neuroplasticity research (Rosenzweig, Diamond, Greenough,
cortical reorganization in amputees and stroke patients), the text argues the nervous
system rewires quickly (within minutes, not years) around whatever movement pattern is
repeated, and lists practical inferences: avoid machines that restrict joint movement to
one plane/pattern (they can reprogram the brain toward that restricted pattern and reduce
sport-specific capability); avoid over-reliance on ergogenic devices (lifting belts, wrist
wraps, shoe wedges) that can make efficient unassisted movement harder later; favor
planned variation of means, methods, and exercises over fixed repetition of the same
weights or machines; respect individual movement style rather than forcing one stereotyped
technique on every athlete. (PDF pp. 19-20, printed pp. 8-9.)

**Why it works** — The underlying neuroscience (adult cortical plasticity, rapid synaptic
change, constraint-induced reorganization in rehab patients) is well established. The
extension to healthy-athlete strength training — that machine use or ergogenic aids will
measurably "reprogram" sport-specific neural patterns — is the text's own inference, not a
finding directly tested in athletes in this section.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this can be used as a rationale for favoring
free-weight, multi-planar, compound movement over single-joint machine work when the goal
is direct transfer to a sport skill, and for planning intentional exercise variation
across a training block rather than running the same fixed machine circuit indefinitely.
**Eric's baseline:** the department teaches "knowledge from experience" as an operating
value: keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything
advanced, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work
(`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy and decision principles," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5`, `week1-lecture.md p.12`). **Inference:**
that basic-movement-first philosophy is broadly consistent with this heuristic's caution
about restrictive machine patterns, though the baseline material does not itself cite a
neuroplasticity mechanism or single out machines specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this should be treated as contested where it
implies routine machine use or belts during max lifts causes lasting neural harm to sport
skill; the text (PDF pp. 19-20, printed pp. 8-9) gives no dose-response evidence for that
extension, and machines and supportive equipment remain standard tools in most strength
programs with no established injury or transfer cost at typical use levels documented
anywhere in this ingest. **Inference:** do not use this heuristic to argue against belts
for heavy compound lifts, where the safety benefit is well established elsewhere and not
addressed by this section of the text at all.

**Example** — **Inference:** Programming a hip-thrust machine as the sole posterior-chain exercise for a
sprinter, with no free-weight hip hinge or sprint-pattern work anywhere in the week, is the
scenario this heuristic warns against; it does not warn against occasional supported
machine use as part of a varied program.

**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]].
######## heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: heuristic

topic: training age and program complexity
category: [programming, training-age, individualization]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26

# Beginners Respond to Load Alone; Advanced Athletes Need the Full Variable Set

**What it is** — Load, reps, and sets are described as the traditional core variables of a
weight program, but the text lists a much longer set of variables that matter more as
training age rises: contraction type, movement speed by phase, acceleration at critical
points, rest interval length and type (active/passive), exercise sequence,
agonist/antagonist and stabilizer/mover strength balance, static/dynamic range of motion,
individual strength deficit, training history, injury history, and level of sports
proficiency. The proficiency factor is called out as especially important: exact
sequencing of strength, strength-speed, and hypertrophy work barely matters in a
beginner's first weeks/months but matters a great deal for an experienced athlete. Loads
as small as 40% of 1RM can measurably strengthen a beginner but do nothing for an elite
athlete. (PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp. 11-12.)

**Why it works** — A novice's nervous system and tissue are both far from their adaptive
ceiling, so almost any consistent stimulus produces a training effect; an advanced
athlete has used up most of that low-hanging adaptive room, so the remaining gains depend
on precisely managing the variables that were negligible for the novice.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this supports a rule for how much programming detail is
worth the coaching time — spend detailed variable-management effort (sequencing, rest
structure, ROM, asymmetry work) on advanced/experienced athletes, and keep novice
programming simple and consistency-focused. This library's Bompa book makes a related point
from the development-model side ([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological
vs Chronological vs Training Age]]), though that entry addresses age-grouping and injury
risk rather than Verkhoshansky's programming-variable-complexity angle specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't use "they're a beginner" as an excuse to
ignore movement quality, technique, or safety variables; the text's simplification applies
to programming complexity (sequencing, minor load percentages, PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp.
11-12), not to coaching attention on how an exercise is performed — this distinction is
this entry's own reading, not stated explicitly in the text. **Inference:** an older
athlete new to formal training still has a low training age by this logic and should be
treated as a beginner by this rule, not by chronological age; Verkhoshansky's text does not
draw that chronological-vs-training-age distinction itself in this section.

**Example** — **Inference:** A true freshman gains strength on almost any structured 3x/week program with
straightforward load progression; a fourth-year starter needs exercise sequencing,
recovery structure, and asymmetry correction actively managed to keep progressing.

**Related** — [[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]].
######## heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: heuristic

created: 2026-09-26

# Strength Deficit Size Points to a Different Training Method

**What it is** — If an athlete's strength deficit (see
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]) is large for a given muscle
group, the text recommends near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (weightlifting or
plyometric methods) or, if very large, Compensatory Activation Training (CAT) with 5-8RM
loads. If the deficit is small, it recommends submaximal hypertrophy work (bodybuilding-
style loading) followed by maximal efforts against heavy loads. Verkhoshansky's own
research is cited as finding the strength deficit increases as external resistance and
movement time decrease, meaning it matters most for fast, low-resistance actions such as
running, jumping, and throwing, and matters less for slow, high-resistance actions. (PDF
p. 21, printed p. 10.)

**Why it works** — A large deficit means there is untapped voluntary/neural capacity
still available, so training that improves recruitment and rate of activation (max effort
or reactive/plyometric methods) has the most room to produce gains. A small deficit means
the athlete is already recruiting close to their ceiling voluntarily, so further gains
require growing the tissue itself (hypertrophy) before neural methods can express more
force.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** as a screening question for method selection in
explosive/team-sport athletes: for actions with little time to produce force (change of
direction, sprint push-off, jump takeoff), a large SJ/CMJ-style deficit would, by this
heuristic's logic, point toward reactive-strength and max-effort work over added
hypertrophy volume, and a small deficit toward a hypertrophy or general-strength emphasis
instead. This specific application to team-sport screening is not stated in the text.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky's Compensatory Activation Training (CAT) with 5-8RM
loads (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10) is not a validated modern method name; **Inference:**
treat it as historical terminology for near-maximal effort training, not a specific
protocol to prescribe as written. **Inference:** do not use this rule to skip hypertrophy
work in an athlete simply because their sport is "fast" — the size of the individual's own
measured deficit, not the sport category alone, should drive the decision, and no deficit
was actually measured with a validated modern tool in this text; this caution is this
entry's own judgment.

**Example** — **Inference:** A running back with a large gap between static-start and countermovement
jump height is a better fit for added reactive/plyometric work in that block; a running
back with almost no gap between the two jumps, but comparatively low absolute strength, is
a better fit for a strength/hypertrophy emphasis first.

**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]].
######## principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.2"
topic: mass-acceleration equivalence and specificity
category: [biomechanics, specificity, exercise-selection]
confidence: proven
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# The Same Force (F = ma) Produced Different Ways Trains Differently

**What it is** — Newton's second law (F = ma) means the same force can be produced with a
large mass and small acceleration (powerlifting-style, heavy load), a small mass and large
acceleration (many track and field actions), a moderate mass and moderate acceleration
(bodybuilding-style hypertrophy training, roughly 8-12 reps), or near-zero acceleration
under isometric/isokinetic conditions. Despite equal force output, these methods are
argued and shown in practice not to produce the same training effect, because different
neural, muscular, and metabolic processes are engaged in each case. (PDF pp. 32-33,
printed pp. 21-22.)

**Why it works** — Force alone does not specify the movement's velocity, duration, muscle
action type, or motor unit recruitment/firing pattern, all of which independently affect
the training stimulus; two efforts that reach the same peak force via different mass-
acceleration combinations are mechanically equal on that one variable but different on
several others that matter physiologically. This is the mechanistic backbone of the
general specificity-of-training principle, which is well established independent of this
text.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a reasoning check against choosing exercises
solely by "how much force does this produce," when the intended adaptation (max strength
vs. explosive power vs. hypertrophy vs. isometric endurance) requires matching the
mass-acceleration profile, not just the force magnitude, to the target quality. This
generalized application is this entry's own extension of the four loading-option
comparison (PDF pp. 32-33, printed pp. 21-22).

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states isokinetic training (option d, F = k.R)
correlates poorly with actual sporting performance despite producing meaningful
non-specific strength gains in a lab setting (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22, citing Rosentzweig
& Hinson 1972, Ostemig 1986). **Inference:** don't treat isokinetic results as a proxy for
how an athlete will perform in ballistic, free-loading sport actions; this specific
caution is this entry's own restatement of that finding's practical implication.

**Example** — **Inference:** A powerlifting-style heavy squat and an Olympic-style ballistic
clean pull can both produce a similar peak force at the bar, but the clean pull's high
acceleration under a lighter relative load trains rate of force development and ballistic
coordination that the heavy, slow squat does not, and vice versa for maximal-tension
adaptation.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].
######## principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.2"
topic: force-velocity relationship
category: [biomechanics, testing, strength-speed]
confidence: proven
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26

# The Force-Velocity Relationship, and Why Strength Doesn't Guarantee Speed

**What it is** — Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve: velocity of contraction is
inversely related to load; large force cannot be produced at very high velocities under
constant conditions; heavy strength training shifts the curve upward, particularly in
beginners (raising force at all velocities, called training for "strength-speed"); light,
high-velocity training shifts the curve's velocity maximum rightward (called training for
"speed-strength"). Because power = force x velocity, both shifts raise power, just at
different points on the curve. Critically, there is no correlation between an athlete's
maximal strength and their maximal velocity — they are described as different motor
abilities. (PDF pp. 30-31, printed pp. 19-20; Zatsiorsky & Matveev 1964, Komi 1979,
Zatsiorsky 1995.)

**Why it works** — The F-V relationship reflects the cross-bridge cycling and motor unit
recruitment limits of muscle contraction; it has been confirmed for whole-body sporting
movement as well as isolated muscle, and is the direct ancestor of the force-velocity
profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others) used in modern sprint and jump testing.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** justifies programming that targets a specific region of
the force-velocity spectrum rather than assuming "more strength" automatically transfers to
speed: heavy-load, low-velocity work develops the force end; light-load, high-velocity
(including ballistic/plyometric) work develops the velocity end. **Inference:** usable as
the conceptual basis for choosing between a strength-speed or speed-strength emphasis block
for an athlete whose limiter has been identified (e.g., via jump testing or sprint
force-velocity profiling); this specific screening application is not stated in the text.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't treat "no correlation between max strength and
max velocity" (PDF p. 31, printed p. 20) as license to ignore strength training for a
speed-limited athlete; a certain strength floor is plausibly still necessary before
speed-specific training pays off. **Eric's baseline:** the Vermeil hierarchy of athletic
development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill) is
repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10,18-19`).
**Inference:** that sequencing is broadly consistent with treating a strength floor as a
prerequisite, though neither this text's cited section nor the baseline states the two
frameworks are equivalent. Verkhoshansky himself flags the classic hyperbolic F-V curve as
not universally accurate: research on the lumbar erector spinae shows a "yielding" drop in
force during constant-velocity eccentric stretching that the standard curve doesn't predict
(Sutamo & McGill, 1995; PDF p. 30, printed p. 19) — the model is a strong generalization,
not a universal law for every muscle group.

**Example** — **Inference:** Two athletes with equal back squat 1RM (similar max force) can have very
different unloaded sprint speeds; that gap is F-V curve position, not raw strength, and
argues for velocity-end training (sprint work, light-load ballistics) rather than more
heavy squatting to close it.

**Related** — [[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]],
[[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]].
######## principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1"
topic: neural basis of strength
category: [strength, neural, adaptation]
confidence: proven
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Strength Increase Is Initiated by Neuromuscular Stimulation, Not Muscle Size

**What it is** — "The fundamental principle of strength training... is that all strength
increase is initiated by neuromuscular stimulation." Strength is framed as a function of
how powerfully and efficiently muscle is activated by the nervous system first, with
hypertrophy as a downstream, longer-term structural consequence of a given stimulus
regime, not the driver of early gains. (PDF pp. 17-18, printed pp. 6-7.)

**Why it works** — Hypertrophy is a slow structural adaptation; force output can rise
well before meaningful cross-sectional area change through improved recruitment,
firing rate, and coordination of the muscle already present. This is one of the more
independently replicated findings in strength physiology outside this text (early-phase
strength gains preceding measurable hypertrophy is a standard finding in resistance
training research), which is why this entry is rated `proven` rather than `supported`
despite the book being the citation vehicle here.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this principle explains early-training-block strength
gains in novice athletes that outpace any visible muscle growth. **Eric's baseline:**
Tracy Fober's "use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer" standard prioritizes
movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM
numbers, especially early in a training cycle (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21`; `week1-lecture.md p.46`).
**Inference:** that coaching standard is consistent with this principle's emphasis on
coordination before load, though the baseline material does not itself cite the
neuromuscular-primacy mechanism. **Inference:** the same logic likely explains why
detraining strength loss can outpace measurable muscle loss (neural efficiency degrading
faster than tissue), though this text does not state that extension explicitly.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states maximal strength "depends to a great extent"
on adequate muscle cross-section (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7), so hypertrophy is not
unimportant at higher training ages. **Inference:** this principle should not be used to
justify skipping hypertrophy-phase work for athletes past the early-adaptation window,
where structural gains matter more for continued strength progress; this caution is not
stated in the text itself.

**Example** — **Inference:** A freshman who has never lifted seriously often adds meaningful strength in
the first 4-6 weeks of a program with little visible size change; that gain is
predominantly neural (coordination, recruitment, reduced antagonist co-contraction), not
tissue growth.

**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] (the
mechanisms by which this happens).
######## principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.1"
topic: rate of force development
category: [strength, testing, explosive-strength]
confidence: proven
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Rate of Force (or Tension) Development Is a Separate Limiter from Maximal Force

**What it is** — Sporting performance does not depend simply on the ability to produce
maximum force, because many sporting actions happen too fast to recruit an adequate
number of muscle fibres in the available time. Rate of Force Development (RFD) / Rate of
Tension Development (RTD) — how quickly force rises, not just its ceiling — is named as an
independently important limiter, worth assessing on its own alongside maximal-force
deficits. (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10; cross-referenced to 2.2.1 for more detail.)

**Why it works** — Many athletic actions (sprint ground contact, jump takeoff, change of
direction) last far less time than it takes to reach true maximal voluntary force. An
athlete can have high 1RM strength but a slow force-time curve, and still underperform in
short-duration actions, because the task ends before peak force is reached. This
distinction (peak force vs. rate of rise to a sub-maximal time point) is well established
in modern force-time curve analysis, independent of this text.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** force-plate metric selection follows the
Output/Driver/Strategy/Fluffy (ODSF) framework, picking 1-2 output metrics, 1-3 driver
metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force), and 1-3 strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations)
rather than reporting peak values alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`, credited to Hawkin Dynamics, not
Eric's own framework). **Inference:** this principle's force-vs-rate distinction supports
that driver-metric emphasis and argues for testing and reporting RFD-type variables
separately from 1RM or peak-force values, especially for athletes in short-ground-contact
positions; this specific link between the ODSF framework and Verkhoshansky's RFD argument
is not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states RFD/RTD deficits are developed further in
later chapters on strength-speed and explosive strength (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10,
cross-referenced to Ch3, Ch5), implying the two qualities are trainable somewhat
independently. **Inference:** don't substitute a single RFD number for the full force-time
curve when the movement or time window matters (RFD at 0-50ms is a different quality than
RFD at 100-200ms); this time-window caution is this entry's own addition, not stated in
this section of the text.

**Example** — **Inference:** Two athletes with the same back squat 1RM can produce very different sprint
starts if one reaches a given force threshold in 100ms and the other takes 200ms; testing
and training that difference requires RFD-sensitive measures, not another max-strength
test.

**Related** — [[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]].
######## principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.7"
topic: amortization phase and elastic energy
category: [plyometrics, stretch-shortening-cycle, reactive-strength]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# A Short Transition (Amortization) Between Stretch and Shortening Preserves Stored Elastic Energy

**What it is** — Actin-myosin cross-bridges have a limited lifetime, 15-120 milliseconds
(Edman et al., 1978). For stored elastic energy from a stretch to be used in the
following concentric contraction, the transition period between the end of the eccentric
(stretch) phase and the start of the concentric (shortening) phase must be brief; a longer
delay lets cross-bridges detach and the elastic potential dissipates as slippage rather
than being used for work. A greater velocity of stretch during the eccentric phase also
increases elastic energy storage (Rack & Westbury, 1974). Much of the extra positive work
seen in rapid eccentric-concentric (plyometric) actions is attributed to this stored
elastic energy plus a separate pre-loading/pre-stretch effect (tension at the start of the
concentric phase is already elevated by the preceding stretch). Tendon-based elastic energy
storage during locomotion largely happens via near-isometric muscle contraction with
minimal muscle fibre length change, which is also more metabolically efficient than
dynamic contraction. (PDF pp. 55-56, printed pp. 44-45.)

**Why it works** — The cross-bridge attachment window is a hard physiological time
constraint; the mechanics of elastic energy return depend on catching that window, which
is why a fast stretch-to-shorten transition (a short "amortization phase," in later
plyometrics terminology) is functionally different from a slow, paused transition even if
the stretch magnitude is identical.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the underlying mechanism behind coaching cues
for minimizing ground-contact/amortization time in plyometric and reactive-strength work
(depth jumps, bounds, sprint ground contacts), and behind why reactive strength index
(RSI/mRSI, already the department's chosen daily readiness marker) is sensitive to contact
time as well as jump height — a longer amortization phase indicates the athlete is not
capturing the SSC benefit this mechanism describes.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the cited cross-bridge lifetime range (15-120ms) is
a cellular-level parameter, not a directly coachable or measurable field variable; do not
try to cue an athlete toward a specific millisecond target. Use it as the "why" behind a
qualitative cue (minimize ground contact time, avoid pausing at the bottom of a jump), not
as a number to program.

**Example** — **Inference:** cueing an athlete to "spend as little time on the ground as
possible" during a depth jump, rather than pausing briefly before jumping, is a practical
application of keeping the stretch-to-shorten transition inside the cross-bridge
attachment window.

**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]],
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]].
######## principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.4"
topic: specificity of training
category: [specificity, exercise-selection, programming]
confidence: proven
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Strength Training Adapts Along (at Least) Ten Independent, Narrow Dimensions

**What it is** — Strength gains transfer narrowly, not generally, across at least ten
independent dimensions: type of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region/range of
movement, velocity of movement, force of contraction, muscle fibre recruitment,
metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility, and fatigue. Training that improves one
dimension often produces little or no improvement on the others, even when the same
muscle groups are involved. Specificity is explicitly distinguished from simulation:
mimicking a sport movement with added resistance is not the same as training the specific
factors above, and can actually distort the neuromuscular programming needed for the real
skill because of changes in center of gravity, moment of inertia, and mechanical
stiffness introduced by the resistance. (PDF pp. 38-39, printed pp. 27-28.)

**Why it works** — Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
muscular systems together (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
adaptation. This is one of the more broadly replicated findings in strength and
conditioning research, independent of this text.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a master reasoning check before assuming an
exercise "transfers" to a sport skill: ask which of the ten dimensions the exercise
actually matches, not just whether it uses similar muscles. **Eric's baseline:** the
Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of
movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production,
and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise transfers, and
is taught in HHPR 5355 (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`, `week1-lecture.md p.34`). **Inference:**
Dynamic Correspondence (this book's Ch4.3, not yet ingested) is plausibly the applied
extension of this same ten-dimension specificity logic to exercise selection, though this
chapter does not itself state that link.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't use "specificity" as an argument against any
general preparation work; this book's own 1.1 material and this library's Bompa
multilateral/LTAD entries support building a general base before narrowing to sport-specific
work. This principle governs which dimensions transfer, not whether general work has value
at an earlier training age; that distinction is this entry's own reading, not stated as
such in this passage of the text.

**Example** — **Inference:** Heavy squat strength does not automatically transfer to high-velocity sprint
force production (different point on the velocity dimension) even though both use similar
musculature; each needs its own specific training exposure.

**Related** — [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]],
[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]].
######## principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.2"
topic: torque and lifting technique
category: [biomechanics, technique, safety]
confidence: proven
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Strength Expression Depends on Torque Management, Not Just Load

**What it is** — Torque (force times the perpendicular distance from the force's line of
action to the joint fulcrum) determines effective loading on a joint, independent of the
absolute weight lifted. Bringing a load closer to a joint reduces the torque at that
joint for the same weight: flexing the elbows reduces shoulder torque during dumbbell
raises/flyes/bench press; keeping a bar close to the body during the clean or deadlift
reduces torque at the lumbar spine and hips, allowing a heavier load to be lifted more
safely. Swinging the bar away from the body during a snatch pull, or a javelin away from
the shoulder during wind-up, are cited as inefficient uses of torque. (PDF pp. 28-29,
printed pp. 17-18.)

**Why it works** — Torque = force x moment arm; for a fixed external force (a given
weight), shortening the moment arm directly lowers the rotational demand on the joint,
which is standard, independently-established biomechanics, not specific to this text.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a coaching cue and technical-fault-diagnosis
tool for any lift where the bar or load can drift away from the body's midline (clean,
snatch, deadlift, overhead press) or away from a joint (dumbbell raises, flyes); keeping
the load's path close to the relevant joint is both a safety cue and a load-capacity cue.
This general coaching application is this entry's own extension of Verkhoshansky's
worked examples (PDF pp. 28-29, printed pp. 17-18).

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a mechanical principle about joint
loading, not a complete safety framework; it does not account for tissue tolerance,
technique proficiency, or fatigue-related form breakdown on its own, and the text does
not claim that it does. **Inference:** reducing joint torque is not always desirable if
the goal is specifically to overload that joint's musculature for rehabilitation purposes
(e.g., some hip- or shoulder-isolation rehab work intentionally increases moment arm at a
target joint under controlled load); this rehab caveat is not addressed in this section of
the text.

**Example** — **Inference:** Cueing an athlete to keep the bar against the shins and thighs during a
clean pull, rather than swinging it forward, reduces lumbar torque for the same bar
weight and is both a technique and a load-management fix.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].
######## principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.8-1.11"
topic: triphasic muscle action
category: [biomechanics, plyometrics, injury-risk]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# All Dynamic Movement Is Triphasic: Isometric, Then Concentric/Eccentric, Then Isometric Again

**What it is** — Classifying muscle action as simply "static" (isometric) or "dynamic"
(concentric/eccentric) is described as an oversimplification. Every dynamic action must
begin from an isometric phase (the muscle must first develop enough tension to
counterbalance the load before any movement starts: concentric if tension exceeds the
load, eccentric if it doesn't), and every movement ends in another isometric phase before
reversing or stopping, because Newton's laws require the system to momentarily come to
rest at a direction change. In ballistic/ fast movement, the transition isometric phase is
very brief; in slow maximal efforts (e.g. a powerlifting squat or bench), it can be much
longer. The brief isometric phase in a plyometric movement is specifically termed
"explosive isometric" action and is central to speed-strength training and movements like
the weightlifting jerk, shot put, and high jump. Movement termination/reversal can also
involve any combination of agonist eccentric or isometric action, antagonist concentric or
isometric action, stabilizer action at the joint or nearby joints, and passive connective-
tissue damping — not simply "antagonist opposes agonist" as popular descriptions suggest.
(PDF pp. 65-66, printed pp. 54-55.)

**Why it works** — This follows directly from Newtonian mechanics (a moving system must
have zero velocity at the instant it reverses direction) combined with the physiological
fact that muscle tension must build before it can move a load; the "explosive isometric"
phase is the same brief coupling window discussed in
[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]], described here from the
whole-joint-action perspective rather than the cross-bridge perspective.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces that "isometric strength" is not a separate,
niche quality but a phase present in every dynamic lift and sprint/jump action, which
supports including isometric testing (IMTP) and isometric-emphasis training as directly
relevant to dynamic performance, not a side quality. Also a caution for kinesiology
teaching (e.g. HHPR 5355): movement termination is not simply "antagonist stops agonist";
several structures can share that role, so a simplistic agonist/antagonist explanation for
a given movement's braking phase may be incomplete.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky himself notes inappropriate antagonist activation
opposing a strongly contracting agonist is a recognized injury mechanism (e.g. hamstrings
rupturing when they fire to oppose the quadriceps during sprinting or kicking, PDF p. 60,
printed p. 49); **Inference:** this triphasic framework describes normal, coordinated
movement termination, and should not be conflated with that pathological
premature-antagonist-activation injury pattern, which is a distinct, unwanted phenomenon
rather than part of the normal triphasic sequence.

**Example** — **Inference:** a sprinter's ground-contact phase is not purely
"eccentric-then-concentric"; it necessarily includes the brief isometric coupling phase
this principle describes, which is the same window where the reactive-strength/elastic
mechanism in [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]] operates.

**Related** — [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]],
[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]].

3	SUPERTRAINING
4	STRENGTH AND THE  
5	MUSCULAR SYSTEM
6	Objective
7	It is the objective of this book to explore the phenomenon of strength and to apply to physical conditioning the 
8	discoveries arising from this quest, with a particular emphasis on the development of special fitness and  
9	preparedness for sporting performance  at the highest level. In meeting this objective, the concepts of work 
10	capacity, fitness and preparedness, as well as the different types of strength are examined in detail to provide the 
11	necessary framework for research and practical application of all findings.
12	It analyses the different types of strength, their roles in human movement and how they may be developed 
13	efficiently. In illustrating how scientific research may be applied in training or rehabilitation, it discusses the 
14	various means and methods of strength training, ranging from resistance training with weights to impulsive 
15	('plyometric') loading without weights. It identifies which specific types of strength fitness are required by the 
16	athlete, the forms in which strength is produced over the range of a given sporting movement and the most 
17	appropriate sequences for developing the different types of strength fitness over a prolonged training period.
18	Since considerable research reveals that strength is not a single fundamental fitness factor like cardiovascular 
19	endurance, as is often implied, this textbook introduces the reader to the exquisite complexity of strength via an 
20	understanding of the biomechanics, functional anatomy and physiology of the human movement system. This is 
21	not done simply as an intellectual exercise, but to prevent the reader from devising sport specific training 
22	programmes based on deficient traditional schedules which may have ignored the nuances of the different types of 
23	strength and the specificity of training for a given sport and individual.
24	This text, although aimed primarily at the exercise scientist, specialist high level coach and physical educator, 
25	also has direct relevance to the sports medical practitioner or therapist who may be involved with rehabilitating 
26	athletes whose return to top level competition depends on restoration of the necessary type of strength fitness.
27	What is Strength ?
28	Strength is an essential component of all human performance and its formal development can no longer be 
29	neglected in the preparation of any athlete. Successful strength conditioning depends on a thorough understanding 
30	of all processes underlying the production of strength by the body. Therefore, it is appropriate that this text 
31	commences with an outline of the structure and function of the more important systems involved in producing all 
32	types of strength.
33	Strength is the product of muscular action initiated and orchestrated by electrical processes in the nervous 
34	system of the body. Classically, strength is defined as the ability of a given muscle or group o f muscles to  
35	generate muscular force under specific conditions.  Thus, maximal strength  is the ability of a particular group of 
36	muscles to produce a maximal voluntary contraction in response to optimal motivation against an external load. 
37	This strength is usually produced in competition and may also be referred to as the competitive maximum  
38	strength, CFmax. It is not the same as absolute strength,  which Zatsiorsky (1995) calls Fmm, the maximum of all 
39	maxima, and which usually is associated with the greatest force which can be produced by a given muscle group 
40	under involuntary muscle stimulation by, for example, electrical stimulation of the nerves supplying the muscles 
41	or recruitment of a powerful stretch reflex by sudden loading.
42	For certain practical purposes, absolute strength may be regarded as roughly equivalent to maximal eccentric 
43	strength, which is difficult or impractical to measure, because a maximum by definition refers to the limit point 
44	preceding structural and functional failure of the system. Thus, it is apparent that specific neural feedback 
45	mechanisms, like governors in a mechanical engine, exist to prevent a muscle from continuing to produce force to 
46	the point of mechanical failure. This is why it probably would be more practical to use the maximum explosive 
47	isometric strength (produced under so-called maximum plyometric conditions or explosive thrust against a 
48	dynamometer, as discussed in Ch 5) as a working approximation to absolute strength (or Fmm). To prevent 
49	confusion, it also should be noted that the term ‘absolute strength’ sometimes is used to define the maximum 
50	strength which can be produced by an athlete irrespective of bodymass.
51	1
52	
53	=========== IDX 13 | printed 2 | viewer p.14
54	SUPERTRAINING
55	It is vital to recognise a training maximum  TFmax or training 1RM (single repetition maximum), which is 
56	always less than the competition maximum CFmax in experienced athletes, because optimal motivation invariably 
57	occurs under competitive conditions (Fig 1.1). Zatsiorsky states that the training maximum is the heaviest load  
58	which one can lift without substantial emotional excitement , as indicated by a very significant rise in heart rate 
59	before the lift (Medvedev, 1986). It is noteworthy that, in the untrained person, involuntary or hypnotic 
60	conditions can increase strength output by up to 35%, but by less than 10% in the trained athlete. The mean 
61	difference between TFmax and CFmax is approximately 12.5 ±  2.5% in experienced weightlifters, with a larger 
62	difference being exhibited by lifters in heavier weight classes (Zatsiorsky, 1995).
63	The merit of identifying the different types of strength or performance maximum lies in enabling one to 
64	prescribe training intensity more efficiently. Intensity is usually defined as a certain percentage of one's maximum 
65	and it is most practical to choose this on the basis of the competitive maximum, which remains approximately 
66	constant for a fairly prolonged period. The training maximum can vary daily , so, while it may be of value in 
67	prescribing training for less qualified athletes, it is of limited value for the elite competitor.
68	It is relevant to note that competitions involve very few attempts to reach a maximum, yet they are far more 
69	exhausting than strenuous workouts with many repetitions, since they involve extremely high levels of 
70	psychological and nervous stress. The high levels of nervous and emotional stress incurred by attempting a 
71	competitive maximum require many days or even weeks to reach full recovery, even though physical recuperation 
72	would appear to be complete, so that this type of loading is not recommended as a regular form of training.
73	In other words, any attempt to exceed limit weights requires an increase in nervous excitation and interferes 
74	with the athlete's ability to adapt, if this type of training is used frequently. In attempting to understand the 
75	intensity of loading prescribed by the apparently extreme Bulgarian coaches who are reputed to stipulate frequent 
76	or daily use of maximum loads in training, one has to appreciate that training with training maxima  (which do not 
77	maximally stress the nervous system) is very different from training with competitive maxima  (which place great 
78	stress on nervous processes).
79	F i g u r e  1.1 Different types of maximal strength. Absolute strength (or Fmm, maximum of maximum forces) is produced under 
80	involuntary conditions, whereas the other two maxima are the result of voluntary action. The strength deficit, the difference between 
81	absolute strength and maximal strength, is discussed later in this section.
82	Strength is a relative phenomenon depending on numerous factors, so it is essential that these conditions are 
83	accurately described when strength is being assessed. For instance, muscular strength varies with joint angle, joint 
84	orientation, speed of movement, muscle group and type of movement, so it is largely meaningless to speak of 
85	absolute strength without specifying the conditions under which it is generated. Sometimes, the term relative 
86	strength is introduced to compare the strength of subjects of different bodymass. In this context, relative strength 
87	is defined as the strength per unit bodymass produced by a given individual under specific conditions (e.g. 
88	executing a well-defined lift or combination of lifts, such as the squat, snatch or the weightlifting Total).
89	It is also useful to recognise that one may define isometric, concentric and eccentric strength maxima, since 
90	every sport requires distinct levels of each one of these types of maximum. The importance of these maxima is 
91	discussed later in the subsection entitled 'Strength Deficit', As a matter of interest, these maxima given in order of 
92	magnitude are: eccentric, isometric, concentric.
93	Later, several other important strength-related terms such as explosive strength, starting-strcngth, 
94	acceleration-strength and speed-strcngth are analysed in detail. In particular, this text discusses strength and 
95	musculoskeletal conditioning in terms of the following fundamentals:
96	• The physiology of muscle action
97	2
98	
99	=========== IDX 14 | printed 3 | viewer p.15
100	SUPERTRAINING
101	• The biomcchanics of strength production
102	• Neuromuscular stimulation and control
103	• Adaptation to physical loading
104	• The various types of strength fitness
105	• The specificity of muscular and neuromuscular training
106	The Origins of Strength Training Science
107	Strength training has always been synonymous with the so-called 'Iron Game', a broad generic term for the 
108	competitive lifting of heavy objects by strong men during the last century or so. Feats of lifting strength, 
109	however, have appeared throughout the history of most nations, but it has only been in very recent times that 
110	training to produce strength has become a scientific discipline. This science did not arise overnight: it is the 
111	culminating point of thousands of years of trial-and-error methods of training.
112	The earliest reference to formal strength training occurs in Chinese texts dating to as far back as 3600BC, 
113	when emperors made their subjects exercise daily (Webster, 1976). During the Chou dynasty (1122-249BC), 
114	potential soldiers had to pass weight-lifting tests before being allowed to enter the armed forces. There is 
115	abundant evidence of weight-training used in ancient Egypt and India, while the Greeks left numerous sculptures 
116	and illustrations of their athletes training with stone weights. In fact, the 6th century BC was known as the 'Age 
117	of Strength' and weight-lifting competitions involved the lifting of huge stones. The renowned ancient physician, 
118	Galen, referred frequently to exercising with weights (halteres), with his treatise Preservation o f Health  even 
119	classifying exercises into 'quick' exercises without weights and 'violent' exercises which are performed with 
120	weights. The Roman poet Martial (40-104AD) pondered: "Why do the strong men labour with their stupid 
121	dumbbells? A far better task for men is digging a vine trench". Weight training was not confined to men: a wall 
122	mosaic from a Roman villa in Piazza Almeria in Sicily depicted a girl exercising with weights.
123	It should not be surprising, then, that the quest for superior strength led to numerous systems of strength 
124	training, thereby laying a solid experiential foundation for the far more refined methods of today. During the 16th 
125	century in Europe, books on weight-training began to emerge, with Sir Thomas Elyot's text on the topic being 
126	published in England in 1531. Several universities in France and Germany offered weight training and in 1544, 
127	Joachim Camcrius, a lecturer at Leipzig University, wrote several books recommending weight training as an 
128	essential activity for the model school. In 1728, John Paugh published A Physiological, Theoretic and Practical  
129	Treatise on the Utility of Muscular Exercise for Restoring the Power to the Limbs , revealing that even then it was 
130	recognised that weight training offered therapeutic benefits. In the 1860s, the Scot, Archibald MacLaren, 
131	compiled the first system of physical training with dumbbells and barbells for the British Army and formalised a 
132	crude form of progressive overloading. Some of his ideas appeared in McMillan’s Magazine (1863) in his article, 
133	“National Systems of Bodily Exercise”, which compared various systems of physical training used at that time.
134	Pioneers of Strength Training
135	The path to strength training science is synonymous with the history of many of the legendary heroes of 
136	yesteryear, ranging from the biblical Samson and the bull-lifting Milo of Italy to the Russian superheavy 
137	wcightlifter, Alexeyev. The showmen and strong man entertainers of 19th century Europe in particular, laid the 
138	most solid foundations for the systematic development of formal strength and physique training methods and the 
139	eventual acceptance of the use of these methods in the general fitness and sports specific strength training 
140	revolution of today. Space permits the mention of only a few of these pioneering strong men of the past, so the 
141	history-minded reader is well advised to read David Webster’s fascinating and thorough book, “The Iron Game”, 
142	which presents the feats of these men from the distant past to 1975, upon which this brief summary is based.
143	On the basis of many years of research, Webster isolates the Italian circus and fairground performer, Felice 
144	Napoli, as the initiator of the strong man boom on an international scale. Born in 1820, some of his most 
145	illustrious disciples included Professor Attila (Louis Durlacher) and Eugen Sandow (Frederick Muller). The 
146	German-born Attila, in turn, became so well-known that he attracted as his pupils some of the world’s most 
147	famous physical culturalists and many rulers of Europe. Royalty whom he taught included King George of 
148	Greece, King Edward of England (while he was Prince of Wales), Crown Prince Frederick who became King 
149	Haakon of Norway, the six children of King Christian of Denmark, the Queen Mother Alexandra of England, 
150	Princess Dagmar (who became Empress of Russia and mother of Tsar Nicholas), and the Duchess of Cumberland.
151	3
152	
153	=========== IDX 15 | printed 4 | viewer p.16
154	SUPERTRAINING
155	At the time, the training of royalty, the wealthy and the famous with weights and specialised exercises was a 
156	well-established and desirable profession, predating the current generation of so-called personal trainers by about 
157	150 years. The fame and fortune of the strongmen of those days were a result of their regular and well-publicised 
158	one-on-one stage challenges and entertainment hall competitions using some highly individual and unusual one and 
159	two arm lifts, swings, supports and manoeuvres against loads of vehicles, humans and specially contrived barbells 
160	and dumbbells. These events, much like the music hall performances of famous composers and musicians, were 
161	often attended by royalty and the wealthy, and served to publicise these men, not only as entertainers, but also as 
162	teachers or mentors o f‘physical culture’.
163	The great Sandow, bom in Koningsberg in East Russia in 1867, was sought out by presidents and rulers from 
164	all around the world, with his book. Life is Movement  being received enthusiastically by nine kings and queens 
165	and many princes of Europe, as well as US Presidents William Taft and Woodrow Wilson. Besides defeating 
166	many strongmen of his time, he was a generous sponsor of many charitable causes and an early champion of more 
167	hygienic conditions of working and living for all, including the central role of formal fitness and health 
168	management. As part of his vision, he pressed for the introduction of physical education and sport as 
169	compulsory school subjects, and the regular examination of pupils by school doctors and dentists. At the same 
170	time, he toured the world lecturing to promote physical culture as a means of improving quality of life, with his 
171	contributions being described as follows by the Mirror of Life and Sport  (8 April 1911):
172	His Majesty King George has conferred an unique honour upon Mr. Eugen Sandow, the world-renowned  
173	exponent and founder o f scientific physical culture . Mr. Sandow just having had the honour o f being  
174	appointed Professor of Scientific Physical Culture to his Majesty.
175	The keen interest which the King has always taken in the physical welfare of his people is well-known, and  
176	there is no desire more dear to his Majesty's heart than to improve the conditions of life for the masses.
177	Mr. Sandow's appointment must be regarded as a striking recognition of the undoubted benefits of  
178	scientific physical culture, and there is no doubt that the interest shown by his Majesty in the subject will  
179	considerably increase the popularity of the science of which Mr. Sandow is the principal authority.
180	Mr. Sandow is a man who has risen by his own unaided effort to a position in which he is not only a  
181	national but a world factor in the science of improvement o f the human body and the combating of that  
182	physical degeneracy which in former eras has always accompanied the advances of civilisation.
183	In many respects, therefore, Sandow was one of the most important founding fathers of the fitness revolution, 
184	with the history of his efforts revealing that the modem phenomenon of science-based physical training is by no 
185	means novel or innovative. Interestingly, Sandow’s methods focused largely on the development of strength and 
186	skill as the foundation of health, an approach which was almost completely deposed more than half a century 
187	later by cardiovascular scientists such as Dr Kenneth Cooper of the USA, who massively downplayed the role of 
188	these fitness qualities and stressed ‘aerobic’ fitness as being far more important to general health. It has taken 
189	more than 25 years for the quality of strength advocated by Sandow to return to academic acceptance.
190	In Russia, during this same period, the eminent Polish-born physician, Vladislav Krayevsky (or Krajewski), 
191	founded the St Petersburg Amateur Weightlifting Society (1885), having visited various German towns to 
192	familiarise himself with what was already known throughout Europe as weightlifting or ‘heavy athletics’ (or 
193	’Tyazhelaya Atletika’, the name still used in Russia to describe this sport), because of his great interest in the use 
194	of physical culture for the prevention and treatment of illness. Many prominent scientists, artists and athletes 
195	became his pupils, including another famous strongman, George Hackenschmidt, who credited Krayevsky for 
196	teaching him all that he knew. Hackenschmidt, in his book, The Way to Live , added that some of the world’s

245	The Divergence of Training Philosophies
246	The development of different scientific and educational cultures in the West and the East had a profound impact 
247	on the growth of the different aspects of strength and general fitness training. In the earliest days of the strength 
248	game, most of the strong men travelled extensively to learn from colleagues and teachers with different outlooks 
249	and were keen to be apprenticed to those whose knowledge attracted widespread attention. With the advent of 
250	World War I, the growth of the USA into a great power, the advent of communism and other controversial 
251	philosophies and economies, nationalism reached greater heights than ever before in Europe. The Great 
252	Depression followed a few decades later, leading to World War II and the partitioning of the world into an 
253	Eastern and a Western bloc.
254	The increasing ideological isolation of nations and well-protected prestige of sporting success meant that 
255	research in all fields, including sport, took different directions. During the years after both World Wars, Russia 
256	and Europe still continued to promote the virtues of physical strength and power, whereas research in the West 
257	rapidly veered in the direction of cardiovascular fitness, assuming great impetus with the running for health and 
258	‘aerobics’ crazes, associated closely with Swedish endurance exercise research and popular fitness books such as 
259	Kenneth Cooper’s Aerobics.  This resulted in a vigorous promotion of the cardiovascular doctrine , the paradigm 
260	which maintains that cardiac and general health depends predominantly on prolonged endurance or ‘aerobic’ 
261	exercise. At the same time, proponents of this doctrine fairly vigorously denigrated the health benefits of strength

298	data base from the following distinct sources (the details in parentheses refer to the purpose of each discipline):

309	The Fundamental Principle of Strength Training
310	The production and increase of strength both depend on neuromuscular processes. Strength is not primarily a 
311	function of muscle size, but one of the appropriate muscles powerfully contracted by effective nervous 
312	stimulation. This is the foundation of all strength training.
313	Several centuries ago, when electricity, less still bioelectricity, was not of much scientific interest, this 
314	principle was already anticipated by Sir Isaac Newton, who wrote in his Principia Mathematica (1687) of "a
