2327	1.8 Classification of Muscle Actions
2328	In producing the various directions of movement, many muscles are simultaneously involved in controlling the 
2329	action from its beginning to its end. This orchestration of diverse contributing muscles has led to different roles 
2330	being allocated to each muscle group. One of the typical classification schemes recognizes the following traditional 
2331	roles:
2332	• Igonta Muscles acting as the so-called prime movers of the action. Prime movers  produce the most 
2333	significant contribution to the movement, while assistant movers  play a more secondary role in assisting this 
2334	prune action. Some authorities recognise emergency muscles  as a special class of assistant movers which come 
2335	into play only when maximal force must be generated during a particular movement. In physiotherapy, the 
2336	phenomenon of assistant movers being recruited by significant increases in loading is referred to as overflow.  The 
2337	value of training periodically against near maximal or maximal resistance then becomes obvious.
2338	' Antagonists: Muscles acting in direct opposition to the agonists. As emphasized by Basmajian (1978), this 
2339	action does not necessarily accompany every agonistic contraction, but only under certain circumstances. Central 
2340	nervous processes are sufficiently refined to control agonist activity without routine reliance on opposition by  
2341	antagonists. After all, in engineering situations it is rarely necessary to use two motors in opposition to offer 
2342	sophisticated control of any movement. All that is necessary is a single sufficiently powerful motor with rapid 
2343	feedback processes to ensure accuracy, control, appropriate force and appropriate speed throughout the defined 
2344	movement range.
2345	Moreover, it is important to note that reciprocal inhibition  of the antagonist usually occurs whenever an 
2346	agonist is strongly activated (see 3.5.3). In other words, the antagonist invariably relaxes when the agonist 
2347	contracts, except when the action is extremely rapid and some 'antagonists' come into play to prevent joint 
2348	damage due to the large momentum of the moving limb. The inappropriate activation of'antagonists' to oppose 
2349	strongly contracting agonists, however, is recognised as one of the causes of musculoskeletal injury. For instance, 
2350	the hamstrings can rupture if they contract to oppose the quadriceps while an athlete is sprinting or kicking. 
2351	Russian researchers have shown that antagonist inhibition occurs most readily during rhythmic activity associated  
2352	M ih motor learning.
2353	So-called 'antagonists' may act continuously or in periodic spurts throughout a movement. Moreover, the 
2354	presence of antagonist activity may be due to motor learning and not inherent reflexes. Sometimes, the existence 
2355	of antagonistic activity is a sign of unskilled movement or nervous abnormality. Clearly, the automatic labelling of 
2356	specific muscle actions as antagonistic needs to be tempered with caution, unless confirmed by careful 
2357	electromyography (recording of electrical signals from the muscles).
2358	49

2360	the term includes all the different types of strength, while endurance refers to both muscular endurance and 
2361	cardiovascular endurance, factors which relate directly to the onset of fatigue during stabilisation or mobilisation.
2362	The relationship between stability and mobility forms a vital part of physiotherapeutic PNF (proprioceptive 
2363	neuromuscular facilitation), whose means and methods of physical conditioning may be extended to offer an 
2364	extensive system of strength training (see Ch 6).

2369	carry out a movement involving other joints. During static stabilisation,  the muscles cither contract isomctricaLH 
2370	or quasi-isometrically (very slowly). An example is the action of the spinal erectors (erector spinae) durinj 
2371	pushups. They maintain an isometric contraction to prevent the spine from hypcrcxtcnding (sagging) while tin 
2372	pectoral and anterior deltoid muscles produce the up and down movement of the upper body relative tot 
2373	ground. During dynamic stabilisation,  the musclcs arc in continuous contraction while simultaneously carrying 
2374	out a mobilising role. For instance, during running and walking, the quadriceps contract not only to extend t 
2375	knee, but also to stabilise it during the ground contact phase of each stride. Stabilising muscles often augment

2378	assistant or emergency stabilisers  which are recruited to assist the 'prime' stabilisers during very intensive effor 
2379	by the prime and assistant movers. This principle is used in rehabilitation by physiotherapists to recruit 'lar 
2380	muscles.

2382	movements. An example is offered by situps, in which the internal and external obliques contract simultaneous 
2383	to produce trunk flexion. Singly, these muscles tend to produce lateral flexion and rotation of the trunk 
2384	Simultaneously contracting, they oppose one another to cancel these movements and thereby assist the rectui 
2385	abdominis musclcs in producing pure trunk flexion. Similarly, the anterior and posterior heads of the deltoi 
2386	muscles neutralise one another’s tendencies to elicit medial/lateral rotation and horizontal flexion/cxtensioi 
2387	thereby assisting the medial head in producing pure abduction (raising of the arm laterally).
2388	Variations on these categories exist, such as the division of muscles into two classes: synergists , wtei 
2389	cooperate to produce a movement, and antagonists  which act in opposition to the direction of movemefi 
2390	However, it must be emphasized that all muscles operate synergistically  in the normal person; they all cooperal 
2391	by contributing forces in the most appropriate directions to produce the desired motion, although not necessan 
2392	with maximum efficiency. It is preferable to remember that all muscles interact to produce the two fundamenti 
2393	characteristics associated with all human movement: stability and mobility (see 1.7.4). To do this, the same muse 
2394	may act as a mover at one time and a stabiliser at another. It is inappropriate to identify a muscle as one of th r 
2395	above types under all circumstances. Accurately speaking, a muscle may only be identified as carrying ou:  
2396	specific role in a specific situation.  Thus, it is imprecise to refer to specific muscles as being agonists, antagonists 
2397	stabilisers, synergists and so forth: it is more accurate to state that each muscle plays a specific role at a give: 
2398	moment (or during a certain movement phase) in a given situation.
2399	Muscles are also categorised as being tonic (postural or anti-gravity) to offer stability and resist gravity,* 
2400	phasic  (dynamic) to provide movement. Tonic muscles are usually penniform, contain a higher proportion i 
2401	slow twitch muscle fibres, generally cross only one joint, lie deeper below the surface and perform exteow 
2402	actions including abduction or lateral rotation. Phasic muscles usually occur more superficially, contain more & r 
2403	twitch muscle fibres, often cross more than one joint and perform flexor functions, including adduction and m cdu 
2404	rotation.
2405	1.9 Cocontraction and Ballistic Movement
2406	In general, muscles will cooperate to produce two kinds of action: cocontraction  and ballistic movernc 
2407	(Basmajian, 1978). In cocontraction , agonist and antagonist musclcs contract simultaneously, with dominances 
2408	the former producing the external motion. Ballistic movement involves bursts of muscular activity followed 
2409	phases of relaxation during which the motion continues due to stored limb momentum. The term 'ballistic' is 
2410	sincc the coursc of action of the limb is determined by the initial agonist impulse, just as the flight of a bullet 
2411	determined by the initial explosive charge in the cartridge.
2412	Skilled, rapid ballistic and moderately fast continuous movements are preprogrammed in the central nerv o u s. 
2413	system, whereas slow, discontinuous movements are not. The ballistic action rarely involves feedback process? 
2414	during the course of the movement. Feedback  from the muscles and joints to the central nervous system pennr 
2415	the ensuing motion to be monitored continuously and to be modified, if necessary. The resulting movenia 
2416	becomcs accurately executed and the relevant soft tissues arc protected from injury by changes in muscle tensa 
2417	and by the activation of appropriate antagonists to control and terminate the motion.
2418	50
2419	
2420	=========== IDX 62 | printed 51 | viewer p.63
2421	SUPERTRAINING
2422	If no sensory or proprioceptive feedback is implicated, the mode of control is termed feedforward  or 'open- 
2423	loop' control (Smith & Smith, 1962; Green, 1967). Here, control is preprogrammed into the central nervous and 
2424	ncuromuscular systems by the visual and auditory systems before movement begins, so that ongoing monitoring 
2425	mechanisms arc not involved. The first sign of impending programmed action is the inhibition of antagonist 
2426	contraction preceding agonist action, as revealed by the electromyograph. Premature activation of the antagonists 
2427	may not only diminish skill, but it can cause muscle injury. During ballistic and other rapid movement, antagonist 
2428	contraction is appropriate only to terminate further motion of the limb concerned. Not only is there no antagonist 
2429	activity during ballistic movements, but it is also absent during discontinuous motion (Brooks, 1983). The 
2430	advantage offered by feedforward processes is speed of action, whereas its main disadvantage is the lack of 
2431	flexibility which can be offered by feedback. Nevertheless, the importance of feedforward processes in human 
2432	movement should not be underestimated, as implied by the Russians in using regimes of visualisation and 
2433	autogenic training in sports preparation.
2434	1.10 Types of Muscle Action
2435	Traditionally, the following types of muscic “contraction” (or, more accurately, “action”) beginning with the 
2436	prefix '-iso' (meaning 'the same') are defined: isotonic  (constant muscle tension), isometric  (constant muscle 
2437	length), isokinetic (constant velocity of motion) and isoinertial (constant load). In addition, movement may occur 
2438	under concentric (so-called “muscic shortening”) and eccentric (so-called “muscic lengthening”) conditions. Before 
2439	these terms are unquestioningly applied to exercise, it is important to examine their validity.
2440	In all of the above cases, it is more accurate to speak about muscle action taking place under various 
2441	movement conditions. It is well known that a muscle can only contract or relax relative to its resting or 
2442	inactivated state, so that it is a misnomer to refer to eccentric muscle action as a “contraction” in which a muscle 
2443	contracts and lengthens simultaneously. Actually, this means that a muscle which has contracted under concentric 
2444	or isometric conditions is simply returning under eccentric conditions to its original resting length. To avoid 
2445	confusion like this, it is preferable to define muscle action as follows:
2446	• Concentric - Action in which the proximal and distal muscle attachments move towards one another
2447	• Eccentric - Action in which the proximal and distal muscle attachments move away from one another
2448	• Isometric - Action in which the proximal and distal muscle attachments do not move relative to one another
2449	Isometric literally means 'same length', a state which occurs only in a relaxed muscle. Actually, it is not muscle 
2450	length, but joint angle which remains constant. Contraction means 'shortening', so that isometric contraction, like 
2451	all other forms of muscle contraction, involves internal movement processes which shorten the muscle fibres. 
2452	Isometric contraction may be defined more accurately to mean muscle action which occurs when there is no 
2453	external movement or changc in joint angle (or distance between origin and insertion). It occurs when the force 
2454	produced by a muscle exactly balances the resistance imposed upon it and no movement results. Although not 
2455	incorrect, the term isometric may be replaced by the simple word static, without sacrificing any scientific rigour. It 
2456	is interesting to note that, during isometric action, mechanical work, some of which is absorbed by the tendinous 
2457	tissue, is generated by the shortening of muscle fibres (Masamitsu et al, 1998).
2458	The term isotonic, however, should be avoided under most circumstances, since it is virtually impossible for 
2459	muscle tension to remain the same while joint movement occurs over any extended range. Constancy is possible 
2460	only over a very small range under very slow or quasi-isometric (almost isometric) conditions of movement for a 
2461	limited time (since fatigue rapidly decreases tension). Naturally, constant tone also exists when a muscle is 
2462	relaxed, a state known as resting tonus. Whenever movement occurs, muscle tension increases or decreases, since 
2463	acceleration or deceleration is always involved and one of the stretch reflexes may be activated.
2464	European and Russian scientists prefer the term auxotonic, which refers to muscle action involving changes in 
2465	muscle tension and length and thus is often synonymous with isoinertial action (note that ‘auxotonic’ applies to 
2466	action of the muscle whereas ‘isoinertiaP applies to the load). Other authors use the term allodynamic , from the 
2467	Greek'alios' meaning 'other' or 'not the same'. These terms are all more accurate than isotonic in this context.
2468	Isotonic action is most likely to occur under static conditions, in which case we have isotonic isometric  action. 
2469	Even then, as is the ease with all muscic activation, there is rise time of tension build up, an intermediate phase of 
2470	maximal tension and a final decay time of tension decrease. For any prolonged action, the tension oscillates 
2471	irregularly over a range of values. If the load is near maximal, the muscles are unable to sustain the same level of 
2472	static muscle tension for more than a few seconds and the situation rapidly becomes anisotonic isometric.  In
2473	51
2474	
2475	=========== IDX 63 | printed 52 | viewer p.64
2476	SiJPERTRAINING
2477	general, the term isotonic should be reserved for the highly limited, short-movement range situations in which 
2478	muscle tension definitely remains fairly constant.
2479	The word isokinetic  is encountered in two contexts: firstly, some textbooks regard it as a specific type of 
2480	muscle contraction, and secondly, so-called isokinetic rehabilitation and testing machines are often used by 
2481	physical therapists. The term isokinetic contraction  is inappropriately applied in most cases, sincc it ii 
2482	impossible to produce a full-range muscle contraction at constant velocity. To producc any movement from rest, 
2483	Newton's first two Laws of Motion reveal that acceleration must be involved, so that constant velocity cannot 
2484	exist in a muscle which contracts from rest and returns to that state. Constant velocity can occur only over a part 
2485	of the range of action.
2486	Similarly, it is biomechanically impossible to design a purely isokinetic machine, since the user has to starta 
2487	given limb from rest and push against the machinc until it can constrain the motion to approximately constant 
2488	angular velocity over part of its range. The resistance offered by these devices increases in response to increase 
2489	in the force produced by the musclcs, thereby limiting the velocity of movement to roughly isokinetic conditions 
2490	over part of their range. They are designed in this way sincc some authorities maintain that strength is besi 
2491	developed if muscle tension is kept at a maximum at every point throughout the range, a proposition which ij 
2492	neither proved nor universally accepted with reference to all types of strength. Moreover, research has shown 
2493	that torque (and force) produced under isokinetic conditions is usually much lower than that produced

2643	Slow and Fast Twitch Muscle Fibres
2644	Earlier we discussed the actin and myosin components of muscle. We now note that the myosin plays a special 
2645	role in determining the contractile characteristics of the muscle via one of its specific components, namely the 
2646	myosin heavy chain (MHC). This chain appears in three different varieties or isoforms, referred to as type I, Ha 
2647	and II* isoforms, as are the muscles fibres which contain them (i.e., I, IIA and ILX). Type I fibres are also referred 
2648	to as slow fibres, while the other two fibres are known as fast fibres, because the latter contract far more rapidly 
2649	than the former (type I1X fibres contract approximately 10 times faster than type I fibres, with the contraction 
2650	velocity of IIA fibres lying intermediate to types 1  and NX (Andersen et al, 2000).

2652	themselves: there are also hybrid fibre types which contain mixtures of slow and fast myosin isoforms.

2654	exhibit less than 5% of this variety. On the other hand, in older adults this value rises to over 30% and becomes 
2655	the dominant fibre type in very old adults (Andersen et al, 2000).

2657	contracting, slow fatiguing fibres at one extreme and the fast contracting, fast fatiguing fibres at the other. Most

The muscle models presented in this text emphasize that fitness training should focus not only on musck

Research into this issue was instigated to probe the reason why muscle strength can increase without increase in 
muscle size or density of muscle filaments (sec earlier subsection entitled 'Strength and connective tissue').
The hypertrophy produced by strength conditioning and the enhancement of neuromuscular efficiency b) 
appropriate speed-strength and impulse training can also influence the storage and use of elastic energy. Since 
this hypertrophy is associated with an increase in the quantity and strength of connective tissue and an increase 
in the number of cross-bridges, the potential for storage of elastic energy can also increase, especially if the 
training has included suitable neuromuscular stimulation. This can be very important for improving performance 
both in acyclic power sports such as weightlifting and field athletics, as well as in cyclic endurance events suchai 
distance running and cycling.
1.7.3 Implications of the Muscle Model for Flexibility
Mobility and stability both rely heavily on flexibility and strength-flexibility, so it is important to understand the 
implications of the integrated muscle complex model for actions which involve stretching of the soft tissues of the 
body. This model reveals that the different types of stretching have specific effects on the different components 
of the muscle complex and that all-round preparation of the athlete depends on using the various types of stretck 
conditioning during the appropriate periods. This issue is covered in detail in Section 3.5.
1.7.4 The Relationship between Stability and Mobility
The fundamental principle of animal motion is that all activity is the result of balance between stability am  
mobility in the body. All sporting performance and training involve the learning and perfection of processes which 
produce the appropriate and effective interaction of mechanisms which stabilise and those which mobilise the 
joints from instant to instant during a given activity. As discussed in the next section, certain muscles act ini 
phasic role as prime movers or assistant movers, while others act in a tonic or postural role as stabilisers. 
Sometimes the roles of the muscles will interchange during certain activities and stabilisers will become moven 
and vice versa. The balance between stability and mobility depends on the neuromuscular integration of factors 
such as strength, endurance and range of movement, as well as the mechanical properties of the tissues involved 
(in particular, mechanical stiffness and damping ratio). This process is summarised graphically in Figure 1.24.
Neuromuscular processes, including the various reflexes of the body, orchestrate the overall interpla;. 
between stability and mobility to produce motor skill. Range of movement and stiffness are intimately related to  
flexibility, where the 'stiffness' referred to here is the mechanical stiffness of the tissues comprising the muscle 
complex (the spring constant k in the Hooke's Law equation relating force F to extension x: F = k.x) and not 'join!

tissues to store elastic energy (EE = x/i k.x2). Damping efficiency, the ability to absorb and dissipate shock or

1.8 Classification of Muscle Actions
In producing the various directions of movement, many muscles are simultaneously involved in controlling the 
action from its beginning to its end. This orchestration of diverse contributing muscles has led to different roles 
being allocated to each muscle group. One of the typical classification schemes recognizes the following traditional 
roles:
• Igonta Muscles acting as the so-called prime movers of the action. Prime movers  produce the most 
significant contribution to the movement, while assistant movers  play a more secondary role in assisting this 
prune action. Some authorities recognise emergency muscles  as a special class of assistant movers which come 
into play only when maximal force must be generated during a particular movement. In physiotherapy, the 
phenomenon of assistant movers being recruited by significant increases in loading is referred to as overflow.  The 
value of training periodically against near maximal or maximal resistance then becomes obvious.
' Antagonists: Muscles acting in direct opposition to the agonists. As emphasized by Basmajian (1978), this 
action does not necessarily accompany every agonistic contraction, but only under certain circumstances. Central 
nervous processes are sufficiently refined to control agonist activity without routine reliance on opposition by  
antagonists. After all, in engineering situations it is rarely necessary to use two motors in opposition to offer 
sophisticated control of any movement. All that is necessary is a single sufficiently powerful motor with rapid 
feedback processes to ensure accuracy, control, appropriate force and appropriate speed throughout the defined 
movement range.
Moreover, it is important to note that reciprocal inhibition  of the antagonist usually occurs whenever an 
agonist is strongly activated (see 3.5.3). In other words, the antagonist invariably relaxes when the agonist 
contracts, except when the action is extremely rapid and some 'antagonists' come into play to prevent joint 
damage due to the large momentum of the moving limb. The inappropriate activation of'antagonists' to oppose 
strongly contracting agonists, however, is recognised as one of the causes of musculoskeletal injury. For instance, 
the hamstrings can rupture if they contract to oppose the quadriceps while an athlete is sprinting or kicking. 
Russian researchers have shown that antagonist inhibition occurs most readily during rhythmic activity associated  
M ih motor learning.
So-called 'antagonists' may act continuously or in periodic spurts throughout a movement. Moreover, the 
presence of antagonist activity may be due to motor learning and not inherent reflexes. Sometimes, the existence 
of antagonistic activity is a sign of unskilled movement or nervous abnormality. Clearly, the automatic labelling of 
specific muscle actions as antagonistic needs to be tempered with caution, unless confirmed by careful 
electromyography (recording of electrical signals from the muscles).

ground. During dynamic stabilisation,  the musclcs arc in continuous contraction while simultaneously carrying

Simultaneously contracting, they oppose one another to cancel these movements and thereby assist the rectui

However, it must be emphasized that all muscles operate synergistically  in the normal person; they all cooperal 
by contributing forces in the most appropriate directions to produce the desired motion, although not necessan 
with maximum efficiency. It is preferable to remember that all muscles interact to produce the two fundamenti 
characteristics associated with all human movement: stability and mobility (see 1.7.4). To do this, the same muse

above types under all circumstances. Accurately speaking, a muscle may only be identified as carrying ou:

stabilisers, synergists and so forth: it is more accurate to state that each muscle plays a specific role at a give: 
moment (or during a certain movement phase) in a given situation.

1.9 Cocontraction and Ballistic Movement
In general, muscles will cooperate to produce two kinds of action: cocontraction  and ballistic movernc 
(Basmajian, 1978). In cocontraction , agonist and antagonist musclcs contract simultaneously, with dominances 
the former producing the external motion. Ballistic movement involves bursts of muscular activity followed 
phases of relaxation during which the motion continues due to stored limb momentum. The term 'ballistic' is 
sincc the coursc of action of the limb is determined by the initial agonist impulse, just as the flight of a bullet 
determined by the initial explosive charge in the cartridge.
Skilled, rapid ballistic and moderately fast continuous movements are preprogrammed in the central nerv o u s. 
system, whereas slow, discontinuous movements are not. The ballistic action rarely involves feedback process? 
during the course of the movement. Feedback  from the muscles and joints to the central nervous system pennr 
the ensuing motion to be monitored continuously and to be modified, if necessary. The resulting movenia 
becomcs accurately executed and the relevant soft tissues arc protected from injury by changes in muscle tensa 
and by the activation of appropriate antagonists to control and terminate the motion.

If no sensory or proprioceptive feedback is implicated, the mode of control is termed feedforward  or 'open- 
loop' control (Smith & Smith, 1962; Green, 1967). Here, control is preprogrammed into the central nervous and 
ncuromuscular systems by the visual and auditory systems before movement begins, so that ongoing monitoring 
mechanisms arc not involved. The first sign of impending programmed action is the inhibition of antagonist 
contraction preceding agonist action, as revealed by the electromyograph. Premature activation of the antagonists 
may not only diminish skill, but it can cause muscle injury. During ballistic and other rapid movement, antagonist 
contraction is appropriate only to terminate further motion of the limb concerned. Not only is there no antagonist 
activity during ballistic movements, but it is also absent during discontinuous motion (Brooks, 1983). The 
advantage offered by feedforward processes is speed of action, whereas its main disadvantage is the lack of 
flexibility which can be offered by feedback. Nevertheless, the importance of feedforward processes in human 
movement should not be underestimated, as implied by the Russians in using regimes of visualisation and 
autogenic training in sports preparation.
1.10 Types of Muscle Action
Traditionally, the following types of muscic “contraction” (or, more accurately, “action”) beginning with the 
prefix '-iso' (meaning 'the same') are defined: isotonic  (constant muscle tension), isometric  (constant muscle 
length), isokinetic (constant velocity of motion) and isoinertial (constant load). In addition, movement may occur 
under concentric (so-called “muscic shortening”) and eccentric (so-called “muscic lengthening”) conditions. Before 
these terms are unquestioningly applied to exercise, it is important to examine their validity.
In all of the above cases, it is more accurate to speak about muscle action taking place under various 
movement conditions. It is well known that a muscle can only contract or relax relative to its resting or 
inactivated state, so that it is a misnomer to refer to eccentric muscle action as a “contraction” in which a muscle 
contracts and lengthens simultaneously. Actually, this means that a muscle which has contracted under concentric 
or isometric conditions is simply returning under eccentric conditions to its original resting length. To avoid 
confusion like this, it is preferable to define muscle action as follows:
• Concentric - Action in which the proximal and distal muscle attachments move towards one another
• Eccentric - Action in which the proximal and distal muscle attachments move away from one another
• Isometric - Action in which the proximal and distal muscle attachments do not move relative to one another
Isometric literally means 'same length', a state which occurs only in a relaxed muscle. Actually, it is not muscle 
length, but joint angle which remains constant. Contraction means 'shortening', so that isometric contraction, like 
all other forms of muscle contraction, involves internal movement processes which shorten the muscle fibres. 
Isometric contraction may be defined more accurately to mean muscle action which occurs when there is no 
external movement or changc in joint angle (or distance between origin and insertion). It occurs when the force 
produced by a muscle exactly balances the resistance imposed upon it and no movement results. Although not 
incorrect, the term isometric may be replaced by the simple word static, without sacrificing any scientific rigour. It 
is interesting to note that, during isometric action, mechanical work, some of which is absorbed by the tendinous 
tissue, is generated by the shortening of muscle fibres (Masamitsu et al, 1998).
The term isotonic, however, should be avoided under most circumstances, since it is virtually impossible for 
muscle tension to remain the same while joint movement occurs over any extended range. Constancy is possible 
only over a very small range under very slow or quasi-isometric (almost isometric) conditions of movement for a 
limited time (since fatigue rapidly decreases tension). Naturally, constant tone also exists when a muscle is 
relaxed, a state known as resting tonus. Whenever movement occurs, muscle tension increases or decreases, since 
acceleration or deceleration is always involved and one of the stretch reflexes may be activated.
European and Russian scientists prefer the term auxotonic, which refers to muscle action involving changes in 
muscle tension and length and thus is often synonymous with isoinertial action (note that ‘auxotonic’ applies to 
action of the muscle whereas ‘isoinertiaP applies to the load). Other authors use the term allodynamic , from the 
Greek'alios' meaning 'other' or 'not the same'. These terms are all more accurate than isotonic in this context.
Isotonic action is most likely to occur under static conditions, in which case we have isotonic isometric  action. 
Even then, as is the ease with all muscic activation, there is rise time of tension build up, an intermediate phase of 
maximal tension and a final decay time of tension decrease. For any prolonged action, the tension oscillates 
irregularly over a range of values. If the load is near maximal, the muscles are unable to sustain the same level of 
static muscle tension for more than a few seconds and the situation rapidly becomes anisotonic isometric.  In

general, the term isotonic should be reserved for the highly limited, short-movement range situations in which 
muscle tension definitely remains fairly constant.
The word isokinetic  is encountered in two contexts: firstly, some textbooks regard it as a specific type of 
muscle contraction, and secondly, so-called isokinetic rehabilitation and testing machines are often used by 
physical therapists. The term isokinetic contraction  is inappropriately applied in most cases, sincc it ii 
impossible to produce a full-range muscle contraction at constant velocity. To producc any movement from rest, 
Newton's first two Laws of Motion reveal that acceleration must be involved, so that constant velocity cannot 
exist in a muscle which contracts from rest and returns to that state. Constant velocity can occur only over a part 
of the range of action.
Similarly, it is biomechanically impossible to design a purely isokinetic machine, since the user has to starta 
given limb from rest and push against the machinc until it can constrain the motion to approximately constant 
angular velocity over part of its range. The resistance offered by these devices increases in response to increase 
in the force produced by the musclcs, thereby limiting the velocity of movement to roughly isokinetic conditions 
over part of their range. They are designed in this way sincc some authorities maintain that strength is besi 
developed if muscle tension is kept at a maximum at every point throughout the range, a proposition which ij 
neither proved nor universally accepted with reference to all types of strength. Moreover, research has shown 
that torque (and force) produced under isokinetic conditions is usually much lower than that produced 
isometrically at the same joint angle (see Figs 2.8, 2.9). In other words, it is impossible to use isokinetic machines 
to develop maximal strength throughout the range of joint movement.
The presence of any acceleration or deceleration always reveals the absence of full-range constant velocity.

1.12 Types of Muscle Fibre
Skeletal muscle does not simply comprise an extremely large number of the same type of fibre, further subdivided 
into actin, myosin and other components. Research has revealed that muscle fibres may be classified in terms of 
factors such as colour, contractile properties, content of myoglobin (the pigment which binds oxygen in the 
blood), relative content of metabolic enzymes, and the content of mitochondria.
Slow and Fast Twitch Muscle Fibres
Earlier we discussed the actin and myosin components of muscle. We now note that the myosin plays a special 
role in determining the contractile characteristics of the muscle via one of its specific components, namely the 
myosin heavy chain (MHC). This chain appears in three different varieties or isoforms, referred to as type I, Ha 
and II* isoforms, as are the muscles fibres which contain them (i.e., I, IIA and ILX). Type I fibres are also referred 
to as slow fibres, while the other two fibres are known as fast fibres, because the latter contract far more rapidly 
than the former (type I1X fibres contract approximately 10 times faster than type I fibres, with the contraction 
velocity of IIA fibres lying intermediate to types 1  and NX (Andersen et al, 2000).
The type I, IIA and IIX fibres or pure fibres are not the only form in which the various isoforms express 
themselves: there are also hybrid fibre types which contain mixtures of slow and fast myosin isoforms. 
Interestingly, these hybrid fibres are scarce in young people, with vastus lateralis studies showing that the latter 
exhibit less than 5% of this variety. On the other hand, in older adults this value rises to over 30% and becomes 
the dominant fibre type in very old adults (Andersen et al, 2000).
Research indicates that all muscle fibres appear to lie on a continuum which extends between the slow 
contracting, slow fatiguing fibres at one extreme and the fast contracting, fast fatiguing fibres at the other. Most 
classification schemes refer to the these extremes as Type I red, slow twitch (ST) fibres and Type II white, fast 
twitch (FT) fibres, where the difference in colour is due to the fact that red fibres have a higher content of 
myoglobin. Since slow fibres rely largely on aerobic metabolism and fast fibres depend more on anaerobic 
metabolism, endurance athletes are heavily reliant on a large percentage of slow fibres and short distance or 
strength athletes require a large percentage of fast fibres.
In general, ST (Type I)  fibres are slow contracting, slow fatiguing reddish fibres with a small diameter, high 
oxidative capacity and low glycolytic capacity (ability to rely on stored glycogen as an energy source for 
resynthcsizing ATP). They are efficient in maintaining posture and sustaining prolonged, low intensity activity 
such as distance running, particularly since they usually contain a large number of mitochondria and use ATP 
slowly. These fibres may be tonically or phasically active for prolonged periods, being known to fire at fairly low 
rates for as much as 20-35% of the day (Edstrom & Grimby, 1986).
FT (Type II) fibres have usually been subdivided into several sub-classes, the most frequently mentioned 
being FTa (Type ILA) and FTb (Type IIB or IIX in humans). Type IIA (FTa)  fibres are also called fast twitch, 
oxidative-glycolytic (FTOG), since they are able to draw on oxidative and glycolytic mechanisms for energy. 
They are apparently suited to fast, repetitive, low intensity movement and are recruited next after Type I (ST) 
fibres. They possess fairly large numbers of mitochondria and therefore tend to be reasonably resistant to fatigue 
and can recover fairly rapidly after exercise. Some authorities believe that they are Type II (FT) fibres which are 
adapted for endurance activity. Bodybuilders often tend to have a high relative percentage of these fibres, which 
has led some researchers to propose that these fibres may be especially able to adapt to hypertrophy in response 
to suitable training stimuli (Jurimae et al, 1997).
TypellX (IIB or FTb) fibres are fast contracting, whitish, low myoglobin fibres with a large diameter, high 
glycolytic capacity, low oxidative capacity and few mitochondria. They are suited to high power output and are 
usually recruited only where very rapid or very intense effort is required, as in field athletics and weightlifting, 
where athletes in these sports exhibit high percentages of these fibres (Abemethy, 1994; Tesch, 1998). They

Further research reveals that this high intensity is not necessarily dependent on the use of 1RM (1 repetition 
maximum) or near IRM loads, but the degree to which the relevant muscle fibres are recruited during the effort. 
In this respect, the terms fast twitch  and slow twitch  do not necessarily mean that fast movements recruit 
exclusively FT fibres and slow movements ST fibres. To analyse the involvement of different fibre types, it is 
vital to determine the force that needs to be produced. If large acceleration of the load is involved, Newton's 
Second Law of Motion decrees that the resulting force will be large. Thus, the maximal force generated during 
rapid acceleration of a 100kg bench press easily can exceed the maximal force produced during a slowly accelerated 
150kg bench press. Both a small load accelerated rapidly and a heavy load accelerated slowly strongly involve the 
FT fibres. Likewise, explosive movements rely heavily on the action of FT fibres.
59

=========== IDX 71 | printed 60 | viewer p.72
SUPERTRAINING
Moreover, rapid movements often recruit the muscle stretch (myotatic) reflex, which can elicit a powerful 
contraction. Relevant to this process is Starling's Law, which states that the strength of contraction is 
proportional to the original length of the muscle at the moment of contraction. The ideal relationship between 
tension and length in a sarcomere occurs when the muscle is slightly stretched and the actin and myosin filaments 
just overlap slightly. However, in applying this law, it has to be remembered that the advantage offered by the 
stretching may be diminished in cases where this stretching occurs at large joint angles which provide poor 
leverage. The well-known prestretch  principle in bodybuilding training and the plyometric method in speed- 
strength training rely on this phenomenon. Many gymnasium machines are seriously limiting in that they do not 
allow the user to begin a movement with a pre-stretch. Not only does this diminish the force which can be 
generated, but it also exposes joints to a greater risk of injury because the movement begins without muscular 
support for the ligaments.
The importance of the nervous system in developing strength cannot be ignored. As stated earlier, the 
development of strength is related to the number of appropriate muscle fibres firing simultaneously, which is 
entirely a function of the nervous system. An additional finding is that, if the nerve which normally supplies a 
ST muscle fibre is surgically interchanged (‘cross reinnervated’) with one which supplies a FT fibre, the ST fibre I 
will behave like a FT fibre (e.g. Bacou ct al, 1996; Baijot ct al, 1998). These studies, carried out on rabbits, suggest 
that sensitivity to motor innervation increases from the glycolytic to oxidative types of fibre, in the order: IIB > I 
IIX/IID > ILA> I (where the IID, like the IIB fibre types occur in small mammals as analogues of the human IK I 
type). In other words, the behaviour of muscic would appear to be determined by the activity of the nerve fibres I 
which supply it, a deduction which is discussed further in the next section.
The rate and number of fibres firing depends on voluntary and involuntary processes, the voluntary ones 
being related to personal motivation and biofeedback techniques, and the involuntary ones to feedback information , 
from the proprioceptive system, including the various stretch reflexes.
Thus, the simple act of motivating or emotionally willing yourself, through methods such as self-talk or 
guided imagery to produce greater or faster efforts can recruit a greater number of muscle fibres at an increased rate 
of firing. Encouragement by a training partner can also play a useful role in this regard, if done at appropriate 
stages during an exercise. Interestingly, the method of training with progressively heavier loads or at larger i 
accelerations is a valuable way of learning how to motivate yourself at progressively higher levels of performance, n 
The carry-over of this may well benefit one in all aspects of daily life.
Further Aspects of Muscle Plasticity
A great deal of ongoing research is investigating the plasticity, or structural-functional change, of muscic in 
response to various conditions, such as active and passive loading, different types of neural activation, lack of 
loading and electrical stimulation. Some of this work has been reported elsewhere in this book, but it is relevant to 
include some further information on other recent findings in this regard.
One of the prominent hypotheses is that the pattern of neural activation determines the quantity and quality j 
of contractile proteins (myosin and actin isoforms) and metabolic proteins (glycolytic and oxidative enzymes) I  
which the muscles express (Roy et al, 1991). This thesis emerged from studies which showed that typical FT 
muscle after very prolonged daily low frequency stimulation (24 hours a day) produces physiological, biochemical 
and structural changes which resemble those found in ST muscle (Lomo et al, 1974; Pette & Vrbova, 1985). This | 
seemed to reinforce work first done by Buller et al (1960), who crossed nerves over from one group of muscic to 
another and found that this apparently caused the muscle fibres to change their type. They pointed out, however, i  
that “the neural influence on muscle speed is not exerted by nerve impulses as such”, but could also have been due 
to neural growth processes associated with hormonal factors (e.g. thyroid hormone and testosterone).
Hormonal effects generally seem to depend on the type and level of activity of the muscle fibres involved i 
The muscle fibre types involved in the anabolic properties of estrogens have not yet been clearly described, but io 
the case of growth hormone and insulin, mainly the ST type is affected, partly via an increased secretion of 
somatomedins (Insulin-like Growth Factors - IGFs) or by interaction on IGF receptors (Vigneron et al, 1989). I 
The other hormones in the body tend to produce a shift toward more vigorous fast contracting activity, which 
increases the percentage of fast glycolytic fibres. Anabolic hormones such as the androgens, catecholamines and 
bcta-agonists enlarge these fibres, whereas excess quantities of thyroid hormones or glucocorticoids promote their

2952	The powerful influence of androgenic and anabolic steroids such as testosterone on muscle hypertrophy and 
2953	function are well known, which has led directly to their huge abuse in sport. Less well known is the potent effect 
2954	of thyroid hormone in this same regard. The first study to reveal this was conducted by Gold et al (1970), who 
2955	showed that thyroid state influences the contractile properties of slow skeletal muscle. They found in rat soleus 
2956	muscle that the hypothyroid state decreased the normal shortening velocity by 60%, while hyperthyroidism 
2957	increased this velocity by 20%. Other work revealed that in the solcus muscle hyperthyroidism converts some 
2958	slow  Type I fibres to Type IIA and IIX fibres and shifts the force vs frequency curve to the right (Caiozzo et al, 
2959	1991). At the same time, hypothyroidism completely suppresses the expression of FT fibres in soleus. Even 
2960	though soleus comprises only about 15% of FT fibres, this FT to ST conversion produces significant changes in 
2961	the solcus force-frequency curve, which implies that the small relative population of FT fibres in soleus plays a 
2962	vital role in determining the mechanical properties of this muscle (Caiozzo & Haddad, 1996). Thyroid state, 
2963	however, has far less effect on FT muscles, such as plantaris (Caiozzo et al, 1991).
2964	Hypothyroidism also retards the rate and extent of muscle growth, although the change in maximal muscle 
2965	tension per unit cross-sectional area is insignificant. Another aspect of this work is the fascinating discovery that 
2966	there appears to be a subset of the ST fibre group which is unresponsive to hormonal, mechanical or electrical 
2967	stimuli and which have been called refractory Type I fibres (Caiozzo et al, 1993).
2968	In summary, this research, which is part of an effort to understand altered gene expression for specific 
2969	isoforms as a central process in muscic adaptation, shows that thyroid hormone and mechanical activity can 
2970	produce rapid qualitative and quantitative changes in muscle protein expression and possibly also on overall 
2971	muscle function (Caiozzo & Haddad, 1996). Although any suggestion of athletes experimenting with ingestion of 
2972	thyroid hormone in a private quest for enhanced performance should be deemed as potentially very hazardous, 
2973	this research implies that significant alterations in one’s natural thyroid hormone status may be associated with 
2974	undesired changes in muscle performance.
2975	Other recent research concerning the plasticity of muscle has shown that (Roy ct al, 1991):
2976	I Muscle atrophy produced by lack of stimulation, nerve damage or reduced gravity proceeds in the following 
2977	order: atrophy in the slow extensors is greater than in the fast extensors, which in turn is greater than in the 
2978	fast flexors. Conversely, regular progressive overloading increases the mass of fast muscle more than slow 
2979	muscle, with fast extensors hypertrophying more than fast flexors. Possibly this is a rational manifestation of 
2980	some survival mechanism, since rapid extensor actions, which are associated with striking an assailant or 
2981	thrusting him away, generally are involved more in self defense processes than flexion activities.
2982	1 Muscles display regional change in response to the effects of activation or deactivation. Typically, the deeper 
2983	regions of the muscle, namely those with the highest proportion of oxidative (ST) fibres, tend to atrophy more 
2984	than the superficial regions, while the same regions also seem to show the greatest hypertrophy after 
2985	functional overload.
2986	3. The concept of variation in muscle fibre size as a function of fibre type fails to take into account the existence 
2987	of many exceptions to this often proliferated rule. Popularly, FT (Type II) fibres are assumed to 
2988	consistently have larger diameters than Type I, an observation which seems to be borne out in the superficial 
2989	muscle regions, but not in deeper regions, where the two fibre types have similar diameters. Moreover, in 
2990	predominantly slow muscles such as soleus, vastus intermedius and adductor longus, animal studies show that 
2991	the fast fibres are consistently smaller than the slow fibres. In human males, the Type II (FT) fibres of 
2992	vastus lateralis are larger than the ST fibres, but the opposite tends to occur in females (Saltin & Gollnick, 
2993	1983).
2994	4. The largest muscles tend to atrophy and hypertrophy the most, irrespective of fibre type. When this change 
2995	is calculated in the form of a relative percentage, it is often the same in slow and fast muscle.
2996	5 The fastest rate of muscle atrophy takes place in the initial 1-2 weeks of inactivity, especially regarding the 
2997	degradation of contractile proteins (like slow myosin in soleus), after which this rate progresses more slowly. 
2998	The situation concerning hypertrophy is more complicated. Muscle mass increases markedly within a few 
2999	days of functional overload (despite the assumptions that all initial changes are mainly neural), but, during the 
3000	first week or so, this increase in cross-sectional area offers little or no increase in strength. After this initial 
3001	latency period during which relative muscle strength decreases, this trend reverses and normal concurrent 
3002	increases in hypertrophy and strength proceed for several weeks or months. After about 2-3 months, the rate 
3003	of increase slows down, as is the case with atrophic changes after a similar period.

3008	6. Prolonged muscle stimulation does not increase muscle strength and hypertrophy, but can actually decrease 
3009	both after several weeks of electrical stimulation (Eisenberg et al, 1984). Moreover, fibres that are the least 
3010	active, as based on the sequence of accepted recruitment patterns, usually are the largest fibres in normal 
3011	mammals. This raises questions about the practicc of continued long periods of intense resistance training, 
3012	These findings suggest that excessive strenuous training can produce stagnation or decrease of hypertrophy 
3013	and muscle function and that the condition which optimally promotes hypertrophy and strength increase is the  
3014	production ofsome minimum level offorce for some minimum amount of time.
3015	7. There is a close association between enzymes associated with myosin ATP metabolism and those involved 
3016	with glycolysis, suggesting that there may be some functional advantage for the maximal rates of glycogen and 
3017	ATP breakdown to coincide, as happens during intense muscle contraction. Since this would match the rate of 
3018	energy expenditure during myosin activity with an immediate replacement of energy by glycolysis, this 
3019	concept seems logically compelling. This idea is supported further by the fact that fast myosin hydrolyses 
3020	ATP twice as rapidly as slow myosin, which is reflected by very a marked increase in the flux of energy 
3021	substrates via the process of glycolysis. It would not be unexpected to find that the expression of proteins 
3022	associated with specific myosin type and the glycolytic capabilities of a fibre indeed are closely linked.
3023	8. Musclcs and motor units can atrophy without altering their fatiguability, with slow muscle fibres showing 
3024	prolonged capacity to metabolically support the amount of contractile proteins left in the atrophying muscic 
3025	cells. However, if the whole body is involved in producing strength output, the atrophied muscles will become 
3026	more easily fatigued because of recruitment of larger numbers and types of muscle fibres, many of which may 
3027	well be susceptible to fatigue.
3028	9. Although most research has stressed that training increases the size of muscle fibres, some studies show that 
3029	muscles adapt sarcomere number and rest length in response to different patterns of use. For instance, fixing a I 
3030	joint in a flexed or extended position that lengthens some musclcs and shortens others causes the muscle fibres 
3031	to lengthen or shorten to establish a new mean sarcomere length which ensures that active force production is 
3032	maximal at the maintained joint position (see review by Lieber R, "Skeletal Muscic Structure and Function" ) I 
3033	Work done by Morgan and colleagues (Lynn & Morgan, 1994) on rat vastus intermedius muscle fibres 
3034	revealed that eccentric exercise produces a greater increase in sarcomere number than concentric training, but 
3035	Koh and Herzog (1998) found no significant increase cither in sarcomere number or muscle length in rabbit 
3036	dorsiflexor muscles in response to eccentric training. The differences between these two studies may relate to 
3037	species differences, or different exercise regimes, stressing that more work needs to be done in this area.
3038	These findings collectively add further support for the view (stated in the previous section by Goldspink anc 
3039	others) that the relative expression of isoforms of myosin in skeletal muscle is strongly influenced by the 
3040	degree of mechanical or gravity-related stress imposed on muscle.
3041	The Implications of Ballistic Research
3042	Most of the studies of force generated by muscle have been carried out under isokinetic conditions, which rarely, 
3043	occur in sport. Consequently, Bosco and Komi (1979a) re-examined the force-velocity curves under ballistic 
3044	conditions, particularly with respect to the involvement of the different muscle fibre types. This was done by 
3045	using a force-plate to examine the relationship between force and knee angular velocity in subjects who performed i 
3046	maximal vertical jumps with barbells of different weight on their shoulders (Fig 1.27). In another study, they I 
3047	concluded that vertical jump performance is related to the percentage of FT fibres (Bosco & Komi, 1979b).
3048	More recently, it was found that there is a significant relationship between FT% and the power output of 
3049	the leg extensor musclcs when working dynamically at loads exceeding 23% of the maximal isometric force Fma 
3050	(Thihanyi ct al, 1982). However, when the load increased to over 40% of Fmax. this relationship disappeared.
3051	It would seem that the FT fibres are the main contributors to force production in pure ballistic motion w itfc 
3052	maximal voluntary effort, while the ST contribution rises as the muscle contraction time increases from 100 to  
3053	1000 milliseconds. This deduction agrees with the relationship found between FT% and the time taken for the 
3054	force to increase from 10 to 30% of Fmax (Viitasalo & Komi, 1978, Viitalaso et al, 1982). This relationship: 
3055	between fibre composition and contraction time is not exhibited when the time taken for force to increase froti \ 
3056	60% to 100% of Fmax is measured. Moreover, no definite relationship has been found between Fmax and muscle 
3057	fibre composition.

3062	Fifurel .27 The relationship between average force and angular velocity of the knee, obtained from subjects performing squat jumps 
3063	with different weights on the shoulders. The percentage contributions of the different fibre types are shown, as suggested by Bosco. 
3064	Gmphi based on the work of Bosco & Komi (1979a).
3065	Therefore, muscic cross-sectional area may be most important for production of maximal strength, regardless of 
3066	muscle composition (Ikai & Fukunaga, 1968), whereas power or explosive maximal strength depends more on 
3067	FT%  (Bosco & Komi, 1979b). It should be noted that ST fibres appear to predominate in most graded 
3068	movements requiring less than approximately 20% of the maximum force capability of the given muscles and 
3069	produced at submaximal speeds (see Fig 1.26).
3070	However, if the movements involve producing large forces of short duration at very high velocity, then the 
3071	FT fibres appear to be recruited, while some inhibition may be exerted over ST fibres (Minagawa et al, 1978). 
3072	Therefore, the pattern of muscle fibre recruitment is related to the mcchanical pattern of muscle contraction and 
3073	the plasticity of the central nervous system enables the body to select the most efficient pattern of muscic 
3074	activation to carry out a wide variety of movements of different intensity, duration and speed (Bosco, 1982).
3075	Bosco (1982) compares the patterns of muscle fibre recruitment in different cases to illustrate the limitations 
3076	of the recruitment schcmc of Figure 1.26. Firstly, he points out that walking at moderate speed (ground contact 
3077	tim e about 700ms) produces a vertical ground reaction force of over 700 Newtons, relying entirely on ST action 
3078	according to Figure 1.26.
3079	Secondly, if a person pushes a car from rest, the development of force is graded and progressively involves 
3080	more and more FT fibres (see Fig 1.26). Finally, if a subject lies supine with knees flexed to 90° and then 
3081	performs a maximal effort knee extension by thrusting against the foot plate of a horizontal leg press machine, the 
3082	musclcs approach their highest shortening velocity. However, the force produced in this case is usually less than 
3083	the force developed during walking although it is the result of entirely FT action. Bosco concludes that the 
3084	jehema presented in Figure 1.26 may be suitable for graded, progressive loading, but it is unsuitable to describe 
3085	ballistic motion. He suggests that Figure 1.27 may be more appropriate under these circumstances. He remarks 
3086	on the implications of this for isokinetic training.
3087	He notes that the velocity of efficient isokinetic apparatus is adjustable to enable it to more closely match the 
3088	requirements of specific sports, but cautions that this type of training is not advisable for athletes engaged in any 
3089	sports involving predominantly ballistic motion (Bosco, 1982). Much of the international literature contends that 
3090	the isokinetic training method is the most effective for neuromuscular reasons, whereas dynamic auxotonic training 
3091	is highly effective for promoting power development and muscle hypertrophy, an hypothesis which has caused 
3092	considerable confusion among training specialists. It must be pointed out that maximal effort on an isokinetic 
3093	device usually produces the same maximal motor unit activation for both concentric and eccentric contraction 
3094	iKom i. 1973b), even though prolific research reveals that fewer motor units are recruited during maximal eccentric 
3095	w ork to produce greater muscle tension than during concentric work.
3096	Similarly, no change in myoelectric activity was found during maximal vertical jump performance performed 
3097	•aith or without additional loads (Bosco et al, 1982). This means that maximal motor unit activation can be 
3098	elicited by ballistic action, regardless of muscle shortening velocity and pattern of force production during 
3099	concentric work (Fig 1.28).

3125	(Bosco, 1982). Whether this is the result of positive changes in the myotatic stretch reflex, the structure of the

3132	action may raise the threshold at which significant inhibition by the Golgi apparatus takes place. This has

3134	1.13 The Mechanism of Muscle Growth
3135	Living tissue grows by increase in the size of its components ( hypertrophy) or  by increase in the number of its 
3136	components (hyperplasia). This growth in structure is an adaptation to the functional demands placed on the 
3137	given system, where adaptation occurs at a molecular level within the genetic structure of the cells.
3138	Research by Meerson discovered a link between the volume of loading imposed on the cells and their genetic 
3139	structure. He learned that stimulating cellular function activates the genetic apparatus and increases the speed of 
3140	transcription, translation, protein synthesis and build-up of certain structures (Nikituk & Samoilov, 1990). He 
3141	propounded the concept of intensity of functioning of structures  (IFS), which posits that the functional capacity of 
3142	a system is related to its mass. Thus, the more intense the required function, the greater the mass of the working 
3143	structure needed to perform the function. In the light of the discussion in Section 1.6, the mass involved should 
3144	be understood to be the 'active mass'.
3145	We are now in a position to examine the increase in muscle mass as an adaptation to resistance training. In 
3146	the case of muscic fibres, the occurrence of hypertrophy  in response to strength training is a well-established fact, 
3147	but there is considerable debate concerning muscle hyperplasia.  Gonyea (1980) has presented evidence of 
3148	hyperplasia in cats subjected to heavy resistance training, but other researchers have criticised this work, pointing 
3149	out that there may be fibre splitting, but not proliferation of new fibres. Certain Russian research also suggests 
3150	that increase in muscle mass occurs not only through hypertrophy of muscic fibres, but as a result of an increase 
3151	in fibre number by means of the splitting of hypertrophied muscle fibres and the development of muscle fibres 
3152	from  muscle 'buds' and satellite cells (Gudz, 1968, 1976). In addition, it has been suggested that muscle 
3153	hyperplasia may occur with extremely intense resistance training, but current evidence from human subjects is 
3154	still by no means unequivocal.
3155	However, the contention that skeletal muscle enlargement in adult animals is solely due to changes in fibre is 
3156	now being seriously challenged by recent evidence which suggests strongly that fibre hyperplasia may also 
3157	contribute to muscle mass increases in mammals under certain extreme conditions (Antonio & Gonyea, 1993). 
3158	Research involving direct counts of muscle fibres using nitric acid digestion techniques have shown that both 
3159	exercise and stretch overload result in significant increases in the number of muscle fibres, plus indirect fibre counts 
3160	using histological measurements of muscic cross-sections have suggested fibre hyperplasia. In addition, the 
3161	expression of embryonic myosin isoforms has furnished indirect evidence for the formation of new fibres in bird 
3162	flight muscles subjected to long-term stretch overloading (with weights attached to their wings). Moreover, satellite 
3163	cells, which can activate new cell formation, have been shown to be involved in muscle fibre hyperplasia in 
3164	stretching and dynamic exercise. Hyperplasia may also occur due to fibre splitting of large fibres that subdivide into 
3165	two or more smaller fibres (Hather et al, 1991; Tamaki et al, 1992; Antonio & Gonyea, 1994).
3166	With regard to hyperplasia in humans, Antonio states that evidence for its occurrence is indirect. He points 
3167	out that one study showed that elite bodybuilders and powerlifters had upper arm circumferences 27% greater than 
3168	normal sedentary controls, although the cross-sectional area of their triceps muscle fibres were not different from 
3169	the control group (Yamada et al, 1989). Larsson and Tesch (1986) found that bodybuilders displayed thigh 
3170	circumference measurements 19% greater than that of control subjects, yet the average size of their muscle fibres 
3171	A cre not significantly different from that of the controls. Furthermore, Nygaard and Neilsen (1978) did a cross- 
3172	sectional study in which they found that the overall size of deltoid muscles was greater in swimmers than in 
3173	controls, despite their having smaller Type I and IIA muscle fibres.
3174	Furthermore, Alway et al. (1989) compared the biceps brachii muscle in elite male and female bodybuilders and 
3175	found that the cross-sectional area of the biceps muscle correlated to both fibre area and number, unlike other 
3176	workers who have shown that bodybuilders have larger fibres instead of a greater number of fibres when compared 
3177	to a control population (Haggmark et al, 1978; McDougall ct al, 1984; Schantz et al, 1981). Some scientists counter 
3178	these findings by suggesting that many bodybuilders or other athletes have the same sized or smaller muscle fibres 
3179	versus untrained controls is because of a greater genetic endowment of muscle fibres. In other words, they must 
3180	have been born with more muscle fibres. Antonio points out that, if this were true, then the prolonged periods of 
3181	intense training performed by elite bodybuilders and other strength athletes has produced at best average size fibres. 
3182	This implies that they were bom with a system of below average size fibres that training simply enlarged to average 
3183	size, which is a generally unlikely and implausible.
3184	65

3186	=========== IDX 77 | printed 66 | viewer p.78
3187	SUPERTRAINING
3188	Antonio considers that the question which needs to be asked is not whether muscle fibre hyperplasia actual!; 
3189	occurs, but rather under what conditions it does occur. The prolific amount of evidence which shows that increas 
3190	in muscle mass most commonly is associated with an increase in muscle cross-sectional area certainly emphasize 
3191	that hyperplasia does not take place as a simple matter of course, but under very special conditions which warran 
3192	further research.
3193	Although the existence of hyperplasia of muscle fibre may be uncertain or rare, hyperplasia o f structures  
3194	within the muscle fibre and cell docs occur.  Nikituk and Samoilov (1990) identify two types of subfibral 
3195	hyperplasia:
3196	• Sarcoplasmic hyperplasia^  which involves an increase in the number of sarcoplasmic organelles
3197	• Myofibrillar-mitochondrial hyperplasia , which involves increase in the number of myofibrils and
3198	mitochondria.
3199	Increase in muscle diameter is due to enlargement of individual muscle fibres by an increase in the number and size 
3200	of individual myofibrils (Goldspink, 1980), accompanied by an increase in the amount of connective tissue 
3201	(McDonagh & Davies, 1984), as discussed in Section 1.6. This increase in muscle protein is produced by 
3202	increased protein synthesis and decreased protein degradation (Goldberg et al, 1975). Two types of muscic 
3203	hypertrophy may occur (Fig 1.30):
3204	• Sarcoplasmic hypertrophy.  In this case, the volume of non-con tractile protein and semifluid plasma between 
3205	the muscle fibres increases. Although the cross-sectional area of the muscle increases, the density of muscle 
3206	fibres per unit area decreases and there is no corresponding increase in muscle strength.
3207	• Sarcomere hypertrophy.  Here there is an increase in the size and number of the sarcomeres which comprise 
3208	the myofibrils. These may be added in series or parallel with the existing myofibrils, although only the 
3209	parallel growth will contribute to an increased ability to produce muscic tension. The area density of 
3210	myofibrils increases and there is a significantly greater ability to exert muscular strength.
3211	Except for a few sports, such as bodybuilding and sumo wrestling, in which an increased bodymass without

3349	1.14 Neurophysiological Aspects of Exercise
3350	All-round preparation of the athlete necessitates physical and psychological training, not as separate components, 
3351	but as closely interrelated aspects of human performance. The mental and physical systems interact continuously 
3352	and it is vital to remember that the highly-skilled, superbly conditioned body is of little value in competition 
3353	without the right frame of mind. For instance, an emotional upset can prevent the athlete from relaxing or 
3354	concentrating to produce the necessary degree of physical efficiency. Similarly, a slight physical injury may 
3355	disturb one sufficiently to diminish confidence, concentration and skill.
3356	The body may be viewed as a living cybernetic (control and communication) system in which the central 
3357	nervous system, including the brain and spinal cord, controls the functions of the body via two major 
3358	communication systems: the nervous system (autonomic and voluntary systems) and the hormonal system 
3359	(endocrine glands).
3360	The hormonal system is involved with control of the slower bodily processes such as growth, metabolism, 
3361	sexual function, excretion and temperature regulation. The nervous system is concerned mainly with rapid 
3362	processes such as sight, hearing, thinking and muscular contraction. However, these two systems interact in 
3363	numerous processes, the link between them being the hypothalamus, situated near the middle of the brain. The 
3364	hypothalamus is linked with the brain's limbic system (intimately connected with emotion) and the pituitary 
3365	gland (sometimes called the master gland of the body). It may be inferred immediately that physical efficiency 
3366	«i;pends on proper utilisation of thought processes, emotions and muscles.
3367	This may be seen from Figure 1.32 which illustrates how external stimuli from the environment and internal 
3368	stimuli from within the body are received by the specialised transducers of the sensory systems and relayed to 
3369	the relevant parts of the central nervous system for further processing. Not only does the latter system activate 
3370	the muscular system to produce appropriate patterns of movement, but it also relays information to the 
3371	hypothalamus which may produce emotional and glandular responses.
3372	Tbs model offers a simplified foundation for the psychology of sport. The remainder of this section is devoted to 
3373	analysing the different systems of the body and applying this information to physical training and competition.

3383	The kinaesthetic sense depends on information coming from the touch receptors in the skin, from the balance and 
3384	gyroscopic centres of the inner ear and from the proprioceptors in the joints, muscles and tendons. This sense 
3385	provides essential information to the brain to enable movements to be performed by the relevant muscles and 
3386	limbs in specific patterns at a certain velocity and intensity. The importance of the proprioceptors may be 
3387	appreciated when one realises that proprioception is second only to pain in causing the most intense and 
3388	widespread electrical activity in the brain.
3389	The eyes are undoubtedly extremely important in guiding the athlete in execution of the correct movements, 
3390	while the ears may assist him in timing phases of the manoeuvre via feedback of any sound produced by the body 
3391	or apparatus. However, without the kinaesthetic sense, skilled physical activity would be impossible. The 
3392	following is a summary of the main subsystems which contribute essential data to the kinaesthetic sense:
3393	Joint receptors This network of nerves in the ligament capsule surrounding movable joints gives information 
3394	about the angle between the bones of the joints and the rate at which this angle is changing.
3395	Muscle spindles These coiled nerves stretch as the muscles stretch, relaying information back to the central 
3396	nervous system about the relative lengths of and degree of tension in the muscle.
3397	Golgi tendon apparatus  This nerve network, situated in the tendons of the muscles, continuously monitors 
3398	tension and contributes to coordination of the actions of many cooperating muscles. This system is important for 
3399	protecting muscle fibres from excessive loading by decreasing muscle tension after it reaches a critical value.
3400	Vestibular apparatus This system, located close to the inner ear, constitutes an inertial guidance or gyroscopic 
3401	balance mechanism which is sensitive to any changes in position, velocity and acceleration of the head, and 
3402	consequently, of the entire body. The three semicircular canals monitor position and angular velocity, since they 
3403	are too slow to respond to angular acceleration, whereas the hair-and-jelly-like structure of the utricle measures 
3404	acceleration.
3405	The following two types of receptor arc not traditionally kinaesthetic senses, but are also very important in the 
3406	control of skilled movement:
3407	Touch receptors These pressure receptors, which work closely in cooperation with the proprioceptive system, 
3408	cover the surface of the entire body and supply information to the brain of the contact of any part of the body 
3409	with an outside object.
3410	Pain receptors Specific or non-specific pain receptors throughout the body inform the brain about the dangers of 
3411	overstressing or damaging any part of the body. Moreover, certain foci in parts of the brain such as the limbic 
3412	system (also involved with emotion and motivation) receiving stimulation from all the other senses play ac 
3413	important role in the perception of pain.

3434	Scientific understanding of the brain has made massive strides recently and the simple view offered here is not 
3435	intended to provide a thorough physiological treatise. Instead, the more important theories and findings are given 
3436	to enable the reader to base his training methods on a more solid scientific foundation.
3437	At the outset it should be noted that in certain emergency situations the muscles have to react very rapidly 
3438	and. therefore, time cannot be spent in having the input signals pass through the entire computing facility of the 
3439	central nervous system. The body provides for this with its system of reflex loops. For example, if one’s hand 
3440	accidentally touches a hot object, reflex action managed solely at the level of the spinal cord compels one to 
3441	withdraw the hand almost immediately and prevent further injury. During voluntary movements reflex action also 
3442	occurs at the level of the motor cortex and not merely at the level of the spinal cord (Evarts, 1979).
3443	The Russian psychologist Pavlov was the first researcher to recognise that conditioned reflexes could be 
3444	learned by proper methods of reinforcement. In other words, programmes of correctly repeated movements can 
3445	eventually enable these movements to become automatic. This is particularly important in the case of all 
3446	manoeuvres which have to be executed rapidly and cannot accommodate delays caused by active thinking about 
3447	the process.
3448	Repetition of incorrect movements will eventually result in their becoming built-in reflexes which are difficult 
3449	to erase. Any attempt to change faulty technique usually results in a feeling of awkwardness and an inability to 
3450	perform as comfortably as before. This is because the body has adapted to its inefficient movement patterns, and 
3451	the emotional distress caused by apparently useless new techniques can prevent the athlete from implementing 
3452	any changes. Often one will hear a coach or colleague shouting instructions to a competitor to correct faulty 
3453	technique during rapid movements. This is little more than useless because it is not possible consciously to change 
3454	the course of any movement which lasts less than 0.4 second (Thomas, 1970). Moreover, the well-known 
3455	phenomenon of paralysis by analysis  may result if the athlete tries to correct or advise himself immediately before 
3456	or during a skilled manoeuvre.

3461	It is rare for any movement sequence to be controlled entirely by reflex loops; instead, reflexes operate 
3462	together with the entire control system depicted in Fig 1.33. The traditional view was that the motor cortex, 
3463	guided by the cerebellum as a mere servo-control device, is the highest centre for motor integration. Moreover, it 
3464	was assumed that control begins together with or just after initiation of any movement (i.e. via feedback).  Instead, 
3465	research has now discovered that the motor cortex is at a lower level of control, more directly connected to spinal- 
3466	cord motor neurons than either the cerebellum or the basal ganglia. It was also found that the cerebellum, the basal 
3467	ganglia and the motor cortex all become active before any movement begins (Evarts, 1973, 1979). Furthermore, a 
3468	specific brain rhythm of about 9 Hz (the mu rhythm) is blocked in advance of any physical movement (Siff, 
3469	1977). There is also an increase in muscle tone and other changes in activity of the ccrebral cortcx (such as the 
3470	'orientation response’ and ’expectancy waves') preceding the commencement of a motor response (Siff, 1977).

3473	muscular efficiency. The cerebellum can even coordinate movement in the absence of all information from the 
3474	periphery of the body (Llinas, 1975).
